summary: The STOP-PASC trial tested a 15-day course of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Paxlovid) against placebo-ritonavir in 155 adults with long COVID symptoms lasting at least 3 months, most of whom were vaccinated and had been ill for an average of 17.5 months. The primary outcome — pooled severity of six core symptoms (fatigue, brain fog, body aches, cardiovascular symptoms, shortness of breath, and gastrointestinal symptoms) at 10 weeks — showed no statistically significant difference between the treatment and placebo groups; the trial was stopped early for futility when conditional power fell below 10%. Both groups improved over time, and adverse event rates were similar, with dysgeusia more common in the nirmatrelvir-ritonavir group (62% vs 8%) but no serious safety signals attributed to the drug.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary pooled symptom severity outcome at 10 weeks showed no statistically significant difference between NMV/r and PBO/r groups; trial stopped early for futility (conditional power <10%). For the most bothersome symptom, NMV/r was associated with worse odds at 10 weeks (OR 1.99, 95% CI 1.06–3.72, p=0.03).

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested lithium aspartate (10–15 mg/day for 3 weeks) against placebo in 52 adults with long COVID fatigue and cognitive dysfunction, recruited at a neurology clinic. The primary outcome—combined Fatigue Severity Scale and Brain Fog Severity Scale scores—showed no significant difference between groups (mean intergroup difference: −3.6 points, 95% CI −16.6 to 9.5, p=0.59), meaning the low-dose treatment had no detectable benefit over placebo. A small, unblinded follow-up dose-finding study in 3 participants suggested that higher doses (40–45 mg/day) achieving serum lithium levels of 0.18–0.49 mEq/L may produce larger symptom reductions, but this finding is exploratory only and requires a new randomized trial to confirm.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a 3-month personalized resistance exercise program against usual care in 233 adults with persistent symptoms after COVID-19 infection in Scotland, including both community patients and those previously hospitalized. The primary outcome was walking distance on the Incremental Shuttle Walk Test: the exercise group improved by 83 meters versus 47 meters in the control group, an adjusted difference of 36.5 meters (95% CI, 6.6–66.3 m; p=0.02). The intervention also produced statistically significant improvements in quality of life, anxiety and depression scores, and grip strength, with no increase in adverse events or post-exertional malaise.

summary: This phase 2 randomized trial (RECOVER-NEURO) tested three remotely delivered cognitive interventions — adaptive computerized training (BrainHQ), a structured cognitive rehabilitation program (PASC-CoRE) combined with BrainHQ, and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) combined with BrainHQ — in 328 adults with cognitive symptoms persisting at least 12 weeks after COVID-19 infection, across 22 US sites. None of the three active interventions improved self-reported cognitive function (modified ECog2 scale) compared to an active comparator of unstructured computer puzzles over 10 weeks: adjusted mean differences were 0.0 (95% CI −0.2 to 0.2) for BrainHQ vs comparator and 0.1 (95% CI −0.1 to 0.3) for PASC-CoRE+BrainHQ vs comparator. All five arms, including the control, showed roughly equivalent improvement of approximately half a rating point on the 5-point ECog2 scale, and no treatment differences emerged on neuropsychological tests or secondary patient-reported outcomes.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome adjusted mean difference: BrainHQ vs active comparator 0.0 (95% CI −0.2 to 0.2); PASC-CoRE+BrainHQ vs active comparator 0.1 (95% CI −0.1 to 0.3); tDCS-active+BrainHQ vs tDCS-sham+BrainHQ 0.0 (95% CI −0.2 to 0.2) — all null results.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a letter-format secondary analysis of a parent RCT (Méndez-Flores et al. 2022, doi:10.1002/ctm2.763). No per-arm means, SDs, or individual numeric outcome values are reported in the text — only p-value thresholds (p<0.01, p<0.05) for between-group differences. All quantitative biomarker data appear only in supplementary figures (Figures S2-S5) and supplementary tables (Tables S2-S4) which are not included in this text. The network correlation values (rho=0.17, rho=0.36) are reported for male vs female PTIC subgroups only, not as between-arm comparisons. No primary outcome is explicitly designated; all outcomes are biomarker-based (cytokines, chemokines, blood count ratios, physiological network properties). No patient-reported outcomes, clinical outcomes, or adverse events are reported. The analysis focuses on 37 completers (20 PTIC, 17 placebo) from the original 89 randomized, representing very high attrition (~58%). This paper is very poorly suited for quantitative meta-analysis due to absence of extractable numeric effect sizes.

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested polymerised type I collagen (PTIC), an immunomodulatory drug given intramuscularly for 7 days, in 89 unvaccinated adult outpatients with PCR-confirmed COVID-19, with follow-up to 12 weeks to assess post-acute sequelae. The primary analysis focused on physiological network dynamics and inflammatory biomarkers; PTIC-treated patients showed faster reduction in inflammatory markers including IP-10, IL-8, CRP, and eosinophil counts compared to placebo, with sex-dependent effects: women on PTIC showed a larger disruption from baseline network state (network correlation rho=0.17 vs 0.36 in men), indicating stronger early immune remodelling. The analysis was limited to 37 completers (20 PTIC, 17 placebo) out of 89 enrolled, and the primary endpoint was a novel physiological network metric rather than a validated clinical outcome, substantially limiting interpretability.

trial_rating.result_basis: Significant between-group differences in inflammatory markers including IP-10, IL-8, CRP (p<0.01) and IL-1Ra, eosinophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (p<0.05) on day 1 post-treatment; network correlation rho=0.17 (female PTIC) vs 0.36 (male PTIC) at first post-treatment day, but no validated clinical primary endpoint was reported.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested bosentan (62.5 mg twice daily for 30 days), an endothelin receptor blocker, in 313 high-risk COVID-19 outpatients in Iran to determine whether early treatment could prevent post-COVID sarcopenia (muscle wasting). The primary outcome was disease progression (death or hospitalization within 15 days), but this report focuses on the secondary outcome of sarcopenia incidence over 12 months: at 6 months, sarcopenia occurred in 3.2% of bosentan patients versus 14% of placebo patients, an absolute risk reduction of 10.81 percentage points (p<0.001), with significant reductions maintained at all follow-up time points through 12 months. Bosentan was well tolerated with no severe adverse events, though the sample size was calculated for the primary outcome rather than sarcopenia, and sarcopenia was assessed using age-related criteria not specifically validated for post-COVID contexts.

trial_rating.result_basis: Sarcopenia incidence at 6 months: 3.2% bosentan vs 14% placebo; risk difference -10.81% (95% CI -16.9 to -4.71), p<0.001; relative risk 0.23 (95% CI 0.09 to 0.60).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested low-level tragus stimulation (LL-TS) — a non-invasive electrical stimulation of the outer ear that activates the vagus nerve — in 57 adults (mean age 32, 61% female) with POTS following COVID-19 infection. Compared to sham stimulation, one month of twice-daily LL-TS (1 hour per session) significantly reduced the heart rate rise on standing, lowered average and maximum 24-hour heart rates, improved autonomic balance (increased parasympathetic HF power, decreased sympathetic LF power and LF/HF ratio), and reduced plasma neuropeptide Y levels, with effects persisting at one-year follow-up. No device-related side effects were observed, though the study was small (n=31 active, n=26 sham), did not assess broader POTS symptoms such as fatigue or cognition, and lacked a non-POTS control group.

trial_rating.result_basis: Heart rate increase on standing significantly attenuated in LL-TS vs sham at 1 month and 1 year (all p<0.05); HRV parameters (LF, HF, LF/HF ratio) significantly improved during postural test (all p<0.001); NPY levels significantly reduced (p<0.05).

summary: A 12-week home-based telerehabilitation programme (aerobic and strength circuit training, 3 sessions/week via Zoom) was tested against usual daily activities in 120 older adults (age ~65) with post-COVID-19 syndrome in a randomised controlled trial. The primary outcome, peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak), increased in both the telerehabilitation and control groups with no significant difference between them; however, the telerehabilitation group showed significantly greater improvements in exercise test duration (+88.9 seconds), cycle ergometer power output (+25.9 watts), and lean/skeletal muscle mass (+1.4 kg skeletal muscle mass) compared to controls. A notable caveat is that the telerehabilitation group had more severe baseline disease (longer hospitalisation, more ICU admissions, more mechanical ventilation), which may limit direct group comparisons despite the positive physical outcomes observed.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome VO2peak showed a significant interaction effect (p=0.05) but no significant between-group difference (p>0.05); both groups improved (~3.0 vs ~1.9 mL/kg/min). summary: This controlled pilot trial tested intermittent hypoxic-hyperoxic training (IHHT) — alternating cycles of low-oxygen (10-12% O2) and high-oxygen (30-35% O2) breathing — added to standard inpatient rehabilitation in 145 long COVID patients (74% female, mean age 53) at a German rehabilitation centre. The study was non-randomised and open-label, with the IHHT group being on average 5 years younger and having fewer comorbidities (less coronary artery disease and COPD), which limits causal conclusions despite baseline-adjusted analysis; no adverse events were recorded.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT improved 91.7 ± 50.1 m (IHHT) vs 32.6 ± 54.2 m (control), ANCOVA p<0.001, exceeding the 35 m minimum clinically important difference threshold.

summary: This non-randomized feasibility trial tested an 8-week weekly group intervention combining computer-based cognitive training (Fresh Minder 2 software) and CBT-based group psychotherapy in 15 long COVID patients with cognitive complaints at LMU Munich. The intervention group showed significant pre-post improvements across most cognitive domains (attention, memory, executive function) with medium-to-large effect sizes, but when compared against a 15-patient control group who received no intervention, only 3 of 19 cognitive variables showed a statistically significant group-by-time interaction: story memory (p=0.046, r=0.37), story recall (p=0.030, r=0.40), and visuospatial construction (p=0.003, r=0.52). The dominant finding was that both groups improved over approximately 4 months, strongly suggesting spontaneous recovery over time accounts for most cognitive gains; the intervention showed no harmful effects and was rated as helpful by 96% of participants.

trial_rating.result_basis: Only 3 of 19 primary cognitive outcomes showed significant group-by-time interactions: story memory p=0.046 r=0.37, story recall p=0.030 r=0.40, figure copy p=0.003 r=0.52; the remaining 16 variables showed significant time effects in both groups, indicating spontaneous recovery rather than intervention effect.

The primary outcome was physical performance: in the 12-week group, walking distance on the 6-minute walk test increased by 220 meters (from 396 m to 616 m), handgrip strength rose by 10.5 kg, and sit-to-stand repetitions increased by 7.2; the 6-week group showed comparable gains. The 6MWT column header says 's' (seconds) but likely represents meters based on the values reported (520-671 range). Treatment duration of 20 sessions at 2x/week = approximately 10 weeks. SICI and ICF TMS sub-outcomes reported only as medians in Table 3 and are included in the RMT outcome note but not extracted as separate outcomes to manage output size. No primary outcome was explicitly designated; no adverse events were reported. The paper describes the protocol as 'safe' in the conclusions but provides no specific AE data.

summary: This pilot study tested a dual-task augmented reality rehabilitation protocol — combining active physical exercises with concurrent cognitive tasks over 20 one-hour sessions — in 10 non-hospitalized adults with long COVID brain fog and fatigue, compared to 10 similar patients who received no rehabilitation. The primary cognitive outcomes showed significant improvement only in the treatment group: Trail Making Test-B execution time decreased by 15.9 seconds (95% CI 7.6–24.1, p=0.001) and Frontal Assessment Battery score improved by 1.9 points (95% CI 0.8–2.9, p=0.002), indicating better executive function. Fatigue and physical performance measures (six-minute walk test, handgrip strength, fatigue severity scale) improved similarly in both groups with no treatment-specific benefit, and the study was unrandomized with only 10 participants per group, limiting generalisability.

trial_rating.result_basis: TMT-B execution time decreased by 15.9 s (95% CI 7.6–24.1, p=0.001) and FAB score improved by 1.9 points (95% CI 0.8–2.9, p=0.002) in the dual-task group only, with effect sizes pη²=0.275 and pη²=0.306 respectively.

summary: This pilot RCT tested transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) delivered via a home TENS device at three frequencies (10Hz, 25Hz, and 2Hz as a low-dose control) in 35 women with long COVID over 12 weeks. Across all groups, fatigue scores (Brief Fatigue Inventory) fell from a mean of 5.5 to 4.5 points, dyspnea (Borg scale) dropped from a median of 3 to 2 points, and health-related quality of life (SF-36 physical component) improved from 32 to 36 points — but the study used only descriptive statistics with no formal significance testing or placebo comparison. The intervention was generally safe with no serious adverse events, though mild side effects such as ear pain, insomnia, and headaches were reported in roughly one-third of participants; a key caveat is that spontaneous symptom improvement over time cannot be ruled out as the 2Hz 'control' group showed similar gains to the active groups.

trial_rating.result_basis: BFI mean decreased from 5.5 to 4.5 across all groups; no inferential statistics or p-values reported, and no significant between-group differences detected; the 2Hz control group showed comparable improvement, preventing attribution of effects to active stimulation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a post-hoc analysis of a primary RCT (NCT05047952) that focused on cognitive deficits. Depressive symptoms (QIDS-SR-16) were a secondary outcome in the parent trial. The between-group mean difference of -5.41 and within-group changes are from the adjusted GEE model (adjusted for age, sex, education, CRP, TG-HDL, BMI, confirmed COVID diagnosis, IPAQ, nicotine use). In the unadjusted model, time (p=0.776) and treatment (p=0.079) effects were NOT significant, raising concerns about robustness. summary: This 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested vortioxetine (5–20 mg/day) against placebo in 147 Canadian adults with WHO-defined post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) who had depressive symptoms. The primary outcome was change in self-reported depression score (QIDS-SR-16) from baseline to 8 weeks; vortioxetine produced a mean reduction of 4.93 points versus 0.41 points for placebo, a between-group difference of 5.41 points (p<0.001). Participants with higher baseline inflammation (CRP), metabolic disruption (TG-HDL ratio), and elevated BMI showed a more pronounced response to vortioxetine. A key caveat is that this is a post-hoc secondary analysis of a trial primarily designed to assess cognitive outcomes, meaning the depressive symptom analysis was not pre-specified as a primary endpoint.

trial_rating.result_basis: Between-group mean difference in QIDS-SR-16 at 8 weeks: -5.41 points (SEM=1.335, p<0.001); vortioxetine within-group change -4.93 vs placebo -0.41 points.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a feasibility study not powered for efficacy. The CFQ-11 was scored using Likert (0,1,2,3) for change analysis but dichotomous (0,0,1,1) for eligibility screening. The change score of -4.6 and -2.9 are reported in the abstract and Table 3 but the SD of the change scores is not reported, only endpoint SDs. The p=0.01 is from a paired t-test comparing change scores. Table 3 reports multiple conditional analyses (e.g., baseline values for 3-month completers, baseline values for 6-month completers, and 3-month values for those completing both 3- and 6-month follow-ups with N=27). The between-group mean difference of -1.7 was calculated from the change scores (-4.6 minus -2.9). The 6-month comparison is not a controlled comparison as the wait-list group received the intervention after 3 months. SF-12 and EQ-5D-5L were collected but no quantitative results are reported for these outcomes. The paper states no SAR/Es were reported during the 12-week intervention use, reported as a combined statement not per-arm.

summary: This feasibility randomized controlled trial tested a self-administered version of the Perrin Technique — a daily routine of lymphatic drainage massage, spinal mobility and breathing exercises, and alternating hot/cold packs to the upper spine — in 100 adults with long COVID-related fatigue recruited via UK general practice and an NHS research volunteer database. The primary aim was feasibility (recruitment and retention), not efficacy; however, Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire (CFQ-11) scores at 3 months improved by 4.6 points in the intervention group versus 2.9 points in the wait-list control group (p=0.01). The study was not powered for efficacy, the wait-list design inflates apparent effect sizes, and dropout was higher in the intervention arm (30.6%) than in controls (11.8%), limiting conclusions about real-world effectiveness.

trial_rating.result_basis: CFQ-11 change from baseline to 3 months: intervention -4.6 points vs wait-list control -2.9 points, p=0.01; study was not powered for efficacy and used a wait-list design known to inflate effect estimates.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a 6-week supervised telerehabilitation (TR) exercise program — delivered via video call twice weekly — against an unsupervised home exercise brochure in 60 adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome and moderate dyspnea. The primary outcome, dyspnea severity (mMRC scale), improved significantly more in the TR group: a mean reduction of 1.16 points versus 0.36 in controls (between-group difference 0.8, 95% CI 0.5–1.1, p=0.001), exceeding the minimal clinically important difference. TR also produced larger improvements in pain intensity (NPRS reduction 1.44 vs 0.60) and physical function (5-times sit-to-stand improvement 3.8 s vs 1.5 s), with large effect sizes; no serious adverse events were reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: mMRC dyspnea score decreased by 1.16 points in TR group vs 0.36 in controls; between-group difference 0.8 (95% CI 0.5–1.1), p=0.001, exceeding the 0.5-point MCID threshold.

The abstract reports age as mean±SD (45±9 and 39±23) but Table 1 reports median(IQR); these are likely medians with IQR despite abstract notation. The 6MWT control group T1 value of 199.1m appears anomalously low (down from 448.8m at baseline), likely reflecting imputation of very poor values for the 3 dropouts who worsened. summary: This randomized, single-blinded, placebo-controlled pilot study tested pulsed electromagnetic field therapy (PEMF) — 10 sessions of 30 minutes each over 5 weeks using a Papimi Delta device — in 20 adults with post-COVID fatigue syndrome. The intervention group showed clinically meaningful improvements in walking distance on the 6-minute walk test (increase of 55m at end of treatment, 79m at 5-week follow-up, both exceeding the 35m minimal clinically important difference), and in total fatigue scores on the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (improvement of 20.5 units vs a 14.3-unit threshold for clinical relevance), alongside gains in sleep quality, work ability, and quality of life. The study is a small pilot with only 10 participants per arm and no inferential statistics were reported, making it insufficient to draw conclusions about efficacy; three placebo patients dropped out due to worsening fatigue while none in the PEMF group did, which may reflect natural disease progression or a sham-arm bias.

trial_rating.result_basis: No inferential statistics (p-values or confidence intervals) were reported due to small sample size; 6MWT improved by 55m (T1) and 79m (T2) in the intervention group vs a decline of 246m (T1) and recovery of 40m (T2) in controls, but these are descriptive figures only with no significance testing.

summary: A 2-week supervised outpatient cardiopulmonary rehabilitation program was tested in 100 adults with long COVID syndrome (mean age 56.7 years) at Semmelweis University, compared against 100 age-matched controls who received a single check-up. The primary finding was that maximal oxygen consumption (VO2max) continued to improve significantly between 2-month and 3-month follow-up in the rehabilitation group, rising from a median of 1,276 to 1,429.5 ml/min (p=0.033), with weight-adjusted VO2 also improving from 14.6 to 16.0 ml/min/kg (p=0.021). Key caveats include the absence of a control-arm CPET, no baseline CPET measurement, and substantial follow-up dropout: only 73 of 100 participants returned at 2 months and 38 at 3 months, limiting confidence in the long-term estimates.

trial_rating.result_basis: VO2max increased from median 1,276 to 1,429.5 ml/min between 2- and 3-month follow-up (p=0.033); VO2/kg improved from 14.6 to 16.0 ml/min/kg (p=0.021), but these are within-group comparisons only, with 62% dropout by 3 months and no CPET control arm.

The primary outcome was quality of life measured by the WHOQOL-BREF scale; active tDCS produced a statistically significant improvement in the psychological domain compared to sham at end of treatment (p=0.04), but this advantage did not persist at 6 or 12 months. Both groups improved on quality of life immediately and at 6 months (p<0.001 each), suggesting cognitive training alone drives much of the benefit, with the tDCS advantage fading without maintenance protocols.

trial_rating.result_basis: Active tDCS group showed significantly greater improvement in the WHOQOL-BREF psychological domain at end of treatment vs sham (p=0.04), but no significant between-group difference at 6 months or 12 months (p=0.21 at 12 months).

summary: A randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week Pain Informed Movement (PIM) program — combining group pain neuroscience education, individual functional exercise, and relaxation techniques — against usual care plus an educational booklet in 57 adults with long COVID who had developed new-onset persistent pain. The primary outcome, pain intensity (Brief Pain Inventory), was significantly reduced in the PIM group compared to controls, with a mean between-group difference of 2.84 points (p<0.001), exceeding the minimum clinically important difference of 2.0 points; pain interference, catastrophizing, fear of movement, and overall function also improved significantly. The trial was single-blind with a small sample, and a per-protocol rather than intention-to-treat analysis was used, which may overestimate treatment effects.

trial_rating.result_basis: Pain intensity mean between-group difference 2.84 ± 0.62 points (p<0.001, Cohen's d=1.21), exceeding the pre-specified MCID of 2.0 on the Brief Pain Inventory.

The MFIS subscale descriptions in the paper appear inconsistent: the paper states cognitive=9 items, psychosocial=10 items, physical=2 items, but standard MFIS has cognitive=10, physical=9, psychosocial=2 items. summary: This randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial tested 10 sessions of High-Definition transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (HD-tDCS) at 3 mA targeting the left motor cortex, combined with a tailored rehabilitation program, in 70 adults with long COVID-related fatigue (3–12 months post-infection). Active HD-tDCS produced a significantly greater reduction in total fatigue scores than sham (mean MFIS reduction 22.11 vs 10.34 points; group difference 14.03 points, effect size 1.2, p<0.001), with the largest gains in cognitive and psychosocial fatigue domains; physical fatigue did not differ between groups. Active stimulation also reduced anxiety and improved quality of life versus sham, while pain did not change; the only notable adverse event was more skin redness in the active group (37 vs 13 occurrences), with no serious adverse events.

trial_rating.result_basis: Total MFIS group difference 14.03 points, effect size 1.2, 95% CI 7.78–20.28, p<0.001; clinical response rate 77.14% active vs 45.71% sham, NNT=3.

summary: This 12-week randomized controlled trial compared aerobic exercise (AE), resistance exercise (RE), and combined AE/RE (each added to diaphragmatic breathing) against diaphragmatic breathing alone in 80 men aged 40–60 with chronic post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis. The primary outcomes were forced vital capacity (FVC) and diffusing capacity (DLCO): AE improved FVC by 5.1 percentage points more than the control group (p=0.001, Cohen's d=1.1) and DLCO by 4.6 percentage points more (p=0.001, d=0.8), with AE/RE producing similar gains; resistance exercise alone did not significantly improve FVC or DLCO compared to control. The trial was restricted to men at a single Egyptian centre, and some assessors were unblinded, limiting generalisability.

trial_rating.result_basis: AE vs control: FVC MD=5.1% (95% CI 1.1–9.1, p=0.001, d=1.1); DLCO MD=4.6% (95% CI 0.4–9.7, p=0.001, d=0.8); FVC improvement exceeds the 3% MCID but DLCO improvement does not exceed its 11% MCID.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested high-dose oral vitamin D3 supplementation (9,600 IU/day for 2 days, then 3,200 IU/day for 4 weeks) versus placebo in 1,747 adults recently diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2 infection, recruited from the United States and Mongolia. The primary outcome — rate of healthcare utilization or death within 4 weeks — was not significantly different between groups (incidence 0.28 vitamin D vs. 0.29 placebo). For long COVID at 8 weeks, 21% of the vitamin D group reported ongoing symptoms versus 25% in the placebo group, a non-significant difference (p=0.24); a subgroup analysis of pill-compliant participants showed a 22% lower odds of long COVID symptoms (p=0.07), which did not reach statistical significance. No safety concerns were identified.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (healthcare utilization) incidence 0.28 vs. 0.29, not reported as significant; long COVID secondary outcome 21% vs. 25%, p=0.24; complier subgroup 22% lower odds, p=0.07.

summary: This feasibility trial tested FLEX, an online Cognitive Bias Modification for Interpretations (CBM-I) intervention, in 131 adults with long-term conditions including post-COVID condition, chronic fatigue syndrome, multiple sclerosis, and cancer, all experiencing high levels of fatigue. The primary feasibility outcomes were met: 84% recruitment rate, 70% retention at four months, and 77% full adherence to training sessions. On the key mechanistic outcome—fatigue-related interpretation bias—FLEX produced a large effect versus control at post-intervention (Hedges' g = 0.834, 95% CI [0.472, 1.196]), with small effects on self-reported fatigue and depression but negligible effects on anxiety. This was a feasibility study not powered for significance testing, so symptom effect sizes are exploratory only.

trial_rating.result_basis: Self-reported fatigue (Chalder Fatigue Scale) showed a small, non-significant effect at the primary post-intervention timepoint: adjusted mean difference 1.481 (SE 1.05), Hedges' g = 0.234 (95% CI -0.160 to 0.628); the study was not powered for significance testing.

summary: This double-blind, randomized, sham-controlled trial tested 20 sessions of prefrontal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS, 2 mA) paired with an app-based cognitive training program over four weeks in 60 adults with long COVID cognitive complaints. Compared to sham stimulation plus cognitive training, active tDCS plus cognitive training produced statistically significant but small improvements in inhibitory control (partial η²=0.07, p=0.046), processing speed (partial η²=0.08, p=0.034), and divided attention (partial η²=0.08, p=0.039), while no significant differences were found for verbal memory, working memory, cognitive flexibility, sustained attention, or language. Depression and anxiety symptoms improved similarly in both groups, and blinding was successfully maintained throughout the trial.

trial_rating.result_basis: Three of six primary cognitive domains reached significance vs. sham: inhibitory control η²=0.07 (p=0.046), processing speed η²=0.08 (p=0.034), divided attention η²=0.08 (p=0.039); no correction for multiple comparisons was applied in this exploratory pilot.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT tested co-ultramicronized palmitoylethanolamide/luteolin (PEA-LUT, 700mg+70mg twice daily for 8 weeks) versus placebo in 34 adults with persistent fatigue and cognitive difficulties after mild COVID-19 (average symptom duration ~10 months). The primary outcome was cortical GABA-B activity measured by long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI) using transcranial magnetic stimulation: the PEA-LUT group showed a significant increase in inhibition (LICI decreased from 66.6% to 32.4% of test amplitude) while the placebo group showed no change (66.8% to 71.2%), with a significant treatment-by-time interaction (F=4.92, p=0.034). Cognitive screening scores (MoCA, FAB) did not improve significantly in either group, likely due to a ceiling effect in the instruments used, and no adverse effects were reported.

summary: This double-blind randomised pilot trial tested 12 days of sulphur thermal water (STW) inhalations versus sterile distilled water (placebo) in 30 adults with long COVID and pulmonary sequelae. STW recipients walked 15.9% further in the 6-minute walk test at 3-month follow-up (402.8m to 466.9m, p<0.005), reported a 36.4% reduction in total St George Respiratory Questionnaire score, and showed statistically significant reductions in serum IL-6 (44.6%), IL-1β (48.5%), ACE (93.5%), and S100B (59.5%) compared to no meaningful change in the placebo group. The trial was small (n=15 per arm) and conducted at a single spa facility, limiting generalisability, though no adverse events occurred across the full 3-month follow-up including one pregnant participant.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT distance increased 15.9% in STW vs 2.33% in SDW at T2 (p<0.005); SGRQ total score decreased 36.4% in STW vs 7.2% in SDW; IL-6 decreased 44.6% in STW vs 14.5% in SDW (p<0.05 at T1).

summary: AXA1125, an oral amino acid-based metabolic modulator (leucine, isoleucine, valine, arginine, glutamine, and N-acetylcysteine), was tested against placebo in 41 adults with fatigue-predominant long COVID in a double-blind, randomised phase 2a trial at the University of Oxford. The primary endpoint — change in skeletal muscle phosphocreatine recovery time constant (a measure of mitochondrial function) after 4 weeks — did not differ significantly between groups (LS mean difference 18.2 s, 95% CI −12.7 to 49.1, p=0.24). As a secondary outcome, AXA1125-treated patients reported significantly greater reductions in total fatigue on the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire compared to placebo (LS mean difference −4.30 points, 95% CI −7.14 to −1.47, p=0.0039), though this was an exploratory finding in a small single-centre trial funded by the drug's manufacturer.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (τPCr change) was not significant: LS mean difference 18.2 s, 95% CI −12.7 to 49.1, p=0.24.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This paper reports an acute COVID-19 treatment trial with Long COVID as an exploratory endpoint, not a trial enrolling participants with existing Long COVID. Treatment was a single IV infusion on day 0 during acute infection. Most outcome data reported as percentages without absolute event counts for EQ-5D-5L domains. Individual symptom frequency data (27 symptoms) available in figures (Fig 4) and supplementary tables (eTables 3-6) but not fully extractable from main text. SF-36v2 individual domain scores referenced as being in eTable 6 (p≥0.21 for all). Non-return to usual health reported as wRR=0.72 (95% CI 0.52-0.99) without IPW but the composite with death was wRR=0.65 (95% CI 0.48-0.89). AE data reported in prior publication (Evering et al. Ann Intern Med 2023) covering day 0-28 safety, not repeated in this Long COVID-focused analysis.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (ACTIV-2) tested the monoclonal antibody combination amubarvimab/romlusevimab versus placebo in 780 high-risk, non-hospitalized adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 within 10 days of symptom onset, enrolled January–July 2021. The primary composite outcome—long COVID at 36 weeks or hospitalization/death by 36 weeks—favored treatment (17% vs 24%, weighted risk ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.53–0.93), but this difference was driven entirely by fewer hospitalizations and deaths (4% vs 13%), not by any reduction in long COVID. Among participants who completed the symptom diary, long COVID prevalence was nearly identical: 16% in the treatment arm versus 14% in the placebo arm (weighted risk ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.64–1.27, p=0.55), with no differences in symptom counts, severity, or quality of life at 36 weeks.

trial_rating.result_basis: The primary long COVID-specific outcome (death or long COVID composite) showed wRR=0.90, 95% CI 0.64–1.27, p=0.55; long COVID prevalence was 16% (treatment) vs 14% (placebo), a null result.

The SD column in Table 3 is the standard error of the treatment effect estimate, not the SD of the score. summary: A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase IIa trial tested a single intravenous infusion of rovunaptabin (1350 mg), a DNA aptamer that neutralises autoantibodies against G-protein coupled receptors, in 30 long COVID patients who tested positive for these autoantibodies and had fatigue as a major symptom persisting for at least 3 months. The primary outcome was safety, measured by treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) to day 28: 9 TEAEs occurred in the rovunaptabin group versus 5 in the placebo group, a non-significant difference (p=0.1299). Secondary outcomes showed significant improvements in fatigue and quality of life, including on the FACIT Fatigue Scale (mean improvement 2.91 points, p=0.0378), Bell score (7.54 points, p=0.0004), and Fatigue Severity Scale (-0.43 points, p=0.0088), though a separate phase II trial by the drug's manufacturer was reported to have failed its primary endpoint.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary endpoint (TEAE frequency to day 28) was not statistically significant: 9 events in rovunaptabin group vs 5 in placebo, p=0.1299, CI -14.80% to 63.02%.

summary: This 24-week double-blind randomized controlled trial tested nicotinamide riboside (NR) at 2000 mg/day against placebo in 58 adults with long COVID who had persistent cognitive difficulties and at least two ongoing neurological or physical symptoms. NR reliably raised blood NAD+ levels by 2.6- to 3.1-fold within 5 weeks, but did not significantly improve the primary outcomes of cognitive function (ECog, RBANS, TMT-B; p-values 0.47–0.74) or secondary outcomes of fatigue, sleep quality, depression, or anxiety compared to placebo. Exploratory post-hoc within-group analyses combining all participants during their first 10 weeks on NR showed modest improvements in executive functioning, fatigue (FSS −3.77 points), sleep (PSQI −0.74 points), and depression (BDI −1.67 points), but these are hypothesis-generating only given the absence of placebo-controlled significance and the high dropout rate (51% in the NR arm by 20 weeks).

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary cognitive outcomes showed no significant between-group differences: ECog β=0.08 (p=0.49), RBANS β=6.08 (p=0.47), TMT-B β=−1.83 (p=0.74).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested inhaled aromatherapy (a blend of eucalyptus, lemon, lavender, peppermint, and tea tree oils worn in a diffuser necklace during the day, plus a lavender/ylang-ylang aroma stone at night) in 60 Korean adults with post-COVID-19 symptoms within 45 days of infection onset. The primary outcomes were sore throat and nasal symptoms: sore throat scores were significantly lower in the aromatherapy group than controls on days 3 and 4 (day 4: 1.20 vs 2.63 on a 0–10 scale, p=0.017), but nasal symptom scores did not differ significantly between groups at any timepoint. As a secondary finding, fatigue scores were significantly lower in the aromatherapy group from day 2 onward (day 4: 3.23 vs 5.03, p=0.003); blinding was not possible due to the nature of the intervention, and the 4-day study duration limits conclusions about sustained benefit.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a combination of Liu Zi Jue Qigong exercise and acupressure (QARP) added to standard care versus standard care alone in 128 patients hospitalized with severe COVID-19, following them for 28 months after discharge. At 14 months post-discharge, the QARP group showed significantly greater reductions in breathlessness scores compared to controls (mMRC difference: -0.4, 95% CI -0.6 to -0.2, p<0.001; Borg dyspnea difference: -0.6, 95% CI -0.9 to -0.3, p<0.001), and the Borg dyspnea advantage persisted at 28 months (-0.4, 95% CI -0.7 to -0.1, p=0.024). trial_rating.result_basis: Primary Borg dyspnea score (MBS) difference at 14 months: -0.6 (95% CI -0.9 to -0.3, p<0.001); mMRC difference: -0.4 (95% CI -0.6 to -0.2, p<0.001); both exceeding pre-specified minimal clinically important differences of -0.5 and -1.0 respectively.

summary: REGENECYTE, an allogeneic cord blood-derived hematopoietic progenitor cell therapy, was tested in 30 adults (aged 18-65, 70% female) with post-COVID syndrome lasting 6-18 months in a phase IIa randomized placebo-controlled trial. Participants received three intravenous infusions over 6 weeks (20:10 treatment:placebo ratio); the primary endpoint was safety, while the key secondary endpoint was change in fatigue measured by the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire (CFQ-11). REGENECYTE produced a large, sustained reduction in fatigue: CFQ-11 Bimodal scores fell from 6.75 to 1.00 in the treatment group versus 7.70 to 5.20 in placebo by week 26 (p<0.001), with physical fatigue showing the greatest benefit; safety was favorable, with only 2 of 20 treated patients (10%) experiencing mild, treatment-related adverse events and no serious adverse events. The trial is small, single-site, single-blind, and funded entirely by the manufacturer, all of which limit confidence in the findings.

summary: The OVID trial follow-up (Post-OVID) tested whether 14 days of prophylactic enoxaparin (40 mg subcutaneously once daily) given during acute COVID-19 improved 2-year outcomes in 439 ambulatory patients over age 50 in Switzerland and Germany, compared to no anticoagulation. The primary outcome — all-cause hospitalization or death within 24 months — occurred in 8.3% of the enoxaparin group versus 10% of controls (relative risk 0.83; 95% CI 0.5–1.5), a non-significant difference. Long COVID symptoms were reported by 44% of the enoxaparin group and 47% of controls, with no difference in functional status (15% in each group had PCFS grade 1–3; odds ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.6–1.7) or quality of life scores.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome RR 0.83 (95% CI 0.5–1.5), p=0.5; no statistically significant difference between enoxaparin and control groups.

summary: This randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested SIM01 — a synbiotic containing three Bifidobacterium strains plus galacto-oligosaccharides, xylo-oligosaccharides, and resistant dextrin — taken twice daily for 6 months in 463 Hong Kong adults with post-acute COVID-19 syndrome (long COVID). At 6 months, significantly more participants in the SIM01 group had alleviation of fatigue (63% vs 43%, OR 2.27), memory loss (42% vs 27%, OR 1.97), difficulty in concentration (62% vs 39%, OR 2.64), gastrointestinal upset (70% vs 54%, OR 2.00), and general unwellness (77% vs 59%, OR 2.36) compared to placebo, all surpassing the Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold. Adverse event rates were similar between groups (10% SIM01 vs 11% placebo), and the trial was single-centre with an exclusively Chinese ethnic population, which limits generalisability.

summary: This RCT tested ENO Breathe, a 6-week online programme using singing-based breathing retraining developed by the English National Opera, in 150 adults with persistent breathlessness following COVID-19 (mean 320 days since symptom onset), recruited from 51 UK long COVID clinics. The primary outcome was change in health-related quality of life measured by the SF-36 mental health composite (MHC) and physical health composite (PHC) scores; ENO Breathe improved the MHC score by 2.42 points more than usual care (95% CI 0.03–4.80, p=0.047), but did not improve the PHC score (p=0.54). Breathlessness during running improved significantly (between-group difference –10.48 points on a 0–100 scale, p=0.0026), though a post-hoc sensitivity analysis using carried-forward imputation attenuated the MHC result to p=0.095, suggesting the finding is borderline.

trial_rating.result_basis: MHC score improved by 2.42 points vs usual care (95% CI 0.03–4.80, p=0.047); PHC non-significant (p=0.54); sensitivity analysis weakened MHC to p=0.095.

summary: This randomized clinical trial tested AKL-T01 (EndeavorOTC), a smartphone/tablet video game targeting attention and executive control, in 98 adults with cognitive deficits persisting more than 4 weeks after COVID-19 infection. The primary outcome — sustained attention measured by the Digit Symbol Matching Task — did not improve significantly in the intervention group compared to waitlist controls over 6 weeks (p=0.95). Secondary outcomes showed improvements in task-switching and processing speed, and participants in the intervention group reported reduced disability, better quality of life, less cognitive fatigue, and lower anxiety scores compared to controls. Funding from Akili Interactive (the developer of AKL-T01) and the lack of an active control group are notable limitations.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (Digit Symbol Matching Task sustained attention) showed no significant difference between intervention and control: F[3,261]=0.12, p=0.95, η²=0.001.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested two home-based respiratory muscle training programs — inspiratory muscle training (IMT) alone or combined inspiratory and expiratory training (RMT) — delivered via telerehabilitation over 8 weeks in 88 adults with long COVID who had persistent fatigue and breathlessness for at least 3 months. summary: This phase II double-blind randomised controlled trial tested therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) — a procedure that filters inflammatory substances, autoantibodies, and other potentially harmful molecules from the blood — against a sham procedure in 50 adults with moderate-to-severe long COVID (Post-COVID-19 Functional Status scale grade 3–4), with an average of approximately two years since initial SARS-CoV-2 infection. Six sessions of TPE over three weeks produced no improvement over placebo on any efficacy measure, including functional status, symptom burden, fatigue, quality of life, cognitive performance, or blood biomarkers. Both groups had similarly favourable safety profiles with no serious adverse events, though musculoskeletal adverse events were more frequent in the TPE arm (13.1% vs 6.9% of events).

trial_rating.result_basis: At day 90, functional improvement (PCFS score 1-2) was seen in 24% of TPE participants vs 40% of placebo participants; no statistically significant differences were found between groups on any efficacy parameter.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This paper is primarily a cost-effectiveness analysis alongside the ReDIRECT RCT. Clinical outcomes (fatigue, breathlessness, anxiety/depression symptom scores, weight change) are referenced but reported in a separate primary outcome paper (Combet et al., Nat Med, 2025). Per-arm SDs for utility at 3 and 6 months are not reported (only means from AUC table). Adjusted values from Table 2 and Table 3 are used where available. The treatment effect for hours of work missed (1.91, 95% CI -1.01 to 4.83) represents the adjusted difference favouring greater reduction in the intervention arm. Healthcare resource use at 6 months showed a non-significant mean difference of -£47.03 (95% CI -£236.83 to £142.77). Cost-effectiveness acceptability curve probabilities: 72% at £20k/QALY, 89% at £30k/QALY (NHS/PSS); 93% at £20k/QALY, 96% at £30k/QALY (societal); 74% cost-saving at £0/QALY (societal).

summary: The ReDIRECT trial tested the Counterweight-Plus remotely delivered weight management programme (dietitian-supported total diet replacement followed by food reintroduction and maintenance) in 234 UK adults with long COVID and overweight or obesity. This paper reports the economic evaluation alongside the trial: from an NHS perspective, the intervention cost £14,754 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained — well below the NICE £30,000/QALY threshold — with an 89% probability of being cost-effective at that threshold. When broader societal costs (lost productivity, food expenditure) were included, the intervention became cost-saving overall, driven largely by reduced work absenteeism in the intervention group.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial tested hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) — 40 sessions of 100% oxygen at 2 atmospheres — against a sham procedure in 60 long COVID patients (average age ~47) with persistent symptoms for at least 3 months after confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (GLS in full cohort) group-by-time interaction p=0.237 (non-significant); significant result only in post-hoc reduced-GLS subgroup (p=0.041, N=29).

summary: This 10-week randomized crossover trial tested two intermittent fasting regimens in 58 adults with long COVID (mean symptom duration 24.6 months, average 20.5 symptoms at baseline): an intense fasting protocol (daily 16:8 time-restricted eating plus one 23–60 hour water-only fast per week, combined with a no-added-sugar diet) versus mild time-restricted eating (daily 10–12 hour eating window with the same no-sugar diet). The intense fasting regimen reduced the composite long COVID symptom severity score by 10.2 points versus 2.8 points for mild TRE (p=0.008), and cut the number of symptoms by 5.0 versus 1.4 (p=0.002); across the full 10 weeks, mean symptom severity fell 51.8% and symptom count fell 40.6%. Ninety percent of participants experienced at least one symptom flare-up, with 58% of flare-ups during the fasting period attributed to the fasting treatment, though no participants withdrew due to adverse events and only one hospitalization was possibly fasting-related.

summary: This randomized trial tested transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) over two brain targets — the primary motor cortex (M1) or the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) — each combined with 15 sessions of adaptive computerized cognitive training, in 63 long COVID patients with confirmed fatigue (average symptom duration 32 months, 81% female). The trial lacked a sham control group, so placebo effects cannot be excluded, and follow-up was limited to one month.

summary: This pilot randomized controlled trial tested high-dose versus low-dose transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) worn daily for 4 weeks in 25 long-COVID patients experiencing chronic widespread pain, fatigue, and gait impairment resembling fibromyalgia. High-dose TENS produced a significantly greater reduction in pain interference scores (BPI-I mean difference = 2.61 points, p = 0.008, Cohen's d = 1.12) compared to low-dose TENS, and improved gait measures including cadence (5.6–9.5% depending on task) and stride time (4–8%) from baseline. Among the subset of 5 participants meeting formal fibromyalgia criteria, high-dose TENS also significantly improved fatigue scores (GFI improvement of 6.08 points, p = 0.005). The trial was small, unblinded at 4 weeks with high subsequent dropout, and the intervention group had lower baseline pain severity than controls, limiting interpretation of the between-group comparison.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome BPI-I between-group mean difference = 2.61 points favouring high-dose TENS, p = 0.008, Cohen's d = 1.12.

summary: This RCT tested a brief 'awe intervention' — four weekly one-hour online sessions teaching long COVID patients to deliberately notice and cultivate moments of awe in daily life — against a waitlist control group in 68 US adults meeting CDC long COVID criteria. The primary outcomes were stress, anxiety, depression, and well-being; the awe group showed significant reductions in depression symptoms (17% decrease vs. 2% increase in controls, d=0.96), stress (12% decrease vs. 2% increase, d=0.78), and a 16% increase in well-being, all with medium-to-large effect sizes. Anxiety did not improve significantly. The trial is small (N=30 intervention, N=38 control), used a waitlist rather than active control, and was conducted at a single time point in April 2023, limiting generalisability and ruling out placebo effects.

trial_rating.result_basis: Depression symptoms decreased by 17% in the awe group vs. +2% in controls (t(62.73)=-3.15, p=0.002, d=0.96); well-being increased 16% vs. -8% (t(61.91)=3.88, p<0.001, d=0.96); stress decreased 12% vs. +2% (t(65.82)=-3.34, p=0.001, d=0.78).

summary: This 10-week randomized controlled trial tested a symptom-titrated, individualized concurrent resistance and aerobic exercise program in 118 adults with post-COVID condition who had persistent fatigue (at least 12 weeks) and were largely inactive. Training load was adjusted before each session based on daily fatigue scores, with exercise contraindicated on days of maximum fatigue. Fatigue severity (the primary outcome, measured by the Fatigue Severity Scale) improved significantly more in the exercise group than the control group: from 5.67 to 4.51 vs. 5.49 to 5.29, a between-group difference of 0.93 points (p<0.001). summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial tested heat-treated Lacticaseibacillus paracasei PS23 (HT-PS23, 20 billion cells/day for 6 weeks) in 31 adults (mean age 23) with long COVID symptoms persisting at least 2 months after confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. The intervention was well-tolerated with no adverse events reported, but the small sample (14 vs 17 completers), young homogeneous population, lack of a single primary outcome, and multiple comparisons substantially limit the conclusions that can be drawn.

summary: This small exploratory randomised controlled trial tested leronlimab, a monoclonal antibody that blocks the CCR5 immune receptor, versus saline placebo in 55 adults with long COVID, administered weekly by subcutaneous injection for 8 weeks. The primary outcome — composite symptom score change from baseline — did not reach statistical significance: leronlimab reduced scores by -16.0 points versus -12.0 for placebo, with an adjusted mean difference of -1.0 (not significant). An exploratory finding showed that leronlimab-treated participants had significantly increased cell surface CCR5 expression by week 8 (p<0.0001), particularly among symptom responders, suggesting a possible immune downmodulation mechanism in some long COVID patients. The study was funded entirely by CytoDyn, the drug's manufacturer, and most authors report financial conflicts of interest, which substantially limits confidence in the interpretation of exploratory findings.

summary: This double-blind, sham-controlled pilot trial tested transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) applied to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex — 2 mA for 20 minutes per day over 8 sessions — in 47 long COVID patients with chronic fatigue (average symptom duration ~21 months). The primary outcome, total fatigue score on the Modified Fatigue Impact Scale, did not show a statistically significant difference between active and sham stimulation groups; however, the physical fatigue subscale did improve significantly in the active group compared to sham, with a large effect size (Cohen's d = 1.032 at end of treatment). Adverse events were mild, transient, and equally distributed between groups, but the null result on the primary endpoint and the small pilot sample size mean these findings should be treated as preliminary.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome MFIS-total time-by-group interaction was not significant (F(2,82)=1.730, p=0.184); only the secondary physical fatigue subscale showed a significant interaction (p=0.034).

summary: This pilot randomized controlled trial tested a 12-week home-based asynchronous telerehabilitation program (delivered via smartphone app with exercise videos and therapeutic education) versus a booklet-based rehabilitation program in 35 adults recently discharged from hospital after COVID-19, average age 58, with significant fatigue and psychological distress. The primary outcomes were depression, anxiety, and stress measured by the DASS-21 scale; the telerehabilitation group showed significantly better depression and stress outcomes immediately post-intervention (p=0.048 and p=0.033 by symptom-level analysis), with the advantage in depression persisting at 3 and 6 months (p=0.010 and p=0.036), and a large effect size at the 3-month follow-up (Cohen's d=0.90). The main caveat is the small sample size (17–18 per arm), which limits statistical power and generalizability, and the single-blind design; no safety concerns were reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Depression score at 3-month follow-up: ATG mean 1.44 vs BRG mean 5.11, p=0.031, Cohen's d=0.90; immediate post-intervention level-based depression p=0.048 and stress p=0.033, but continuous scale total scores did not differ significantly post-intervention (depression p=0.458, anxiety p=0.987, stress p=0.967).

summary: This small crossover trial tested a CBD-rich, full-spectrum hemp oil (Formula C, containing 40.7 mg/mL CBD plus terpenes) against a placebo in 31 adults with post-acute COVID-19 syndrome (long COVID), with 24 completing the study. The active treatment group showed statistically significant improvements in dyspnea (p=0.013), anxiety (p=0.006), and sleep disturbance (p=0.041) after 28 days; however, the placebo group also improved across most outcomes because the placebo (hempseed oil) was found to contain unexpected therapeutic concentrations of terpenes, eliminating the validity of the control arm. The trial is effectively uninterpretable as a placebo-controlled study, and its conclusions are further limited by small sample size, single-blind design, and the fact that it was funded by and included equity holders from the product manufacturer.

trial_rating.result_basis: Active group reached significance for anxiety (p=0.006), dyspnea (p=0.013), and sleep disturbance (p=0.041) at day 28, but the placebo arm showed similar improvements and was confirmed to contain therapeutic terpene levels, invalidating the control comparison; between-group differences were not statistically significant.

summary: This Belgian randomized controlled trial tested two brief psychoeducational interventions — one targeting cognitive strategies (metacognition, compensatory techniques) and one targeting affective symptoms (stress management, behavioural activation, CBT techniques) — in 122 long COVID patients with documented cognitive complaints and objective cognitive deficits. Both interventions consisted of four 90-minute in-person sessions; the primary outcome was subjective cognitive complaints at 2 months post-intervention. Both groups showed statistically significant reductions in executive/attention complaints (BRIEF-A) and memory complaints (MMQ) over time, but the cognitive intervention was not superior to the affective intervention — there was no group-by-time interaction for either primary outcome. Improvements were modest (small-to-moderate effect sizes), and despite gains, the majority of patients remained above clinical thresholds for fatigue (85%), sleep difficulties (79%), and psychological distress (56%) at follow-up, indicating limited clinical meaningfulness from a brief 6-hour intervention.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome group-by-time interaction for BRIEF-A: F=0.2, p=0.68; for MMQ composite: F=0.03, p=0.85 — no significant difference between cognitive and affective intervention arms, the pre-specified comparison.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested intermittent hypoxic-hyperoxic training (IHHT) — alternating low-oxygen and high-oxygen breathing sessions — added to standard inpatient rehabilitation in 145 post-COVID patients at a single German rehabilitation clinic. The primary outcome, six-minute walk distance, improved by 91.7 metres in the IHHT group versus 32.5 metres in controls (p<0.001), a difference of approximately 59 metres that exceeds the accepted minimal clinically important difference for the 6MWT. Secondary outcomes all favoured IHHT, including quality of life (EQ5D change +31.3 vs +2.9), fatigue (FAS change -8.9 vs +3.6), and stair climbing time (-1.9 vs -0.5 seconds), with no safety concerns reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT improved 91.7m in IHHT group vs 32.5m in controls (difference ~59m, p<0.001), exceeding the ~25-54m minimal clinically important difference threshold.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a 17-week cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) program called 'Fit after COVID' against care as usual (CAU) in 114 adults with severe fatigue 3-12 months after confirmed COVID-19, the majority of whom had not been hospitalized. CBT significantly reduced fatigue severity compared to CAU, with an overall mean difference of -8.8 points on the CIS-fatigue scale (95% CI: -11.9 to -5.8, p<0.001), representing a medium effect size (Cohen's d=0.69), and this benefit was sustained at 6-month follow-up. At post-treatment, 59% of CBT patients were no longer severely fatigued versus 26% in CAU; CBT also improved physical functioning, social functioning, somatic symptoms, and concentration. The sample was predominantly self-referred, which may limit generalizability to broader clinical populations.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome CIS-fatigue mean difference CBT vs CAU: -8.8 points (95% CI -11.9 to -5.8, p<0.001), Cohen's d=0.69 (medium effect size), sustained at both T1 (-9.3 points) and T2 (-8.4 points).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week supervised cardiopulmonary rehabilitation programme — combining aerobic exercise, resistance training, and respiratory exercises three times per week — in 40 adults (mean age 53) with long COVID who had persistent breathlessness or fatigue. The primary cognitive outcome showed no significant difference between the rehabilitation and control groups on any neuropsychological measure, including executive function, memory, and processing speed. However, the rehabilitation group showed significant reductions in perceived stress (PSS adjusted mean change: −2.46 vs. +3.26 in controls, p=0.002) and depression symptoms (GDS adjusted mean change: −2.39 vs. +2.68 in controls, p=0.015). The trial was underpowered for cognitive outcomes as sample size was calculated for a cardiorespiratory primary outcome, and the study was conducted at a single centre with only 32 participants completing the protocol.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary cognitive outcomes showed no significant group differences on any neuropsychological composite score (all ANCOVA p-values ranged from p=0.17 to p=0.65); secondary psychological outcomes were significant but were not the pre-specified primary endpoint.

summary: A 3-month cardiopulmonary rehabilitation program was tested in 30 convalescent COVID-19 patients, compared to 10 who received no rehabilitation, to assess recovery of right ventricular function and right ventricular-pulmonary artery coupling. The control group was very small (n=10) and patients were not randomised, limiting confidence in the findings.

summary: A 3-month cardiopulmonary rehabilitation program was tested in 60 patients one month after recovery from acute COVID-19, randomized equally to rehabilitation or no intervention. Arterial stiffness (carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity) improved significantly in the rehabilitation group (8.2 to 6.6 m/s, p<0.001) but not in controls (8.9 to 8.8 m/s, p=0.74), and left ventricular global longitudinal strain also improved only in the rehabilitation group (-19.6% to -21.3%, p<0.001). Patients with lower baseline inflammation (IL-1β below 8.4 pg/ml) showed greater benefit in ventricular-arterial coupling improvement than those with higher inflammation (0.14 vs 0.09 m/s%, p=0.04).

trial_rating.result_basis: Arterial stiffness (cf-PWV) improved from 8.2 to 6.6 m/s in the rehabilitation group (p<0.001) versus no change in controls (8.9 to 8.8 m/s, p=0.74); ventricular-arterial coupling improved from -0.43 to -0.31 m/s% in the rehabilitation group (p<0.001).

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested a 4-week, twice-weekly pulmonary telerehabilitation (PTR) program delivered via videoconference against usual medical care in 50 adults with persistent respiratory symptoms after COVID-19 (mostly non-hospitalised, average age 54). The primary outcome was the 1-minute sit-to-stand test: the PTR group improved by 2.1 repetitions versus 1.3 in the control group, a between-group difference of only 0.8 repetitions (95% CI -3.0 to 4.6, p=0.563), which was not statistically significant. summary: This Finnish randomized controlled trial (SOLIDARITY Finland) tested remdesivir (5-day course) plus standard of care versus standard of care alone in 208 adults hospitalized for COVID-19, following them for one year to assess long COVID outcomes. summary: This randomised controlled trial tested whether a 3-month course of supervised endurance training rehabilitation (ETR, two one-hour sessions per week) reduced breathlessness in 60 adults who had been mechanically ventilated for COVID-19-related acute respiratory distress syndrome and remained dyspnoeic at least 3 months after ICU discharge, compared to standard physiotherapy (SP). ETR produced a large, statistically significant reduction in the Multidimensional Dyspnea Profile score at 90 days (mean 26.2 vs 44.8 in the SP group; mean difference -18.6 points, 95% CI -27.8 to -9.4, p<0.0001), and also improved the physical component of quality of life. The trial was stopped early due to declining COVID-19 ICU admissions and enrolled only 60 of the planned 200 participants, limiting statistical power for secondary outcomes.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Critical limitation: The ANOVA tables (Tables 1 and 2) report only sum of squares, df, mean squares, F-statistics, and p-values for between-group comparisons. No per-arm means or SDs are provided in the text or tables for any outcome at any timepoint. Outcome data appears only in figures (Figure 2 shows percentage distributions by level, Figure 3 shows VAS and TTO bar charts with SD bars) without numeric values. All per-arm means and SDs are therefore coded as not_reported. The F-statistics reported in Table 1 (basal) appear inconsistent — F-values for Mobility (6.738), VAS (5.632), and TTO (9.746) at baseline are the same as those at final (Table 2), which is suspicious and may reflect a table formatting/labeling error in the preprint. The p-values at baseline are non-significant for all outcomes (as expected), so the F-values in Table 1 may be erroneous placeholders. Additionally, one patient appears to have been recruited (n=47) but not randomized (n=46 analyzed), with no explanation provided. Adverse events not reported. Note: TR (co-author) is co-founder of Erisea S.A. which produced the supplement — conflict of interest noted.

summary: This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial tested EchA Marine® — a dietary supplement derived from sea urchin eggs containing Echinochrome A, an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant compound — in 46 long COVID patients (aged 18–60) from two Buenos Aires hospitals over 90 days. The primary outcome was health-related quality of life measured by the EQ-5D-3L questionnaire; after three months, the treatment group showed statistically significant improvements in mobility (p=0.013) and pain/discomfort (p=0.005) compared to placebo, and also scored better on overall health by both visual analogue scale (p=0.022) and time trade-off (p=0.003). The trial is a preprint with a small sample (24 treated, 22 placebo), and two of the five EQ-5D dimensions — self-care, usual activities, and anxiety/depression — did not reach significance; additionally, one co-author is a co-founder of the company that produced the supplement.

trial_rating.result_basis: Pain/Discomfort dimension F(1,44)=8.863, p=0.005; Mobility F(1,44)=6.738, p=0.013; VAS p=0.022; TTO p=0.003; three of five EQ-5D dimensions (self-care, usual activities, anxiety/depression) were non-significant.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: FEV1 and VCmax significantly improved in moderate patients at days 28, 90, and 360. DLCO significantly improved in severe patients at day 180. Ground-glass lesion reduction was significant in severe patients at day 90. No significant improvements in moderate patients for lung imaging or in severe patients for FEV1/VCmax. 6-MWD was not significant in either subgroup.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a non-randomized quasi-experimental study (single-arm + external control), not an RCT. The paper reports Hodges-Lehmann estimator as 'Difference' (not a simple mean difference), and all central tendency values are medians with IQRs; no means or SDs are reported for outcomes. The effect_value in between_group_effects fields has been populated with the Hodges-Lehmann estimator as reported. Baseline pulmonary function and 6-MWD data were unavailable (stated as limitation). Per-arm n_analyzed at each timepoint varies and was not fully tabulated in the paper (only aggregated numbers in Figure 1). The lung imaging relative-change data appear primarily in Figure 2 for most timepoints; only the day-90 ground-glass lesion comparison for severe patients had quantitative values explicitly reported in text. Total lesion proportion and solid component change data for moderate patients and total lesion proportion for severe patients were mentioned but numeric per-arm results not provided in text (only in Figure 2). Symptoms (pain, appetite loss, sleep difficulties) and SF-36 data referenced in Supplementary Table 1; D-dimer and IL-6 follow-up data referenced in Supplementary Table 2 — these supplementary tables were not included in the provided paper text. Omitted outcomes (data only in figures or supplementary): total lesion proportion change, solid component change, incidence of pain, incidence of appetite loss, incidence of sleep difficulties, SF-36 scores, D-dimer levels, IL-6 levels at follow-up.

summary: This study tested intravenous infusions of human umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells (UC-MSCs; 4×10⁷ cells on days 0, 3, and 6) versus standard care alone in 110 hospitalized COVID-19 patients (52 treated, 58 controls) at the convalescent stage in China, followed for one year. In moderate COVID-19 patients, UC-MSC treatment produced significantly higher FEV1 (2.75 vs 2.11 L at day 28, p=0.008) and VCmax at days 28, 90, and 360; in severe patients, ground-glass lung lesion volume decreased more in the MSC group at day 90 (-15.13% vs -3.66%, p=0.045), and diffusing capacity (DLCO) improved significantly at day 180 (p=0.004). The study was non-randomized with an external control group, baseline imbalances in IL-6 and viral positivity, and no significant differences in 6-minute walk distance or inflammatory markers, limiting causal interpretation.

trial_rating.result_basis: FEV1 in moderate patients: 2.75 vs 2.11 L at day 28 (p=0.008); ground-glass lesion reduction in severe patients: -15.13% vs -3.66% at day 90 (p=0.045); DLCO in severe patients at day 180 (p=0.004); 6-MWD showed no significant difference at any timepoint.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 spans two parts with complex merged/split rows; some cells are blank for 7-month and 9-month follow-up data (data not reported or not collected for all outcomes at those timepoints). AEs reported pooled across both arms as percentages of total sample (25%, 33%, 34%), not per arm. The Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia-11 is reported as TSK-11 (11-item version) though the methods section mentions TSK-17; extracted values are as reported. The paper states 'Z=1.936, P=.048' and effect size R=0.812 (95% CI 0.715-0.893) for kinesiophobia — this R is a nonparametric effect size statistic, not extracted in between_group_effects (MD extracted instead). Borg scale posttreatment values for the control group appear implausibly high (e.g., 15.50±27.32) compared to baseline (3.17±2.64), suggesting possible data entry error or table parsing artifact. The 'chronicity' variable (mean months since diagnosis) is labeled in Table 1 but appears to represent months since COVID-19 diagnosis. Follow-up at 7 months and 9 months had binary/categorical outcome data for some measures (Activities of daily living limitation, Doing exercise, Presenting symptoms, Returning to work) which are not separately extracted as outcomes here due to complex nested table structure. GRC follow-up means extracted from Table 2 partial data. The Berg balance scale between-group difference CI (0.547 to 3.417) with p=0.11 appears inconsistent (positive CI with non-significant p); reported verbatim.

summary: This pilot randomized controlled trial tested whether adding a weekly evidence-based eHealth education tool (six one-hour telehealth sessions covering COVID-19 pathology, pain neuroscience, breathing exercises, and self-management) to a six-week in-person pulmonary rehabilitation program improved outcomes in 12 post-COVID-19 patients with musculoskeletal symptoms. The only statistically significant between-group difference was in kinesiophobia (fear of movement), with the eHealth group scoring lower on the Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia-11 after treatment (16.0 vs 23.2 points, p=0.048, effect size R=0.812). No significant differences were found between groups in pain scores, functional independence (Barthel index), or six-minute walk test distance. The trial is severely underpowered with only six participants per arm, limiting the reliability of all findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia-11 post-treatment: eHealth group 16.00 ± 2.71 vs control 23.17 ± 5.49, p=0.048, R=0.812; all other primary outcomes non-significant.

All primary and secondary outcome data in Table 2 are reported as percentage change from baseline (median with IQR), not as absolute means with SDs. Absolute endpoint values at t4 and t8 are available only in figures (Figure 2B for CFS longitudinal data), preventing calculation of exact mean differences. The SAGIS Acid Regurgitation direction of effect is ambiguous in Table 2 (VSL#3 median=33.33 increase, but text and Figure 4B indicate improvement); as higher SAGIS scores indicate worse symptoms, a positive % change would indicate worsening — this may reflect a formatting issue in the preprint. There is a 2-week run-in period (t-2 to t0) before treatment begins; weeks_from_randomization are calculated from t0 (baseline/randomization). The paper describes 39 enrolled but 1 excluded for low adherence, leaving 38 randomized (19 per arm); the 1 excluded participant appears to have been in the placebo arm based on context (dismissed post-enrollment before randomization group context is unclear). Table 2 note states 'SCL-90 Somatization' but text refers to 'SCL-12'; likely the same instrument described in Methods as 12-item SCL. No vaccination data reported. summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial tested the probiotic VSL#3 (450 billion CFU/sachet, two sachets twice daily for 4 weeks) against placebo in 38 adults with long COVID who had clinically significant fatigue. VSL#3 produced a statistically significant reduction in fatigue on the Chalder Fatigue Scale compared to placebo (-24% median change vs -4.4%, p=0.0079), with the benefit persisting 4 weeks after treatment ended; overall gastrointestinal symptoms also improved (SAGIS total -22.84% vs 0%, p=0.043). No significant differences were found for anxiety, depression, somatization, performance status, or general wellbeing scores, and no clinically relevant adverse events were reported. This is a small single-centre pilot study (n=19 per arm) and the manufacturer provided funding and the study product.

trial_rating.result_basis: Chalder Fatigue Scale Likert score median change: -24% (IQR -60.9 to -11.6) in VSL#3 group vs -4.4% (-18.8 to 0.0) in placebo group, p=0.0079.

summary: The LISTEN trial tested a personalised self-management support intervention — up to six one-to-one sessions with a trained practitioner plus a co-designed handbook — in 544 non-hospitalised adults with long COVID symptoms lasting 12 weeks or more, recruited across 16 NHS and non-NHS sites in England and Wales. The primary health economic outcome was quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) over 3 months: participants in the LISTEN group gained a mean of 0.005 more QALYs than usual care (95% CI -0.004 to 0.014), a non-significant difference equivalent to roughly 11 additional hours of full health. From an NHS/PSS perspective the intervention cost £491 more per participant and was not cost-effective (ICER £95,304/QALY; only 4% probability of cost-effectiveness at the £20,000 threshold), but from a societal perspective — accounting for lost work, informal care, and out-of-pocket costs — the intervention dominated usual care, with a 95% probability of cost-effectiveness at £20,000/QALY.

trial_rating.result_basis: Adjusted mean QALY difference 0.005 (95% CI -0.004 to 0.014), crossing zero; ICER £95,304/QALY from NHS/PSS perspective with 3.99% probability of cost-effectiveness at £20,000 threshold.

summary: This pilot feasibility trial tested an 8-week personalised health behaviour support programme — comprising weekly one-to-one remote coaching sessions and daily physical activity and symptom diaries — in 32 adults with post-COVID syndrome (symptoms persisting ≥12 weeks). The primary outcome was feasibility of recruitment and randomisation, which was met: 67% of those screened were eligible and all 32 consented participants accepted randomisation, with 84% completing follow-up. Preliminary secondary data showed the intervention group gained 1,240 more steps/day than usual care (95% CI: 555–1,926) and reduced respiratory symptom scores (CAT) by 4 points more than controls, though the trial was not powered to confirm efficacy. No adverse events or symptom exacerbations were reported.

The between-group step count difference was +1,240 steps/day (95% CI: 555–1,926) but no inferential statistics were reported for this as a primary endpoint, and the study was a 32-participant pilot with no formal hypothesis test on clinical outcomes.

Most quantitative outcome data presented in figures only (no table with means/SDs for continuous outcomes). Per-arm means and SDs for PedsQL GI scores and spike antigen concentrations are not reported as numbers in text — data only in figures. CRP at baseline: larazotide mean 144 (SD 96) mg/liter; placebo mean 178 (SD 68) mg/liter — verbatim from Table 1. Win ratio reported as 2.38 (95% CI 1.04-5.43, p=0.04). Spearman correlations reported: IFNgamma vs spike antigen r=0.37, p=0.004; IL-6 vs spike antigen r=0.67, p<0.001; GI symptoms vs spike antigen r=-0.5, p=0.003. Fisher's exact p-values for GI recovery at day 7 and day 14 stated as p<0.001. Irritability continuous comparison by t-test p=0.01 also reported. Outcomes 7, 8, 9 (cytokines, antibodies) have no per-arm quantitative data in text — data only in figures. The effect_measure for binary Fisher's exact comparisons is listed as odds_ratio as a placeholder since no OR was explicitly calculated; the paper reports only p-values from Fisher's exact test without effect sizes. n_analyzed for spike antigen outcomes refers to the subset with spike antigen detected at enrollment (5 larazotide, 3-4 placebo).

summary: This phase 2a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested larazotide — an oral drug that blocks zonulin receptors to strengthen the gut barrier — as an add-on therapy in 12 children (median age 5.7 years) hospitalized with multisystem inflammatory syndrome (MIS-C), a severe post-COVID condition. Children receiving larazotide (n=6) showed faster clearance of circulating SARS-CoV-2 spike protein antigen compared to placebo (n=6), with all 5 antigen-positive larazotide patients clearing antigen by day 21 versus only 2 of 4 antigen-positive placebo patients, and a significantly greater proportion achieving clearance at days 7, 14, and 21 (p=0.002, p<0.001, p<0.0001 respectively). Larazotide-treated children also recovered gastrointestinal symptoms faster (significantly more recovery at days 7 and 14, p<0.001) and returned to usual activities more quickly through 6-month follow-up (p=0.03). The trial enrolled only 12 of a planned 20 participants due to declining MIS-C cases, making the small sample size the primary caveat; no drug-related adverse events were reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Win ratio analysis across all primary outcomes (spike antigen clearance, return to usual health/activities, PedsQL score) yielded a win ratio of 2.38 (p=0.04, 95% CI 1.04–5.43) for larazotide vs placebo; spike antigen clearance significantly greater at day 21 (p<0.0001), but N=12 total.

summary: A 12-week supervised high-intensity interval training (HIIT) program (4×4 minutes, three sessions per week) was tested against standard care in 28 adults previously hospitalised for COVID-19, with cardiac MRI-measured left ventricular mass (LVM) as the primary outcome at 12-month follow-up. The study was small (n=28 at baseline, n=22 completing cardiac MRI at follow-up), limiting the generalisability of findings.
