extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a news article (BMJ Q&A/news piece) summarizing the REGAIN RCT rather than the primary trial paper itself. Per-arm means and SDs are not reported for any outcome — only between-group adjusted mean differences with 95% CIs and p-values are provided. The n_analyzed values for the primary outcome (237 intervention, 250 control) were extracted from a binary outcome description at 3 months and may represent the same analysis population for other outcomes. The primary paper is cited as PMID 38325873 and would contain full quantitative data. The 3-month PROMIS subscores for depression, fatigue, and pain interference are described as driving the primary outcome but the timepoint for these subscores is ambiguous — the text states 'the improvements were largely driven by' these subscores without specifying whether this refers to 3 months or another timepoint; 3 months assumed. The p-value for fatigue is reported as p<0.001, so p_value_exact is set to false and value set to 0.001 as upper bound.

summary: The REGAIN trial tested an eight-week online group rehabilitation programme — combining weekly supervised home-based exercise and psychological support sessions — against usual care (a single advice session) in 585 adults who had been hospitalised with COVID-19 and reported lasting symptoms at least three months after discharge. The primary outcome, health-related quality of life measured by the PROMIS preference score, improved significantly in the intervention group at both three months (adjusted mean difference 0.03, 95% CI 0.01–0.05, p=0.02) and 12 months (0.03, 95% CI 0.01–0.06, p=0.02), driven mainly by improvements in fatigue, depression, and pain. The intervention was safe — only one of 21 serious adverse events was possibly related to the programme — though the trial population was predominantly white and drawn exclusively from post-hospitalisation patients, limiting generalisability to the broader long COVID community.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary PROMIS preference score improved by 0.03 points (95% CI 0.01–0.05, p=0.02) at 3 months versus usual care — statistically significant but a small absolute difference on a 0–1 utility scale.

The paper reports percent-change values in text for several outcomes but Table 2 provides the primary pre/post means and SDs used for extraction. The exercise arm n for analyzed outcomes is noted as 19 (randomized) with 1 withdrawal for commitment; ANCOVA likely analyzed all available data but exact analyzed N per outcome is not explicitly stated—19 for exercise and 20 for control is inferred. The control group FVC eta_p2 is reported as 0.71 in the table which appears to be a typographical error (likely 0.071 or 0.007) as the p-value is 0.141; noted but extracted as verbatim. summary: This RCT tested an 8-week supervised concurrent exercise program (resistance plus aerobic training, 3 sessions/week) against the WHO self-management rehabilitation leaflet in 39 non-hospitalized adults with post-COVID-19 condition lasting more than 12 weeks. The exercise group showed significantly greater improvements across cardiovascular fitness (VO2max +5.7%), lower-limb strength (sit-to-stand time -22.7%), quality of life (SF-12 physical domain +41.5% vs +6.5%), and fatigue (Chalder Fatigue Scale bimodal score -58% vs -16.5%) compared to controls. No adverse events occurred during training sessions, though the trial was small (n=19 per group) and findings may not generalise beyond non-hospitalised, mild-disease patients.

trial_rating.result_basis: VO2max improved by 2.1 ml/kg/min (+5.7%) in the exercise group vs -0.8% in controls (ANCOVA group effect p=0.035, ηp²=0.14); Chalder Fatigue Scale bimodal score -58% vs -16.5% (p=0.007, ηp²=0.23).

summary: This triple-blind randomised controlled trial tested Astragalus root extract (500 mg twice daily for 30 days) against placebo in 64 Iranian hospital nurses with post-COVID-19 chronic fatigue syndrome. No adverse events were reported, and the extract did not affect blood pressure, suggesting short-term safety.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Most quantitative outcome data at 12 weeks (endpoint values) were reported only as least square means with 95% CIs from the linear mixed regression model, not as raw arm-level means with SDs. Per-arm SDs at 12-week follow-up are not reported. Within-group change-from-baseline CIs were reported for peakVO2, VE/VCO2, and CIx. The between-group effect for pp-peakVO2 (delta +18.03%) lacks CI bounds in the text. MIP change-from-baseline p-values reported per arm (IMT p<0.001, UC p=0.075) but no between-group effect statistic explicitly stated; calculated difference (79.4 - 17.3 = 62.1 cmH2O) set as calculated. EQ-5D-3L dimension results at 12 weeks for mobility, self-care, and pain/discomfort dimensions were described as non-significant in text but no numeric effect sizes provided; only baseline data extracted for these. Figure data only: detailed 12-week per-arm endpoint values for EQ-5D dimensions (other than VAS) appear only in figures without tabulated values. BMI reported as median (IQR) for overall sample and arms; individual arm IQR values are 26-32 for IMT and 27-32 for control, but no means/SDs available. Time since infection converted: IMT 385 days / 30.44 = 12.65 months (~12.8), UC 340 days / 30.44 = 11.17 months (~11.3), SD converted from days (97/30.44=3.19, 105/30.44=3.45). The CIx within-group CI for IMT arm (-0.17 to 0.13) appears to span zero, inconsistent with p=0.122 — reported verbatim as stated.

summary: A 12-week home-based inspiratory muscle training (IMT) programme, performed twice daily at 25-30% of maximal inspiratory pressure, was tested against usual care (no intervention) in 26 adults with long COVID who had previously been hospitalised for SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia, on average about one year after discharge. IMT produced a large, statistically significant improvement in peak oxygen consumption (peakVO2), the primary measure of exercise capacity, compared to usual care. The control group's exercise capacity declined over the same period. The trial was small (13 per arm) and single-centre, limiting how broadly the findings can be applied.

trial_rating.result_basis: PeakVO2 increased by +4.46 mL/kg/min in the IMT group vs usual care (95% CI 3.10 to 5.81, p<0.001); the control group declined by -1.09 mL/kg/min (p=0.006).

Follow-up N values (n=200 usual care, n=210 intervention) taken from text and CONSORT diagram. For EQ-5D-5L index and VAS, exact follow-up per-arm n values were inferred by subtracting missing counts from the 3-month follow-up totals (missing: index - 6 intervention, 6 usual care; VAS - 4 intervention, 10 usual care). For GSE scales, 1 missing in usual care at follow-up was noted. For SF-12, 1 missing at baseline in intervention. The paper reports two adjusted models for all outcomes (Model A: adjusted for baseline + site random effect; Model B: additionally adjusted for age, gender, ethnic group, employment status, number of long covid symptoms); both sets of between-group estimates are extracted. The p_value_exact for FIS overall score Model A is set to false because the paper states p<0.001. The 6-week follow-up data were collected for health economic evaluation purposes only and are not reported numerically in the paper. The acceptability/appropriateness/feasibility implementation measures (Table 2) are not extracted as outcomes per se but are noted. The binary responder analysis (odds ratio for achieving MID on primary outcome) is noted: unadjusted OR 1.40 (0.94-2.09), fully adjusted OR 1.46 (0.95-2.25), not extracted as a separate outcome object since it derives from the primary outcome.

summary: The Listen trial tested a personalised self-management support intervention — up to six one-to-one sessions with trained healthcare practitioners plus a co-designed handbook — in 554 adults with long COVID who had not been hospitalised during their acute COVID-19 illness, recruited across 24 sites in England and Wales. The primary outcome, capacity for routine daily activities (Ox-PAQ routine activities scale), showed a small non-significant improvement in the intervention group compared to usual NHS care (adjusted mean difference −2.68 points, 95% CI −5.38 to 0.02, p=0.052), falling well below the pre-specified minimum important difference of 7.51 points. Secondary outcomes showed statistically significant improvements in fatigue (fatigue impact score −7.93, p<0.001), emotional wellbeing (Ox-PAQ emotional wellbeing −5.29, p=0.001), mental health (SF-12 mental component +2.36, p=0.004), and self-efficacy (+2.63, p<0.001), though physical health and social engagement were unchanged; no intervention-related serious adverse events were reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (Ox-PAQ routine activities) adjusted mean difference −2.68 (95% CI −5.38 to 0.02), p=0.052 — non-significant and less than half the pre-specified minimum important difference of 7.51 points.

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested a 16-week home-based exercise training (HBET) programme — three sessions per week of aerobic and strength exercise, semi-supervised via video calls — in 50 adults who had survived severe or critical COVID-19 and been discharged from ICU roughly five months earlier. The primary outcome, the physical component summary of the SF-36 quality-of-life questionnaire, was significantly higher in the exercise group than the control group after 16 weeks (mean difference 16.8 points, 95% CI 5.8–27.9, effect size 0.74). The exercise group also improved lower-limb functional capacity (30-second sit-to-stand: +2.38 repetitions) and had significantly lower rates of persistent muscle weakness (5% vs 35%) and myalgia (19% vs 55%); no adverse events related to the intervention were reported.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled phase II trial tested 10 sessions of hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) — 100% oxygen at 2.4 atmospheres for 90 minutes — versus sham treatment in 80 previously healthy adults aged 18–60 with long COVID at a single Swedish university hospital. The primary outcomes were changes in RAND-36 physical functioning (PF) and role limitations due to physical health (RP) at 13 weeks; neither differed significantly between groups (PF: least square mean difference 0.63, 95% CI −7.04 to 8.29, p=0.87; RP: 2.35, 95% CI −5.95 to 10.66, p=0.57), with both groups improving similarly. An exploratory finding at 52 weeks showed a statistically significant advantage for HBOT in the proportion of patients achieving a clinically meaningful improvement in physical functioning (65.8% vs 40.6%, p=0.033), and the safety profile was broadly comparable between arms, though 49% of HBOT participants had adverse events probably related to treatment versus 24% on placebo.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcomes not statistically significant: PF LSD 0.63 (95% CI −7.04 to 8.29, p=0.87); RP LSD 2.35 (95% CI −5.95 to 10.66, p=0.57).

summary: The PuRe-COVID trial tested a 12-week stepwise pulmonary rehabilitation programme delivered one-on-one by primary care physiotherapists in 76 Belgian adults with long COVID experiencing fatigue and/or respiratory symptoms. The programme included endurance training, strength training, breathing exercises, and inspiratory muscle training across five progressive phases. Patients in the rehabilitation group walked 39 metres further on the 6-minute walk test at 12 weeks compared to controls (95% CI 18–59 m, p<0.001), and also showed greater reductions in fatigue (CIS-fatigue -6 points, p=0.011) and dyspnoea. The trial was stopped before reaching its target of 134 participants (only 76 enrolled), so findings should be interpreted as preliminary; four patients experienced post-exertional malaise during the programme but none withdrew because of it.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome: 6-minute walk distance improved by +39 m in the rehabilitation group versus control at 12 weeks (95% CI 18–59 m, p<0.001), exceeding the 30.5 m minimal clinically important difference.

summary: The COVID-SMART trial randomized 607 adult COVID-19 outpatients at elevated risk for severe disease to either smartwatch-based telemonitoring with 24/7 physician hotline support for 30 days, or standard care, then assessed long COVID symptoms at 12 months. The primary finding was that telemedical support had no effect on depression or anxiety rates at follow-up: 35.4% vs 37.5% screened positive for depression (p=0.604) and 40.3% vs 40.7% for anxiety (p=0.932) in the intervention and control groups respectively. Multivariable analysis identified female sex (OR 2.18 for depression, 2.01 for anxiety), active smoking (OR 1.63, 1.72), and pre-existing asthma (OR 1.63, 2.17) as significant independent risk factors for both outcomes.

trial_rating.result_basis: Depression prevalence 35.4% intervention vs 37.5% control (p=0.604); anxiety 40.3% vs 40.7% (p=0.932); post-hoc power analysis showed only 18.1% power for depression and 5.4% for anxiety outcomes.

summary: The RECOVE trial tested an 8-week supervised concurrent training program (combined resistance and endurance exercise), inspiratory muscle training, or both, versus WHO self-management recommendations in 80 non-hospitalised adults with long COVID lasting over 12 weeks. The primary outcome was estimated VO2max: no statistically significant differences between groups were found, though the concurrent training groups achieved individual within-group improvements of approximately 7.5–7.8% (effect sizes 0.28–0.36). Concurrent training with or without inspiratory muscle training significantly outperformed the other groups on lower-body strength (14.5–32.6% improvement, ES 0.27–1.13), fatigue, and depression scores, and no adverse events occurred during any training session.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome VO2max showed no significant between-group differences (P > 0.05); within-group improvements in CT and CTRM were 7.5% and 7.8% respectively (ES 0.28 and 0.36) but did not reach statistical significance versus comparators.

The between-group p-value for FSS at post-treatment in Table 3 is p=0.034 but the abstract states p=0.022; Table 4 (pre-post change score comparison) reports p=0.022 for FSS, so both values extracted separately. The 'pre-and post-test' comparison in Table 4 represents change-score differences between arms (delta taVNS minus delta sham). For LF power in Table 4, the baseline difference is reported as −123.4 ± 30.5 and post as −53 ± 90.28 with delta −70.4 ± 71.12; these represent taVNS-minus-sham delta values and p=0.029. The HF power between-group p=0.042 (from abstract/Table 4) refers to the change-score comparison, not the endpoint comparison. Cohen's d and Hedges' g values are reported verbatim in the paper for between-group comparisons but not extracted as separate fields per schema. The FSS post-treatment between_group_effects has two entries: one for the endpoint comparison (p=0.034 from Table 3) and one for the change-score comparison (p=0.022 from Table 4). The sham taVNS group baseline HF power SD of 80.67 seems anomalously large compared to the mean of 29.70 — extracted verbatim as reported.

summary: This randomized sham-controlled trial tested transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) — 30 minutes daily for 20 days at 10 Hz — versus inactive sham stimulation in 42 adults aged 18–45 with post-COVID fatigue lasting at least 12 weeks. Both groups showed statistically significant reductions in fatigue severity (Fatigue Severity Scale), but the sham group improved more than the active taVNS group after treatment (mean FSS 4.79 vs 5.05, p=0.034 between groups favoring sham), with only small effect sizes (Cohen's d ≈ −0.19). taVNS did produce autonomic changes consistent with increased parasympathetic activity (decreased SNS index, decreased LF/HF ratio), but the study was likely underpowered and one co-author is a co-founder of the company that manufactured the stimulation device.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary fatigue outcome (FSS) after treatment: sham taVNS mean 4.79 vs taVNS mean 5.05; between-group difference p=0.034 favoring sham, Cohen's d = −0.190 (small effect against active treatment).

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested two yogic breathing techniques — Bhramari Pranayama (humming breath) and Sheetali Pranayama (cooling breath) — practiced for 30 minutes daily over 6 months in 90 post-COVID patients aged 19–40. Both techniques significantly improved lung function: forced vital capacity (FVC) increased by approximately 0.5 L in the Bhramari group and 0.4 L in the Sheetali group compared to controls, with FEV1 improving by 0.3 L in both groups. Heart rate variability also improved, with RMSSD rising by 5.5 ms in the Bhramari group and 4.8 ms in the Sheetali group, indicating enhanced parasympathetic nervous system activity. The study was single-centre with a small sample per arm (28–30 participants), limiting generalisability.

trial_rating.result_basis: FVC improved by mean difference 0.5 L (Bhramari, P<.04) and 0.4 L (Sheetali, P<.04) vs control; RMSSD improved by 5.5 ms (Bhramari, P<.01) and 4.8 ms (Sheetali, P<.02) vs control.

summary: A supervised physiotherapy rehabilitation program — including respiratory training, progressive resistance exercises, and aerobic conditioning — was tested in 23 adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome at a Brazilian outpatient clinic, compared against 10 untreated controls on a waiting list over approximately 8 weeks. The intervention group showed statistically significant improvements in SF-36 quality-of-life domains for physical functioning, physical role limitations, and bodily pain, as well as increased handgrip strength (p<0.05 for all), though no significant improvement was seen in the six-minute walk test distance. The study is substantially limited by its small, non-randomised, convenience sample and notable baseline differences between groups, with the control group being younger and having less severe initial disease.

Between-group factorial ANOVA F and p values are reported in Table 3 and extracted as between_group_effects p_values where they appear to represent the group-by-time interaction; however the abstract reports percent-change comparisons (e.g. FEV1 p=0.005) which differ from the Table 3 ANOVA p-values — the Table 3 values are used here as they are more directly extractable. The abstract states between-group comparisons for FEV1 p=0.005, FVC p=0.003, TLC p<0.001, DLCO p<0.001, 6-MWD p=0.015, but these appear to be based on percentage change comparisons not shown in Table 3; these values are NOT reflected in the Table 3 Factorial ANOVA column. summary: This Tunisian single-centre study tested a 6-week supervised respiratory muscle training programme (twice weekly, including chest physiotherapy, diaphragmatic training, breathing and cough exercises) in 30 patients with persistent symptoms one month after hospitalisation for moderate-to-severe COVID-19 pneumonia, compared to 12 matched controls who received no intervention. The training group showed significant reductions in dyspnea, dry cough, fatigue, and chest pain, and significant improvements in lung function (FVC, FEV1, TLC, DLCO) and 6-minute walk distance (466m to 517m, p<0.001), while the control group improved only in FEV1. The study is limited by its small and unequal group sizes (30 vs 12), lack of blinding, and single-centre design, and respiratory muscle strength (PI max, PE max) did not improve significantly in either group.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6-minute walk distance improved from 466m to 517m (p<0.001) in the training group vs a decline from 526m to 504m in controls (p=0.018); dyspnea prevalence fell from 75.9% to 13.8% (p<0.001) in the intervention group vs no significant change in controls.

summary: This study tested 6 weeks of inspiratory muscle training (IMT) using a pressure-threshold device versus sham training in 18 long COVID patients (9 per arm) who had persistent exertional breathlessness and confirmed diaphragm muscle weakness approximately 31 months after hospitalization for COVID-19. The primary outcome — inspiratory muscle endurance (time to task failure) — improved significantly in the IMT group compared to sham (median 365s at baseline vs 983s post-training, p=0.05), and exertional dyspnea scores (Borg scale) also improved (7 to 6, p=0.03), with benefits persisting 6 weeks after training ended. The trial was very small (9 per arm), largely open-label, and powered for within-group rather than between-group differences, limiting the strength of conclusions.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome: time to task failure improved from 365s to 983s in IMT arm vs 286s to 574s in sham arm, between-group p=0.05; Borg dyspnea score improved from 7 to 6 in IMT arm vs no change in sham, p=0.03.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested Triphala (an Ayurvedic three-herb combination) at 1000 mg/day for 8 weeks in 74 adults with post-COVID-19 condition in Thailand. Within the Triphala group, oxidative stress markers (MDA, protein carbonyl) and inflammatory cytokines (IFN-γ, TNF-α) fell significantly compared to baseline, and SOD antioxidant activity rose; however, none of these changes were statistically significant versus placebo on the primary between-group comparisons. Triphala was safe with no adverse effects on renal or liver function, and secondary analyses showed significantly greater reductions in headache and respiratory symptoms compared to placebo.

trial_rating.result_basis: No primary outcome reached significance between groups: MDA p=0.289 (Cohen's d=0.018), protein carbonyl p=0.184 (Cohen's d=0.028), SOD p=0.516, IFN-γ p=0.187, TNF-α p=0.051.

summary: The LARGO trial tested oral lactoferrin (1200 mg daily for 6 weeks) against placebo in 72 adults with long COVID, recruited within 12 months of PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. The primary outcome — reduction in fatigue measured by the Fatigue Assessment Scale — improved significantly in both groups by week 6 (lactoferrin: 3.9 points, placebo: 4.1 points), but there was no significant difference between the two arms (p=1.0), meaning lactoferrin provided no benefit over placebo. No differences were found for any secondary outcomes including anxiety, depression, cognitive function, or physical performance, and side effect rates were similar in both groups (22% lactoferrin vs 25% placebo).

summary: This Phase II trial tested deupirfenidone (LYT-100), a deuterated form of the antifibrotic drug pirfenidone, against placebo in 185 adults with long COVID respiratory complications who had been hospitalised for severe acute COVID-19 requiring supplemental oxygen. The primary outcome — change in 6-minute walk distance at 91 days — showed no significant difference between groups: deupirfenidone improved by 44.3 m versus 48.8 m for placebo (p=0.70), with both arms showing substantial natural recovery. Deupirfenidone was generally well tolerated, though gastrointestinal side effects were more common (nausea 9.5% vs 1.1%, dyspepsia 6.3% vs 1.1%) and discontinuation due to adverse events was higher in the treatment arm (11.6% vs 4.4%).

trial_rating.result_basis: 6-minute walk distance improved 44.3 m (deupirfenidone) vs 48.8 m (placebo); difference not significant, p=0.70.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested sulodexide (250 LRU twice daily for 8 weeks) in 206 adults with cardiometabolic risk factors who were recovering from moderate-to-severe COVID-19 within 40 days of symptom onset. The primary outcome, thrombomodulin (a marker of endothelial damage), was significantly lower in the sulodexide group at week 8 (25.2 vs 29.9 ng/mL, p=0.03), and secondary markers including vWF, D-dimer, CRP, and IL-6 also showed significant reductions compared to placebo. A notable caveat is that the lead author is a paid consultant for Alfasigma, the manufacturer of sulodexide, which also supplied the study medication.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm means and SDs for outcome trajectories (VAS slopes, EEG power slopes) were not reported in tables or text - only F-statistics, p-values, and effect sizes (partial eta-squared) for the LMM main effects and interactions were provided. Specific raw per-arm means/SDs for AX-CPT behavioral and EEG outcomes are data only in figures. The between-group effect for occipital alpha (outcome 7) is a post-hoc comparison mean difference of 0.06 (sham > verum at post-assessment) with d=0.33, 95% CI [0.07, 0.59], p=0.011 (FDR-corrected). The primary outcome of this paper is subjective state fatigue (VAS slopes); the trial's primary outcome (trait fatigue measured by questionnaires) was reported in a companion paper (Mischke & Zaehle, Brain Stimulation, 2025). The gamified Go/No-Go task was not pre-registered. P50 analysis had reduced n (verum n=19, sham n=16 at pre/post; verum n=18, sham n=15 at follow-up) due to 5 exclusions. The occipital alpha interaction (stimulation x assessment) was significant at F(2,74.45)=4.18, p=0.020, partial eta2=0.10; the sham group showed stronger alpha increase at post vs verum (mean difference=0.06, p=0.011, d=0.33) and reduction from post to follow-up in sham (mean difference=0.05, p=0.010, d=0.35). D-prime in Go/No-Go showed significant stimulation condition main effect (F(1,49)=6.22, p=0.016, partial eta2=0.11) and session x condition interaction (F(3,110.20)=5.57, p=0.001). EQ-5D-5L Index also reported: verum M=0.64 SD=0.26, sham M=0.69 SD=0.28, p=0.562.

summary: This double-blind randomized controlled trial tested four consecutive daily sessions of anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) applied to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in 40 adults with long COVID-related cognitive fatigue. The primary outcome (subjective trait fatigue) showed no significant benefit from active versus sham stimulation; among the secondary outcomes reported here, tDCS also had no significant effect on subjective state fatigue ratings or behavioral performance on a cognitive task. The only notable finding was a statistically significant interaction in occipital alpha brainwave activity, where the sham group showed a greater fatigue-related increase in alpha power at post-assessment compared to the active stimulation group (mean difference = 0.06, p = 0.011, d = 0.33), suggesting a possible but limited neurophysiological stabilizing effect that did not translate into measurable clinical benefit.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary and secondary subjective/behavioral outcomes were all non-significant; e.g., VAS exhaustion slopes: stimulation condition F(1,38.44)=1.12, p=0.296; the only significant finding was a secondary EEG interaction (occipital alpha, p=0.020) with no corresponding behavioral or subjective improvement.

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested 8 weeks of home-based inspiratory muscle training (IMT) in 281 adults with long COVID (average 9 months post-infection, 88% female) whose primary symptom was breathlessness. The primary outcome — overall health-related quality of life measured by K-BILD total score — did not differ significantly between the IMT and control groups in the intention-to-treat analysis (IMT: 58.2±12.3 vs control: 59.5±12.4). However, IMT produced clinically meaningful improvements in breathlessness-specific outcomes: the Transition Dyspnoea Index improved by 2.0 points in the IMT group versus 0.9 in controls (p=0.005), and the K-BILD breathlessness and chest symptoms domains both improved beyond their minimal clinically important thresholds, alongside gains in respiratory muscle strength and estimated aerobic fitness.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome K-BILD total score showed no significant between-group difference in the intention-to-treat population (IMT: 58.2±12.3 vs control: 59.5±12.4, p<0.05 threshold not met for between-group comparison); significant results were limited to secondary outcomes and the per-protocol subgroup.

summary: This interim safety report from the HOT-LoCO trial tested hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBO2) versus sham treatment in 20 previously healthy adults with long COVID (post-COVID condition) at Karolinska University Hospital, Sweden. The interim analysis does not report primary efficacy outcomes — those are physical functioning and role physical scores on RAND-36 at 13 weeks — but documents baseline characteristics and safety data only. The enrolled cohort had severely impaired health-related quality of life (RAND-36 physical functioning score 31.75 vs. population norm of 83.5, p<0.001) and reduced exercise capacity (6-minute walk test 442m vs. 662m norm, p<0.001). Thirty-one adverse events occurred across 60% of subjects, with no serious adverse events; the most common were cough and chest pain/discomfort, and all were transient, leading the independent safety board to conclude HBO2 has a favorable safety profile.

trial_rating.result_basis: No primary efficacy outcome data reported in this interim analysis; baseline RAND-36 physical functioning was 31.75 vs. norm 83.5 (p<0.001), confirming severe impairment at entry, but no between-group treatment effect is yet available.

summary: This double-blind RCT tested whether fluvoxamine 100 mg/day for 10 days, taken during active mild-to-moderate COVID-19, could prevent neuropsychiatric long COVID symptoms in 85 vaccinated Iranian outpatients followed for 12 weeks. Fatigue at 12 weeks was significantly lower in the fluvoxamine group (21.4%) compared to placebo (44.2%), giving a relative risk of 0.48 (95% CI: 0.25–0.95, p=0.026). No other neuropsychiatric symptoms—including anxiety, depression, insomnia, or cognitive complaints—differed significantly between groups, and the trial was underpowered to detect effects on these secondary outcomes.

trial_rating.result_basis: Fatigue occurred in 21.4% of the fluvoxamine group vs 44.2% of placebo (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.25–0.95, p=0.026), a roughly halving of risk, but N=85 completers from a single centre with low pre-specified power (40%).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether adding home-based breathing and chest mobility exercises (3 times per week for 12 weeks) to a standard cardiac rehabilitation program improved cardiorespiratory fitness in 46 long COVID patients with cardiovascular comorbidities such as coronary artery disease and hypertension. Patients who received the additional exercises walked 52 meters further on the 6-minute walk test (467 m vs 415 m, p=0.032), and showed significantly higher peak expiratory flow rate (503 vs 411 L/min, p=0.031) and peak cough flow (465 vs 366 L/min, p=0.016) compared to those on cardiac rehabilitation alone. No significant differences were found in quality of life or inflammation markers (CRP, D-dimer), and no adverse cardiovascular events occurred during the trial.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6-minute walk test: intervention 467 m vs control 415 m, mean difference 52 m (95% CI 4.81–99.96), p=0.032; PEFR difference 91 L/min (95% CI 8.61–173.99), p=0.031.

summary: This RCT tested supervised twice-weekly, 8-week water-based (AQUA) and land-based (LAND) exercise programmes versus no exercise in 74 children aged 10-12 with post-COVID-19 condition characterised by fatigue and respiratory symptoms. Lung function was a secondary outcome; both exercise groups showed significant improvements in FEV1 and FVC compared to controls, who declined (e.g., girls in the AQUA group improved FEV1% predicted by 14.3 percentage points vs a 6.4 point decline in controls). The trial was underpowered for lung function as a secondary endpoint, sample sizes per group were modest (23-26 at baseline), and the study was not blinded due to the nature of the intervention.

trial_rating.result_basis: Secondary outcome FEV1 GROUP×REPETITION interaction: F(2,64)=6.80, p<0.01, η²=0.18; FVC interaction: F(2,64)=4.63, p<0.05, η²=0.13; lung function was not the primary outcome and the trial was not powered for it.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a health economics paper reporting cost-effectiveness of the REGAIN RCT; the primary clinical outcomes (PROMIS-PROPr) are reported only by reference to the companion clinical paper (McGregor et al. BMJ 2024) and are NOT reported with per-arm means/SDs in this paper. The EQ-5D-5L is the primary outcome for economic evaluation. Table 4 (cost-effectiveness results) had heavily merged/garbled cells in the source text; arm-level adjusted cost values (REGAIN £1987 CI 1666-2307; usual care £1681 CI 1406-1955) and QALY values were extracted from partially reconstructed table. The 6-month CI upper bound for EQ-5D utility in Table 3 appears to be a typo (0.67 instead of likely 0.067) — extracted verbatim. Intervention cost per patient: REGAIN £399.92 (n=298); usual care £72.71 (n=287). Resource use cost breakdown by category (medication, outpatient, community care, A&E, inpatient, PSS, nursing home) extracted in Table 2 with complete data across 0-12 months. No adverse events data reported in this economic paper. Time since hospital discharge to randomisation mean 10.6 months reported overall only.

summary: The REGAIN trial tested an eight-week online supervised group rehabilitation programme combining physical exercise sessions and psychological support against best-practice usual care (a single online consultation) in 585 adults with post-COVID-19 condition who had previously been hospitalised. The primary economic outcome was cost-effectiveness over 12 months: the REGAIN intervention cost £305 more per patient (95% CI: -£123 to £732) and generated 0.026 additional QALYs (95% CI: -0.005 to 0.052), yielding an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of £11,941 per QALY, well below the UK NHS £30,000 willingness-to-pay threshold. The 84% probability of cost-effectiveness at that threshold supports offering the programme to hospitalised post-COVID patients, though results are based on modest and statistically non-significant differences in both cost and quality of life, and the findings may not generalise to non-hospitalised patients or minority ethnic groups.

trial_rating.result_basis: Incremental QALYs of 0.026 (95% CI: -0.005 to 0.052) are non-significant; incremental cost £305 (95% CI: -£123 to £732) also non-significant; ICER £11,941/QALY with 84% probability of cost-effectiveness at £30,000 threshold.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a post-hoc analysis of a primary RCT (NCT05047952; primary paper: McIntyre et al., Brain, 2023). The DSST baseline values are reported as combined z-scores. The between-group mean difference of 0.621 (SE=0.313, p=0.047) is from GEE adjusted model moderated by CRP/TG-HDL/BMI — it reflects the interaction-moderated comparison, not a simple overall between-group difference. Week 2 DSST data were collected but no numeric values reported for that timepoint in this paper. Endpoint absolute DSST scores (week 8) not reported — only change-from-baseline values available. The vortioxetine arm TRG-HDL SD (17.19) appears anomalously large compared to placebo (0.99), likely reflecting skewed data or outliers. Adverse events not reported in this post-hoc analysis paper. BMI sub-category means reported in Table 1 but reflect subgroup means within weight categories rather than overall summary statistics.

summary: This 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested vortioxetine (5–20 mg/day) versus placebo in 147 Canadian adults with WHO-defined long COVID, focusing on whether baseline metabolic dysfunction, elevated BMI, and inflammation modified cognitive outcomes. The primary outcome was change in Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DSST) score; vortioxetine produced a statistically significant between-group improvement at 8 weeks (mean difference 0.621 points, p=0.047), with the benefit concentrated in participants who had high baseline CRP, elevated TG-HDL ratio, and higher BMI. This is a post-hoc analysis of a previously published trial, not a pre-specified primary analysis, so the findings are hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.

trial_rating.result_basis: Between-group DSST mean difference = 0.621 (SEM 0.313, p=0.047); vortioxetine within-group change = 1.933 vs placebo 0.289 (p=0.091), but this is a post-hoc subgroup interaction analysis, not the pre-specified primary outcome.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a 12-week home-based pulmonary rehabilitation program — comprising daily walking, diaphragmatic strengthening, and resistance training — against usual medical care alone in 60 adults aged 40–70 with post-COVID-19 syndrome presenting with fatigue, dyspnea, and exercise intolerance. The primary outcome, six-minute walk test distance, improved substantially more in the rehabilitation group (439.7 m) than the control group (347 m) after 12 weeks, a difference of roughly 93 m. The rehabilitation group also showed meaningfully lower fatigue scores (Chalder: 11.1 vs. 13.4), higher physical fitness index (52.3 vs. 36.7), better quality of life on the SF-36 (66.4 vs. 47.6), and greater dyspnea reduction, all at p<0.001, with no notable safety concerns reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT improved to 439.7 m (rehabilitation) vs. 347 m (control), a ~93 m between-group difference, p<0.001; baseline values were comparable (270.7 m vs. 274.1 m).

Per-arm follow-up means and SDs for timepoints 2 and 3 are not provided in tables — only absolute change from baseline means are shown in figures (as mean with SE bars) without numeric values in the text or supplemental tables referenced. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 12 sessions of balneotherapy (thermal mineral water immersion plus aquatic exercises) over one month against a no-treatment control in 98 adults with long COVID, most of whom were middle-aged women with symptoms lasting over one year. The primary outcome was change in questionnaire scores across multiple validated scales; the largest improvements in the balneotherapy group were in musculoskeletal pain (SF-36 pain subscale beta-coefficient -21.6, 95% CI -30.48 to -12.78, p<0.0001) and fatigue (SF-36 energy/fatigue beta-coefficient -17.5, 95% CI -24.23 to -10.66, p<0.0001), with additional significant short-term gains in sleep quality, anxiety, and several quality-of-life domains. Gains in sleep, anxiety, and emotional well-being were not sustained at the one-month follow-up, and 17 of 51 participants in the balneotherapy group reported mild transient worsening of symptoms, primarily fatigue, especially in early sessions.

trial_rating.result_basis: SF-36 pain subscale beta-coefficient -21.6 (95% CI -30.48 to -12.78, p<0.0001) and energy/fatigue beta-coefficient -17.5 (95% CI -24.23 to -10.66, p<0.0001) vs. control at end of intervention.

summary: This non-randomized, open-label dose-escalation trial tested anhydrous enol-oxaloacetate (AEO), a nutritional supplement, in 76 ME/CFS patients (average illness duration 8.9 years, 73.7% women) and 43 long COVID patients with fatigue lasting at least 6 months. The primary outcome was change in Chalder Fatigue Scale score at 6 weeks compared to a historical placebo benchmark of 5.9% improvement; ME/CFS patients showed 22.5–27.9% reductions in fatigue (Likert scoring, p<0.005) and up to 33.3% achieved clinical normalization on bimodal scoring, while long COVID patients at 500 mg twice daily showed up to 46.8% achieving clinical normalization. Key caveats are substantial: the study was unblinded with no concurrent placebo group, was funded by the supplement manufacturer (Terra Biological LLC), one author is a company officer, and dropout rates were high in the long COVID arm, all of which severely limit interpretation of the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: Chalder Fatigue Scale (Likert) improved 22.5–27.9% from baseline in ME/CFS groups vs historical placebo of 5.9% (p<0.005); 33.3% of ME/CFS patients and 46.8% of long COVID patients reached bimodal score ≤4.

summary: Treamid (a bisamide derivative of dicarboxylic acid, BDDA), an oral anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic drug, was tested in 59 adults who had recovered from COVID-19 pneumonia and had persistent lung damage, reduced lung function (FVC and/or DLCO below 80% predicted), and moderate-to-severe breathlessness. After 4 weeks of daily 50 mg oral Treamid versus placebo, 41% of the Treamid group achieved the primary endpoint of clinically significant improvement in FVC and/or DLCO, compared to 17% in the placebo group (p=0.036); Treamid also reduced breathlessness after exercise (Borg scale: -0.9 vs -0.4, p=0.018). The trial was small (roughly 30 patients per arm), industry-funded by the drug's developer, and the female-subgroup benefit was an exploratory post-hoc analysis requiring confirmation in larger trials.

summary: This 1-year follow-up study examined whether intravenous human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell (hUC-MSC) therapy, given during acute severe COVID-19, reduced long-term post-infection sequelae compared to standard treatment alone in 25 discharged patients (8 hUC-MSC, 17 controls). The primary finding was that fatigue remained common overall (60%), but only 25% of the hUC-MSC group reported persistent fatigue at 1 year compared to 76.5% of controls (p=0.028); the hUC-MSC group also had significantly lower KL-6 levels (2585.5 vs 3120.7 U/ml, p<0.001) and lower MDA levels (9.27 vs 9.91 nmol/ml, p=0.036), suggesting reduced lung injury and oxidative stress. No serious adverse events were attributable to hUC-MSC therapy at 1 year, though the study is severely limited by its very small sample size, single-centre design, and non-randomised follow-up attrition.

trial_rating.result_basis: Fatigue rate 25% (2/8) in hUC-MSC group vs 76.5% (13/17) in control group at 1-year follow-up, p=0.028.

summary: This study tested three intravenous infusions of umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs, 4×10⁷ cells/dose) versus placebo in 100 severe COVID-19 patients from Wuhan, with 78 patients assessed at a 3-year follow-up. The primary lung imaging outcome was not statistically significant: 47% of MSC-treated patients showed normal CT scans versus 34% of placebo patients (OR=1.68, 95% CI: 0.65–4.34, p=0.28). The one statistically significant finding was a higher general health score on the SF-36 quality-of-life survey in the MSC group (median 67 vs 50, difference 12.86, 95% CI: 1.44–24.28), with no significant differences in exercise capacity, pulmonary function, or long COVID symptom rates between groups; no increase in tumor incidence or other safety signals was observed over three years.

summary: A 3-month online-supported, app-guided physical activity program (150 min/week of moderate exercise, individually tailored) was tested against a waiting-list control in 62 long COVID patients with significant fatigue (FAS score ≥22) recruited at Hannover Medical School. The primary outcome, peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak), did not improve significantly in either group: the intervention group gained 0.9 ml/min/kg versus 0.3 ml/min/kg in controls, with no significant between-group difference (p=0.098 within intervention group; between-group mean difference -0.6 ml/min/kg, 95% CI -1.8 to 0.8). Fatigue scores improved in both groups equally, likely reflecting natural recovery over time rather than a treatment effect; a post-hoc subgroup analysis found that only patients with moderate fatigue (FAS <35) showed any improvement in exercise capacity, regardless of group assignment.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome VO2peak between-group mean difference was -0.6 ml/min/kg (95% CI -1.8 to 0.8), p=0.098 within the intervention group; no significant between-group difference detected; post-hoc power analysis showed only 12% statistical power, with 810 patients required to detect a significant effect.

The between-group effect for SF-36 Mental Health change score (T1-T0 difference: 1.98 - (-1.26) = 3.24) was calculated from Table 2 data; the paper states p=0.046 for this comparison. Severity of persistent symptoms measured by 1-10 VAS was noted as collected but VAS severity scores are not separately tabulated in outcome tables (only symptom count is reported quantitatively). summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a 4-week supervised aerobic exercise program (12 sessions on a cycling ergometer, using either moderate- or high-intensity interval training) in 24 long COVID patients aged 18–75 with persistent symptoms. The primary finding was that 67.8% of patients in the exercise group showed reduced or resolved symptoms after 4 weeks, compared to 16.7% in the control group (p=0.013). summary: This pilot randomised controlled trial tested at-home, self-administered transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) — a non-invasive device that delivers electrical stimulation to the ear to activate the vagus nerve — in 12 adults with confirmed long COVID symptoms including fatigue, brain fog, anxiety, depression, and others. The primary outcomes were feasibility and safety, not efficacy; the trial was explicitly underpowered to detect clinical effects. Descriptively, participants receiving active taVNS for two weeks saw their reported long COVID symptom burden fall from 46% to 31% of nine tracked symptoms, versus no change in the sham group (68% to 68%), and those completing four weeks of active treatment showed the largest reductions in mental fatigue scores, but no inferential statistics were reported for symptom outcomes. The intervention was safe, with no cardiac adverse events and only two mild cases of skin irritation across all sessions.

trial_rating.result_basis: No p-values or confidence intervals were reported for any symptom outcome; the only quantitative comparison is descriptive: active group symptoms fell from 46% to 31% over two weeks versus sham remaining at 68%, with the study explicitly stated to be underpowered to determine efficacy.

Note: Table 2 headers show N=31 helmet and N=33 HFNC for symptoms, N=30 each for pulmonary function, and N=35/N=36 for quality of life sections — these varying Ns are preserved in arm_results. The 30-s chair stand test p-value (0.65) is reported but no between-group effect size or CI is provided. The EQ-VAS high-flow group IQR in Table 2 has a formatting issue (value '[60-80]' appears on next line); extracted as median=70, IQR 60-80 based on text and table. Outcomes from Table 3 (intubated vs non-intubated subgroup) are captured in subgroup_analyses rather than as separate outcome entries to avoid duplication. Additional outcomes not extracted as separate objects due to space: maximal mid-expiratory flow 25-75 (MEF25-75), alveolar ventilation volume, residual volume/TLC ratio, FEV1<80% binary, FEV1/FVC<80% binary, TLC<80% binary, residual volume<80% binary, 6MWT interruption, 6MWT unable to walk predicted distance, various minor symptoms (dry cough, sore throat, rhinitis, smell disorder, taste disorder, dizziness, myalgia, chest pain, sicca syndrome, inappetence, diarrhoea, decreased visual acuity). summary: This pre-specified follow-up analysis of the HENIVOT randomized trial assessed 6-month outcomes in 71 ICU survivors with moderate-to-severe COVID-19 hypoxemic respiratory failure who had been treated with helmet noninvasive ventilation (NIV) or high-flow nasal oxygen. The primary outcome — the proportion of patients reporting any symptom at 6 months — did not differ between groups (90% helmet vs. 85% high-flow, p=0.71), and no significant differences were found in pulmonary function, physical performance, or quality of life between the two treatments. The only significant between-group difference was lower arthralgia in the helmet group (16% vs. 55%, p=0.002); separately, patients who required invasive mechanical ventilation during the acute illness had significantly worse pulmonary function and quality of life at 6 months regardless of initial treatment assignment.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (proportion with any symptom at 6 months) showed no significant difference: 90% helmet vs. 85% high-flow, p=0.71, OR=1.67 (95% CI 0.36–7.65).

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested two 8-week exercise-based rehabilitation programmes — face-to-face and remote — against usual care in 181 adults with post-COVID syndrome who had previously been hospitalised with COVID-19. Both interventions significantly improved exercise capacity measured by the Incremental Shuttle Walking Test: face-to-face rehabilitation produced a mean gain of 52 metres over usual care (95% CI 19–85 m, p=0.002) and remote rehabilitation produced a gain of 34 metres (95% CI 1–66 m, p=0.047), both exceeding the established 35-metre minimal clinically important difference. Neither intervention improved self-reported quality of life or symptom scores compared to usual care, and an exploratory immune substudy (n=31) found that face-to-face rehabilitation increased CD8+ T-cell and NK cell counts relative to usual care, with no safety signals attributable to the interventions.

trial_rating.result_basis: Face-to-face rehabilitation improved ISWT by mean 52 m (95% CI 19–85 m, p=0.002) and remote by 34 m (95% CI 1–66 m, p=0.047) versus usual care, both exceeding the 35 m MCID.

summary: This study tested oral Actovegin (400 mg three times daily for 60 days) added to standard care in 222 post-COVID-19 patients with cognitive impairment, compared to 222 controls receiving standard care alone; average patient age was 68 years. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) applied for 25 minutes after aerobic exercise in 44 young adults (aged 18-45) with post-COVID syndrome lasting more than 12 weeks. The primary finding was that taVNS enhanced cardiac vagal control during post-exercise recovery: the RMSSD index (a measure of heart rate variability reflecting vagal activity) increased significantly in the taVNS group after stimulation (p=0.028) but not in the placebo group, and the parasympathetic nervous system index showed a greater rate of increase in the taVNS group (p=0.009). However, taVNS produced no significant advantage over placebo for blood lactate clearance or blood pressure reduction, meaning its practical impact on exercise recovery was limited to autonomic signaling measures rather than metabolic or cardiovascular outcomes.

trial_rating.result_basis: RMSSD increased significantly in the taVNS group post-stimulation (p=0.028) vs non-significant increase in placebo; no significant between-group differences in blood lactate (p=0.006 within-group but similar across both groups) or blood pressure (p=0.01 both groups equally).

summary: This double-blind RCT tested daily 1-hour sessions of lower-extremity electrical stimulation (E-Stim) applied to the gastrocnemius muscles for 4 weeks in 18 previously hospitalised long COVID patients with persistent leg muscle weakness and deconditioning. After 4 weeks, only the active E-Stim group showed improved muscle perfusion recovery after stimulation (oxyhemoglobin rose from t60 to t70, p=0.040) and increased gastrocnemius muscle endurance over the 1-hour session (p=0.031), while the sham group showed no improvement in either measure. The intervention was well-tolerated with no adverse events, though the trial was small, the two groups were not well-matched at baseline (the active group had more severe prior illness), and the sample size fell short of the pre-specified target of 32.

trial_rating.result_basis: Active group oxyhemoglobin increased post-stimulation at 4 weeks (p=0.040, d=0.334) vs sham which continued to decline (p<0.001, d=0.632); group×time interaction p=0.022. Muscle endurance increased in active group (p=0.031, d=0.397) with significant group×time interaction (p=0.048).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 12 weeks of Baduanjin exercise training (BET) — a traditional Chinese mind-body practice involving gentle postures, breathing, and meditation — in 40 adults with idiopathic chronic fatigue who had also recovered from COVID-19. The primary outcome, forced vital capacity (FVC), improved significantly in the BET group (from 2.07 L to 2.18 L) compared to no change in controls (2.03 L to 2.02 L), with a between-group difference significant at p=0.001. All secondary outcomes also improved significantly in the BET group, including 6-minute walk distance (298 m to 358 m), fatigue scores, sleep quality, depression, and quality of life, with no changes in the control group; however, the trial is limited by a very small sample (20 per arm), no long-term follow-up, and no objective adherence monitoring.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper reports 'delta score 27.50' for the treatment group and 'delta score 9.50' for the control group in the abstract, but Table 2 shows delta scores of 10.33 and 2.11 respectively. The abstract delta scores appear to be cumulative rank sums (Wilcoxon test statistic) rather than mean differences; Table 2 values were used as primary data. The 95% CI reported in Table 2 for the control group (17.54-20.96) and treatment group (11.04-15.02) appear to be for the post-intervention means rather than for the delta scores. The OR=0.00, p=0.99 reported in the abstract refers to the logistic regression of the intervention itself (Table 3 shows OR=0.81, p=0.26 for WHO Stress Management), creating inconsistency. ISI score baseline comparison p=0.00 is stated in the paper but this seems counterintuitive given that both groups had insomnia at baseline; this may reflect a non-parametric test value rounded to zero. Age was the only demographic characteristic that differed significantly between groups (p=0.03) but exact means/SDs by group were not reported in tables.

summary: This quasi-experimental study tested the WHO Stress Management (WSM) module — a five-session online program combining mindfulness and relaxation — in 36 Indonesian adults with post-COVID insomnia recruited from a Telegram self-isolation group. The WSM group showed a mean Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) score drop from 19.94 to 9.61 (delta 10.33), compared to a drop from 18.56 to 16.44 (delta 2.11) in the sleep hygiene psychoeducation control group (p=0.00 on Wilcoxon and Mann-Whitney tests). However, logistic regression found no significant causative effect of WSM on clinical insomnia improvement (OR 0.81, p=0.26), and the authors note that the online delivery format likely limited participant engagement and masked confounders such as anxiety and depression.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL DATA QUALITY ISSUES: (1) All quantitative data appear only in bar chart figures (Figs 1-5); no tables provided. Percentages are reported verbatim in the results text, but exact n per subgroup are not stated — event counts were back-calculated from stated percentages assuming equal subgroup sizes within each disorder type across the two arms. However, the per-subgroup ns are uncertain: summing inferred subgroup ns (15+23+25+17+25=105) exceeds stated arm 1 total of 80, so the subgroup assignments are not additive across the whole arm (i.e., participants may have had only one disorder type per arm, and the per-subgroup n may represent only that subgroup, not the full arm). The inferred n per subgroup (e.g., 15 per arm for polymenorrhea based on 13.3% = ~2/15) is speculative. (2) No baseline demographic data (age, BMI, time since infection) reported per arm. (3) Allocation method not described — this is NOT a confirmed RCT; described as a controlled study without randomization details. (4) Follow-up duration stated as 3-6 months post-treatment but exact treatment duration not specified. (5) The Ukrainian-language abstract reverses group numbering (group 1 = standard, group 2 = modified) relative to the English text (group 1 = modified, group 2 = standard) — extraction follows English text convention. (6) Adverse event percentages given as ranges (e.g., 15-20%, 60-70%) without exact denominators.

summary: This Ukrainian trial tested a modified multi-component regimen—combining natural estrogen-based oral contraceptives, melatonin, vitamin D3, magnesium-B6, L-arginine, quercetin, folic acid, and vitamin B12—against standard Ukrainian Ministry of Health protocols in 158 women of reproductive age (18–45) who developed menstrual disorders within six months of COVID-19 recovery. Across all five disorder types, the modified regimen produced dramatically lower relapse rates (8.7–23.5% vs. 56–80%) and higher rates of complete menstrual normalization (72–84% vs. 33–52%), with all differences statistically significant at P<0.05. Adverse effects such as edema, breast tenderness, and hypertension were also substantially less frequent in the modified-therapy group (15–20% vs. 60–70%), attributed to the use of natural rather than synthetic estrogens.

trial_rating.result_basis: Complete menstrual normalization achieved in 72–84% (modified) vs. 33–52% (standard), and relapse rates 8.7–23.5% vs. 56–80%, all P<0.05; however, no randomization, blinding, or pre-registration reported, and assignment to groups appears non-randomized.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a quasi-experimental prospective open-label controlled study, not a true RCT; allocation method not described. The study is reported in Russian with English abstract/translation. Arm-level sample sizes for subgroups (Group I, II, III within each treatment arm) were taken from Table 3. The p-value of 0.001 for nasal sIgA between-group comparison in Group I is stated as p=0.007 within-group for treatment arm; the intergroup difference is marked as p<0.001 (#). Between-group effect sizes for nasal sIgA outcomes were calculated as mean difference (arm1 minus arm2 at 30 days). Control group healthy reference values: saliva sIgA 6.45±1.81 mg/ml, nasal sIgA 13.43±3.24 mg/ml (n=15) — not included as a trial arm. Symptom prevalence data from Tables 4 and 5 (acute and post-COVID clinical manifestations) are descriptive/retrospective and not outcomes of the intervention; they are not extracted as outcome objects but all numerical data is present in the paper tables. The paper does not report per-arm demographic data broken down by treatment group.

summary: This open-label controlled study tested intranasal interferon alpha-2b (IFN α-2b) gel, applied twice daily for 30 days, in 65 adults aged 18–60 who had recovered from COVID-19 within the past 1–9 months, compared to 65 untreated post-COVID controls. The primary outcome was secretory IgA (sIgA) levels in saliva and nasal swabs; among patients treated within 1–3 months of infection, salivary sIgA rose more than 3-fold (from 1.84±0.28 to 5.78±1.96 mg/ml, p=0.001) and nasal sIgA rose 1.5-fold (from 28.61±3.0 to 39.83±3.85 mg/ml, p=0.007), while untreated patients showed persistently low sIgA for up to 9 months. No respiratory infections were recorded in the treated group during the study period, versus a 27.6% incidence in the untreated group (p<0.001), and no adverse events were reported in either group.

trial_rating.result_basis: Salivary sIgA increased from 1.84±0.28 to 5.78±1.96 mg/ml (p=0.001) and nasal sIgA from 28.61±3.0 to 39.83±3.85 mg/ml (p=0.007) in the IFN α-2b group at 1–3 months post-COVID.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 10 days of daily 90-minute inhaled 'active hydrogen' (H(H2O)m) inhalation therapy added to standard rehabilitation (physiotherapy, magnesium, B vitamins, L-carnitine) versus standard rehabilitation alone in 60 healthcare workers with post-COVID-19 chronic fatigue syndrome. The primary finding was a large improvement in exercise capacity: the 6-minute walk distance increased from 429m to 569m (+140m) in the hydrogen group versus no significant change in controls, with the hydrogen group walking ~30% further than controls at day 10 (p<0.0001). Additional significant improvements in the hydrogen group included reduced arterial stiffness index (8.8 to 6.8 m/s, p<0.0001), reduced pulmonary shunt fraction (8.98% to 5.34%, p<0.01), reduced venous lactate (2.5 to 1.5 mmol/L, p<0.001), and improved venous oxygen tension (26.9 to 34.8 mmHg, p<0.0001); no adverse events were reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6-minute walk distance increased from 429±45m to 569±60m in the hydrogen group versus no significant change in controls; hydrogen group was ~30% higher than controls at day 10 (p<0.0001).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Crossover design: all 20 participants completed both arms. Per-arm n=20 for all outcomes (each participant contributed data to both conditions). Baseline values for each arm reflect participants at entry into that condition (post-washout values used as pre for second condition). The paper reports intervention x time p-values from two-way ANOVA in Table 2 — these are used as between-group p-values. Calculated between-group mean differences are endpoint post-treatment differences (arm1 post minus arm2 post), which reflects the crossover contrast available from Table 2. The paper's primary between-group p-values (from delta of change comparisons via paired t-test) are: 6MWT p=0.02, TUG p=0.002, Barthel p=0.02; these are reported as between_group_effects p_values. For other outcomes, the intervention x time interaction p-value from two-way ANOVA is used as the between-group p-value. Training cardiopulmonary monitoring data (SpO2, HR, systolic/diastolic BP) appear only as figures with summary statistics in text — these are not extracted as formal outcomes. The 95% CI values in Table 2 are for Hedge's g effect sizes, not for mean differences; they are not entered into the between_group_effects CI fields. Note: the paper states TUG delta-of-change p=0.002 in the results text (Fig 3E) despite the two-way ANOVA intervention x time p=0.01 — the paired t-test p=0.002 is used as the primary between-group comparison. Sequence effects were significant for MRC, PCFS, MoCA, and Barthel Index, indicating potential carryover.

summary: This randomized crossover trial tested 8 weeks of eccentric cycling (ECC) against standard rehabilitation (elastic band strength exercises) in 20 adults who had been hospitalized in an ICU for COVID-19 and were recruited 6 months after discharge. The primary functional outcomes favored eccentric cycling: 6-minute walk distance improved by 140 meters with ECC versus 97 meters with standard rehabilitation (p=0.02 for between-group difference), and Timed Up and Go performance improved 16.5% with ECC versus 8.4% with standard rehabilitation (p=0.002). Both interventions were safe with no adverse events reported, but the two-week washout period between crossover arms was short and some carryover effects were detected, which limits confidence in the between-group comparisons.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT improved 139.5m (315 to 455m) with ECC vs 96.7m (296 to 393m) with STD REHAB, between-group delta p=0.02; TUG improved 16.5% vs 8.4%, p=0.002.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a 12-week multicomponent physiotherapy program (combining strength, resistance, balance, and gait training; twice weekly, 60 minutes per session) in 59 adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome in Brazil. The primary outcomes were functional mobility and quality of life, measured by the 6-minute walk test (6MWT), Berg balance scale, and SF-36 questionnaire. The intervention group improved on all three measures — walking distance increased by 54 meters, Berg score by 3.1 points, and SF-36 score by 6.3 points — but none of these improvements reached statistical significance. High dropout meant only 12 of 31 intervention participants completed all 24 sessions, substantially limiting the study's power.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT improved by 54.1 m in the intervention group vs. -7.3 m in controls, intergroup p=0.13; Berg scale p=0.87; SF-36 p=0.81. No statistically significant primary outcome.

summary: This randomized controlled pilot study tested online occupational therapy (OT) delivered either as live interactive sessions or prerecorded videos over 12 weeks in 158 adults with post-COVID syndrome (mean age 38 years, 86% female) who reported significant fatigue and cognitive impairment. The primary outcome was feasibility and acceptance: 83% of participants in the interactive OT group rated their experience as positive or very positive, compared to 48% in the video group (p=0.001). For secondary efficacy outcomes, participants receiving interactive OT showed significantly greater improvement in health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-3L mean difference +0.11 vs. control, 95% CI 0.05–0.17, p=0.003) and cognitive function (Neuro-QoL mean difference +3.95 vs. control, 95% CI 2.04–5.86, p<0.001) at 12 weeks; the study was unblinded and underpowered for confirmatory efficacy conclusions, and dropout was high (32.5% in the interactive group by week 12).

summary: A 6-week comprehensive rehabilitation program — combining aerobic walking, strength, balance, flexibility, and breathing exercises with patient education — was tested in a randomized controlled trial of 38 long COVID patients aged 25–60 in a low-resource outpatient setting in India. The primary outcomes were functional capacity (six-minute walk test), fatigue (Fatigue Severity Scale), and quality of life (EQ-5D-5L); the intervention group improved six-minute walk distance by 66 metres (well above the 30.5 m minimal clinically important difference), reduced FSS scores by 15 points, and improved EQ-5D VAS scores by 13.5 points, all with large effect sizes (Cohen's d ranging from 0.73 to 1.37). There were no dropouts and no adverse events reported, though the study was single-site with an unblinded outcome assessor.

trial_rating.result_basis: Six-minute walk distance increased by 66.27 ± 15.17 m in the intervention group vs. control (p < 0.0001, Cohen's d = 1.37); FSS decreased by 15.05 ± 5.88 points (p < 0.0001); EQ-5D VAS improved by 13.52 ± 5.46 points (p < 0.0001).

The paper reports almost all quantitative outcomes as percent change from baseline only, without providing absolute pre/post values or SDs — this severely limits effect size extraction. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested three types of balneotherapy (whirlpool baths, 'Biolong' medicated baths, and sodium chloride mineral baths), each combined with exercise therapy, in 160 adults with post-COVID syndrome (median age 50) at an outpatient rehabilitation centre in Moscow. All three active treatment groups showed significant reductions in symptoms such as fatigue, headache, and dyspnoea compared to an untreated control group, with the whirlpool bath group showing a 12.1% increase in forced vital capacity (p<0.01) and 9.6% increase in FEV1 (p<0.05), and the Biolong bath group showing a 26.2% reduction in cortisol (p<0.01) and an 8.3% improvement in 6-minute walk distance (p<0.05). All rehabilitation groups also showed significant improvements in depression, anxiety, and cognitive measures, while the control group showed no meaningful change. The control group was not actively treated rather than receiving a placebo, which limits causal interpretation of the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: Whirlpool bath group: FVC increased 12.1% (p<0.01), FEV1 increased 9.6% (p<0.05); Biolong group: 6-minute walk improved 8.3% (p<0.05), cortisol reduced 26.2% (p<0.01); control group showed no significant change on any measure.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested EEG alpha-rhythm neurofeedback (biofeedback) training versus sham training (identical exercises without feedback) in 20 adults with post-COVID syndrome experiencing anxiety, depression, fatigue, and cognitive complaints. Both groups showed significant reductions in trait anxiety, psychological stress, depression, and fatigue after 12–15 sessions. The neurofeedback group showed additional benefits over sham on general fatigue (U=19.5, p=0.019), immediate word recall (U=25.5, p=0.036), and verbal working memory (U=23.5, p=0.034), though the trial was very small (10 per arm) and lacked pre-registered power calculations, limiting confidence in these findings.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper is in Russian with English translation provided. Tables 1 and 2 present data as M±SD (mean±SD) with numerator=before, denominator=after treatment. Tables 3 and 4 present data as median [Q1; Q3]. The paper states treatment was 15 days (3 weeks). Follow-up was 6 months post-rehabilitation completion. The study study period was 4 months total. Within-group p-values are reported (Wilcoxon test), but between-group p-values are not explicitly stated for most outcomes - the p<0.049 threshold for spirometry and p<0.05 for HRV are noted in the abstract/text as within-group results for arm 1. No between-group statistical comparison results (p-values or effect sizes) are reported. All between_group_effects p_values are set to 0.05 as threshold only where paper indicates significant within-group change in arm 1 but not arm 2. The SDs in Table 1 and 2 may actually represent SE (labeled as M±m in Russian notation where 'm' typically denotes standard error), but are extracted as-is per table labeling. The stroke volume decreased after treatment in the intervention arm (from 53.73 to 48.73 mL) - this may reflect normalization of an initially elevated cardiac output driven by tachycardia. The Tiffenau index (FEV1/FVC ratio) mentioned in methods was not reported in tables.

summary: This open randomised trial tested interval hypo-hyperoxic training (IHHT) — alternating inhalation of low-oxygen (12–15% O2) and high-oxygen gas mixtures using the OXYTERRA device across 15 daily sessions — added to standard rehabilitation versus standard rehabilitation alone in 50 patients (mean age 61.7 years) with post-COVID syndrome persisting more than 3 months. The IHHT group showed statistically significant improvements in lung function (vital capacity, FVC, FEV1, and peak expiratory flow all p<0.05), blood oxygen content (SaO2 rose from 94.3% to 97.2%, p<0.01), heart rate (reduced from 82.8 to 75.7 bpm, p<0.01), and autonomic regulation (total heart rate variability power doubled from 623 to 1265, p<0.05), while the comparison group showed no significant changes in most measures. No adverse events were reported during the intervention or 6-month follow-up, and benefits were reported to persist for 3–6 months post-rehabilitation.

trial_rating.result_basis: FEV1 improved from median 72.2% to 79.1% predicted (p<0.05) in the IHHT group vs no significant change in controls (72.4% to 72.9%); SaO2 improved from 94.3% to 97.2% (p<0.01); heart rate fell from 82.8 to 75.7 bpm (p<0.01); total HRV power rose from 623 to 1265 (p<0.05).

summary: This open-label randomized trial tested sequential transcranial electrical stimulation — combining brain micropolarization (targeting the neocortex) followed immediately by diencephalic brain stimulation (targeting limbic structures) — in 142 adults aged 45–69 with chronic cerebrovascular disease (dyscirculatory encephalopathy) who were 3–4 months post-COVID-19. summary: This Russian randomized controlled trial tested whether adding VedaBiotic, a fifth-generation multisymbiotic (probiotic/prebiotic combination), to a standard physical rehabilitation program improved outcomes in 128 long COVID patients (mean age 57, all with prior bilateral viral pneumonia) at a inpatient rehabilitation centre. The primary finding was that the group receiving VedaBiotic (n=32) showed significantly greater reductions in symptoms and inflammatory markers compared to the rehabilitation-only group (n=64): fatigue resolved in 50% vs 81% still affected, cough resolved completely (0% vs 22% still affected, p=0.001), and D-dimer normalized only in the VedaBiotic group (dropping from 302 to 136 ng/mL, p=0.012, vs non-significant reduction in controls). No adverse events were reported, but the trial has notable limitations including unequal group sizes and open-label design with no placebo control.

trial_rating.result_basis: D-dimer normalized only in VedaBiotic group: 302 [279;440] to 136 [0;177] ng/mL, p=0.012; cough resolved in 100% of VedaBiotic group vs 78% control, p=0.001; fatigue persisted in 50% vs 81%, p=0.009.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper is in Russian with English translation provided. Table 1 reports baseline FVC as 87.90 ± 21.03 in the treatment group (SE noted in caption but values appear to be SD given magnitude); in the text body FVC is described as 88.8 ± 20.50 for treatment and 92.1 ± 17.55 for control — minor discrepancy between table and text for treatment arm FVC (87.90 vs 88.8); Table 1 values used as primary source. The trial is described as 'controlled comparative' but randomization methodology is never described, raising concern about whether true randomization occurred. Change-from-baseline results for FVC (Table 2) are described as 'relative changes' in %; it is unclear whether these represent absolute percentage-point changes in %predicted FVC or true relative (ratio) changes — verbatim values extracted. The mMRC categorical figure (Figure 3) contains proportion data that could not be fully extracted as the image was removed. HRCT change at day 75 favored control group (greater reduction in lesion volume), which is noted but not straightforwardly interpretable as a positive control finding. Between-group effect values for all outcomes are calculated as arm1_mean minus arm2_mean from reported per-arm change-from-baseline values; ANCOVA-adjusted p-values are verbatim from paper.

summary: The DISSOLVE trial (NCT04645368) tested bovhyaluronidase azoximer (Longidase), an enzyme-immunomodulator conjugate that breaks down hyaluronic acid, in 160 adult post-COVID patients with residual lung abnormalities, comparing 15 intramuscular injections over 75 days (n=81) against observation-only controls (n=79) across 13 Russian centres. The primary outcome—reduction in residual lung abnormalities on CT scan—was not significantly different between groups at 180 days (-13.5% vs -13.8%, p=0.327), though treated patients showed significantly greater improvements in forced vital capacity (9.0% vs 5.0% at day 75, p=0.046), oxygen saturation (1.07% vs 0.57% at day 75, p<0.001), 6-minute walk distance (27.8% vs 17.1% at day 75, p=0.049), and dyspnea scores (-0.84 vs -0.58 mMRC points at day 75, p=0.002). The trial was open-label with no blinding or placebo control, and was published with acknowledged support from the drug manufacturer (NPO Petrovax Pharm), limiting confidence in the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (CT residual lung abnormalities) showed no significant between-group difference at day 180: -13.47% vs -13.75%, p=0.327.

summary: This trial tested two Ayurvedic herbal formulations — Femicycle (containing Symplocos racemosa, Asparagus racemosus, Saraca indica, Glycyrrhiza glabra, and Curcuma longa) and Femimens (containing Vitex agnus castus, Withania somnifera, Zingiber officinale, and Trigonella foenum-graecum) — in 53 women aged 18–25 with menstrual disorders that developed within 3 months of moderate or severe COVID-19, compared against 51 women who received only standard rehabilitation (diet, vitamins, psychotherapy). After 6 months, women in the herbal treatment group had significantly fewer menstrual problems: infrequent menstruation affected 1.89% versus 31.37% in the comparison group (OR 0.042 [0.005–0.332]), dysmenorrhea persisted in 11.32% versus 35.29% (OR 0.234 [0.084–0.653]), and PMS in 7.55% versus 29.41% (OR 0.196 [0.060–0.640]). No side effects were reported in the herbal treatment group, though the study lacks blinding, the products appear to be commercially linked to the authors, and the formulations are classified as dietary supplements rather than medicines.

summary: This open-label randomised trial tested L-carnitine (50–75 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks, added to standard rehabilitation therapy) versus standard therapy alone in 90 children, adolescents, and young adults aged 10–25 with long COVID cardiovascular and autonomic symptoms. The primary finding was that 93.3% of the L-carnitine group were symptom-free and had normalised objective status at 6 weeks, compared with 66.7% in the standard-therapy group (p<0.05); ECG repolarisation abnormalities and rhythm disturbances present in 43.3% of patients at baseline resolved completely in the L-carnitine group but persisted in over 50% of controls, and heart rate variability indices (pNN50, rMSSD, SDNN) normalised in 86.7% vs 31.1% of controls (p=0.00). No adverse events requiring drug discontinuation were recorded. Key caveats are the open-label design (no blinding), absence of a pre-specified sample size calculation, and conduct at a single Russian centre, which limit confidence in the results.

trial_rating.result_basis: Symptom-free and normalised objective status at 6 weeks: 93.3% (L-carnitine) vs 66.7% (standard therapy), p<0.05; HRV normalisation: 86.7% vs 31.1%, p=0.00.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: All outcomes reported as median [IQR] due to non-normal distribution (Shapiro-Wilk confirmed). No means or SDs available for any outcome — only medians and IQRs extracted. Between-group effect sizes (mean differences, SMDs) cannot be calculated from medians/IQRs alone. The paper reports percentage reductions (MFI-20: 33.6% vs 14.4%; HAM-A: 55.16% vs 19.74%) but these are not extractable as standardized effect sizes. p<0.05 is reported for both within-group and between-group comparisons for significant outcomes but no exact p-values are given. The HAM-A baseline value for control group is listed as 25.17 in the table — this appears to be a median despite being a non-integer, possibly a rounding artifact or mean. Table 3 (HAM-A) contains 7 subscales; only Tension and Insomnia reached between-group significance in the Cefaly arm. The treatment duration was 10 sessions over approximately 24 days (3 sessions/week for ~3.4 weeks). Percent previously hospitalized: the paper reports 69.93% had inpatient COVID-19 treatment in Cefaly group and 63.27% in control group (from Table 1), but these refer to COVID-19 treatment setting, not ICU hospitalization specifically.

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested transcutaneous supraorbital nerve stimulation (t-SNS) using the Cefaly device — 10 sessions over approximately 3 weeks — added to standard rehabilitation, versus standard rehabilitation alone, in 60 adults aged 60–75 with post-COVID fatigue syndrome at least 6 months after infection. Adding Cefaly to rehabilitation reduced fatigue scores (MFI-20) by 33.6% from baseline versus 14.4% in controls, and reduced anxiety scores (HAM-A) by 55.2% versus 19.7% in controls, with both differences statistically significant. A notable caveat is that both groups still had high residual fatigue scores after treatment (median MFI-20: 42.5 in the Cefaly group vs 63 in controls), underscoring that long COVID fatigue persists substantially even with active treatment.

trial_rating.result_basis: MFI-20 total score reduced from median 70 to 42.5 in Cefaly group (33.6% reduction) vs 71.5 to 63 in controls (14.4% reduction), p<0.05 for both within-group and between-group comparisons; HAM-A total score reduced 55.2% vs 19.7%, p<0.05.
