Baseline imbalances exist: fatigue severity (experimental 2.65 vs control 2.31, p=0.0001) and sleep disorder severity (1.70 vs 1.00, p=0.04) differ significantly at baseline, complicating interpretation. 3. Table 3 p-values are reported as combined pairs (e.g., '0.0001/0.02') where the first value appears to refer to Day 1 between-group comparison and the second to Day 5; this notation is ambiguous and has been interpreted accordingly. 4. For FAS/chronic fatigue outcome (Table 4), only binary classification (above/below threshold of 22) is reported, not continuous FAS scores; no p-value is reported for the between-group comparison at Day 10 (text states 'no statistically significant differences'). 5. The symptom severity scale means in Table 3 are computed across all participants in each group (including those without the symptom, who presumably score 1), not only those with the symptom present. 6. Additional binary outcomes fully extracted from Table 2 but not individually listed as outcomes: shortness of breath, cough, dizziness, chest pain, loss of taste, perverted smell, perverted taste, sleep disorder, anxiety, hair loss, abdominal pain — all had complete n/% data at days 1/5/10. The most clinically important (loss of smell, headache, joint pain, fatigue) are included. 7. The paper notes that 100% of experimental group participants had fatigue and dizziness at all timepoints per Table 2 (binary), though the severity scores improved — this creates an apparent contradiction with Table 3 severity data.

summary: This open-label, non-randomised comparative study tested azoximer bromide (an immunomodulatory drug, 12 mg sublingual daily for 10 days) in 55 adults with post-COVID syndrome — defined as at least two persisting symptoms more than 12 weeks after confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection — compared to 35 untreated controls. By day 10, the treated group showed statistically significant reductions in the frequency and severity of joint and muscle pain (12.7% vs 45.7% still affected), headache (18.2% vs 51.4%), dizziness, impaired concentration, and smell loss, with fatigue severity significantly lower as early as day 5 (mean score 1.71 vs 2.23, p=0.02); no adverse events were reported. The study has substantial methodological limitations: it was open-label with no blinding, had no placebo control, groups were not fully matched at baseline (fatigue scores differed significantly on day 1), and the 10-day follow-up with no post-treatment observation period means durability of effects is unknown.

trial_rating.result_basis: Joint and muscle pain prevalence 12.7% (treated) vs 45.7% (control) at day 10 (p not explicitly stated but marked significant); fatigue severity 1.71 vs 2.23 at day 5 (p=0.02); headache prevalence 18.2% vs 51.4% at day 10 (p<0.05).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. The Schober test is measured in two parts: 'initial' measurement (always 15.00 ± 0.00 cm for both groups/timepoints, as this is the fixed starting mark) and 'final' measurement (the actual flexion endpoint). The 'difference' is the clinically meaningful value. The lateral inclination tests measure the distance from fingertip to floor and are reported similarly in three components: initial (standing upright finger-to-floor), final (in flexion finger-to-floor), and difference. No exact p-values were reported for between-group comparisons at post-intervention — only p<0.05 thresholds with footnote annotations in Table 3. The G2 pain increase was stated as statistically significant (intragroup p<0.05) in the results text. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week supervised exercise program (gym-based aerobic, resistance, balance, and flexibility training, twice weekly) versus home-guidance only in 39 adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome in Brazil. The exercise group showed a statistically significant reduction in pain (VAS score fell from 4.85 to 3.55, p<0.05) and improved functional capacity on the 30-second sit-to-stand test (repetitions increased from 10.45 to 12.45, p<0.05), while the control group's pain scores worsened. The exercise group also showed superior lumbar spine flexibility (Schöber test) compared to controls post-intervention, though muscle strength did not differ significantly between groups.

trial_rating.result_basis: Pain VAS decreased from 4.85 to 3.55 in the exercise group (p<0.05); sit-to-stand repetitions increased from 10.45 to 12.45 (p<0.05); however, baseline imbalance (exercise group had significantly higher pain and lower functional capacity at baseline) limits causal interpretation.

summary: This 30-day observational study tested ammonium glycyrrhizinate (AG, brand name Reglisam), an anti-inflammatory compound, added to standard post-COVID rehabilitation therapy (inhaled corticosteroids, vitamins, anticoagulants) in 40 children aged 7–18 who had COVID-19 with CT-confirmed lung damage. By day 30, children receiving AG had cough scores 2.5 times lower than controls (0.75 vs 1.85 points on a 6-point VAS, p=0.002), weakness scores 2.8 times lower (0.45 vs 1.25 points, p=0.005), and all AG-treated children normalised spirometry versus most controls who did not. Only 2 of 20 AG-treated children reported minor adverse effects (mild headache, dry skin) that did not require stopping treatment.

The primary outcome was physical conditioning measured by the six-minute walk test: the Pilates group increased total distance walked from 480m to 553m (p<0.001), while the control group showed no significant change. The Pilates group also improved chest wall expandability at axillary, mammary, and basal levels (all p<0.05) and reported lower perceived exertion 5 minutes post-test compared to controls (p=0.010); however, the trial was underpowered relative to its pre-specified sample size of 48 per group, and the two groups differed at baseline on education level and weight loss history.

trial_rating.result_basis: Six-minute walk test total distance increased from 480.05m to 552.70m in the Pilates group (p<0.001, IC95% -102.576 to -42.723), with no significant change in the control group (509.00m to 519.73m).

The post-treatment CRP value of 2.5±3.4 mg/L is reported as an average across both groups combined ('снижался в обеих группах и составил в среднем 2.5±3.4 мг/л'), so the same value was applied to both arms with result_source='inferred'. The table (Table 2) shows CRP 2.5±3.4 only in the 'after treatment' column for group 1 and the same value for group 2, consistent with the combined average. The p-value of <0.001 is applied to all outcomes from Table 2 row; individual between-group p-values are not separately reported per outcome. The study reports adverse events for both groups combined (26% of 103 = ~27 patients) mostly attributable to corticosteroids (skin dryness/acne, hyperglycemia), not broken down by arm. The 6-minute walk test is listed as an assessment tool in the methods but no quantitative results are reported in the results section. Quality of life is mentioned (75 points out of 100 at baseline) but no post-treatment value is given numerically per arm, so it was omitted as a separate outcome. The time_since_infection_months values were calculated from the reported days: Group 1: 46.7/30=1.56 months (SD: 13.1/30=0.44); Group 2: 48.7/30=1.62 months (SD: 14.1/30=0.47). Percent female calculated: Group 1 had 49 men out of 53 = 4 women = 7.5% female; Group 2 had 47 men out of 50 = 3 women = 6.0% female. The study was funded by pharmaceutical company Solofarma (manufacturer of Trecresan); authors received a grant. No trial registration number reported.

summary: This open-label randomized trial tested Trecresan (trekrezan), an adaptogen/immunomodulator, added to standard care (corticosteroids, anticoagulants, oxygen therapy) versus standard care alone in 103 hospitalized patients with ongoing symptomatic COVID-19 (symptoms lasting 4–12 weeks after moderate-to-severe infection). The primary outcome was fatigue severity on the MFI-20 scale: the Trecresan group improved from 44.5 to 31.9 points versus 41.2 to 36.7 in controls (p<0.001), and 85% of the Trecresan group reported subjective improvement versus 74% of controls. The study was industry-funded (by Solopharm, manufacturer of Trecresan), was not blinded, and used simple alternating-number allocation rather than true randomization, substantially limiting confidence in the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: MFI-20 fatigue score improved by 12.6 points in Trecresan group (44.5→31.9) vs 4.5 points in controls (41.2→36.7), p<0.001; however the between-group difference is modest and the open-label, industry-funded design inflates the reported effect.

summary: This pilot study tested enhanced external counterpulsation (EECP) — a non-invasive device that applies synchronized compression to the legs to improve circulation — in 30 patients with persistent lung damage and ventilatory impairment an average of 15 months after COVID-19 pneumonia. Patients in the EECP group (n=15) received 20 one-hour sessions over four weeks; controls (n=15) received standard care only. EECP produced significant improvements in total lung capacity (65% to 76%, p<0.001), vital capacity (57% to 73%, p=0.006), FEV1 (65% to 82%, p=0.041), and 6-minute walk distance (313 to 352 metres, p=0.007), while none of these measures improved in the control group; however, lung diffusing capacity (DLCO) did not improve in either group, indicating that underlying structural damage was not reversed. No adverse events were reported, but the study is limited by its very small sample size, non-randomised allocation, and use of the 6-minute walk test rather than cardiopulmonary exercise testing as the exercise measure.

trial_rating.result_basis: Total lung capacity improved from 65% to 76% predicted (p<0.001) and 6-minute walk distance increased by 39 metres from 313 to 352 m (p=0.007) in the EECP group, with no significant change in controls.

summary: This Russian non-randomized controlled trial tested ethylmethylhydroxypyridine malate (an antioxidant drug, 400 mg/day for 14-18 days) against exercise-only control in 24 adults with long COVID (diagnosed 4-12 weeks post-infection) who had fatigue, cognitive impairment, and breathlessness. The treated group showed greater improvement in fatigue (MFI-20 score improved 21% vs 13% in controls) and cognitive function (MoCA improved 20% vs 12.5% in controls), along with metabolomic markers suggesting reduced oxidative stress, including a significant rise in coenzyme Q10 (p=0.005). The study is very small (12 per group), non-randomized, and lacked blinding, making it impossible to rule out confounding; no adverse events were reported in the treatment group.

No serious adverse events were recorded in either group; however, the study was open-label, industry-supported (by the manufacturer of Chondroguard), and conducted without placebo control, substantially limiting confidence in the findings.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL DATA QUALITY ISSUES: (1) Table 5 (HRQOL Parameters Before and After Treatment) reports data ONLY for the insulin/intervention group — no placebo arm data is presented in this table, making between-group effect size calculation impossible for post-treatment comparisons. The p-values reported in Table 5 appear to be within-group pre-vs-post comparisons for the insulin arm only, not between-group comparisons. (2) TDI olfactory score data (primary endpoint from the prior publication, ref 12) is referenced but not reported quantitatively in this paper — only categorical baseline TDI distribution is shown in Table 3. Per-arm means and SDs for TDI are absent. (3) Figure 2 shows consequences of smell loss before and after 4 weeks for both groups, but numeric values are only in the figure (not extractable as text). (4) The n_randomized per arm is not reported — only 48 enrolled total and 20 per arm completed. It is unclear how the 8 dropouts were distributed between arms. (5) The paper does not report control group post-treatment outcomes in tabular form, severely limiting meta-analytic utility. (6) Perception of fire/smoke and emotional satisfaction outcomes shown in Figure 2 could not be extracted as values appear only in figure bars. Omitted figure-only outcomes: perception of fire/smoke, emotional satisfaction (pre/post for both groups from Figure 2).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested intranasal insulin fast-dissolving films (40 IU, three times per week) against placebo films in 40 post-COVID-19 adults with anosmia lasting more than two months. After four weeks, the insulin group showed statistically significant improvements across all key quality-of-life measures compared to baseline, including problems with eating (90% affected before treatment vs. 0% after), personal hygiene difficulties (85% vs. 0%), reduced work ability (75% vs. 0%), and cooking difficulties (50% vs. 0%), all at p<0.0001. The trial was small (20 patients per arm), single-centre, and conducted in Egypt, limiting generalisability; no safety concerns were reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: All primary HRQoL outcomes showed pre-to-post improvement in the insulin group significant at p<0.0001 (e.g. eating problems: 90% before vs. 0% after; work reduction: 75% vs. 0%); no between-group statistical comparison table was reported for post-treatment scores.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested Vardhamana Pippali Rasayana (an Ayurvedic preparation of long pepper, Piper longum, given in an escalating-then-tapering 29-day dose schedule, preceded by castor oil purgation) plus WHO rehabilitation exercises against placebo plus WHO rehabilitation alone in 104 adults with post-COVID syndrome (symptoms persisting beyond 3 months). The Pippali group showed substantially greater improvement across all primary outcomes: Post-COVID Functional Scale scores improved 86.7% vs 25.9% in the placebo group, the six-minute walk test improved 52.5% vs 20.9%, and physical health quality-of-life scores improved 64.5% vs 36.8%, all with p<0.01. The intervention appeared safe with no adverse laboratory signals, though the study was conducted at a single site in India using an Ayurvedic theoretical framework, limiting generalisability.

trial_rating.result_basis: Post-COVID Functional Scale: 86.7% improvement in Group A vs 25.9% in Group B (p<0.01); 6-minute walk test: 52.5% vs 20.9% improvement (p<0.01); physical health QoL: 64.5% vs 36.8% improvement (p<0.01).

summary: A 3-month multicomponent rehabilitation program — combining therapeutic exercises (including the Otago exercise programme), massage, occupational therapy, nutritional guidance, and patient education — was tested in 41 elderly people (aged 60–75) with post-COVID syndrome and sarcopenia, compared against 34 patients receiving standard COVID-19 rehabilitation protocol. The enhanced program produced significantly greater improvements across all primary outcomes: 6-minute walk distance increased by 23.1% (vs 11.5% in the standard group), dyspnoea score fell by 55.9% (vs 16.8%), FVC improved by 15.7% (vs 7.5%), and BMI rose by 10% (vs 3.7%), all p<0.05 versus both baseline and the standard protocol group. The study had no control arm receiving no rehabilitation, and blinding of assessors is not reported, limiting causal interpretation.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6-minute walk distance increased by 23.1% in the enhanced group vs 11.5% in the standard protocol group (390.51 vs 346.23 metres post-intervention, p<0.05); FVC improved 15.7% vs 7.5%; dyspnoea score reduced from 3.58 to 1.58 vs 3.39 to 2.82, p<0.05.

summary: This exploratory crossover trial (n=21 adults with long-COVID and self-reported cognitive complaints) tested whether 3 hours/day of portable supplemental oxygen via a concentrator (POC) for 2 weeks improved cognitive performance compared to standard of care. The primary outcome was the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) total score, which showed no overall difference between POC and control (adjusted mean difference -0.09, 95% CI -1.031 to 0.850); a post-hoc Period 1 analysis suggested a possible advantage for POC (difference 1.705, 95% CI 0.140 to 3.271), driven partly by attention and visuospatial subscores. Only 43% of participants met the pre-defined compliance threshold, and the study was explicitly descriptive with no formal hypothesis testing, making all findings preliminary.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary MoCA outcome: adjusted mean difference -0.090 (95% CI -1.031, 0.850), a null result; post-hoc Period 1 difference was 1.705 (95% CI 0.140, 3.271) but was unplanned and based on n=21 with 43% compliance.

summary: This small Ukrainian RCT tested the addition of Tivorel (levocarnitine 20mg + arginine hydrochloride 42mg, IV then oral) plus quercetin 240mg/day for one month to standard care in 40 hospitalized adults with type 2 diabetes and post-COVID syndrome. Compared to standard care alone, the combination treatment reduced fasting glucose 1.8-fold, lowered HbA1c by 28.2%, cut total cholesterol by 18.2%, raised HDL by 38.6%, and reduced CRP by 50.5% and D-dimer by 25.4%, with all primary group comparisons reaching statistical significance. The study has no blinding, no placebo control, very small arms (n=20 per group), and no pre-registration, making results hypothesis-generating only.

summary: This 3-month physical therapy program tested a geriatric-tailored rehabilitation protocol versus standard COVID-19 rehabilitation guidelines in 75 elderly patients (average age 68.3 years) with post-COVID syndrome and pre-existing sarcopenia. The tailored program, which included therapeutic exercises, functional training, the Otago exercise programme, massage, occupational therapy, nutritional guidance, and patient education, produced significantly greater improvements in dynamic balance and fall risk than standard care: Dynamic Gait Index improved 24.3% and Functional Gait Assessment improved 35.2% in the tailored group versus 9% and 16.4% in the standard care group, with the tailored group exiting the high fall-risk zone. Fear of falling (Fall Efficacy Scale) decreased 33.6% in the tailored group versus 23.1% in standard care, and balance confidence (ABC Scale) improved 44.8% versus 28.4%, though neither group reached the level of healthy controls.

trial_rating.result_basis: DGI improved 24.3% and FGA improved 35.2% in the tailored group vs 9% and 16.4% in standard care, all between-group differences p<0.05; Berg Balance Scale improved 43.3% vs 17.5%.

Patients were blinded to drug vs placebo, but physicians conducting testing were not described as blinded. Study is described as 'blind' without specifying who was blinded.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This study measures electrodermal impedance via EAV (electroacupuncture according to Voll), a device/method with no established clinical validity. The outcomes are not recognized clinical endpoints for long COVID. 2. The intervention is a single-session diagnostic procedure (medicament testing), not a therapeutic intervention in the conventional sense. The 'treatment' and 'follow-up' occur within the same diagnostic session (pre-test vs post-test during the same visit). Duration fields are null as this is a within-session measurement. 3. Table 3 (positive responders) and Table 4 (negative responders) each show per-arm n, pre-test AMV mean±SD, and post-test AMV mean±SD for different meridian subsets. The n values per meridian vary because not all patients had all meridians affected. 4. Table 3 mentions 12 meridians but the text also references 'Ma' (Stomach) as one that showed restoration; however no Ma row appears in the table as extracted — likely a discrepancy in the paper. 5. Figure 2 and Figure 3 contain pre-test EAV readings plotted with means and standard errors, but numerical values are only available in Table 3 and Table 4. 6. P-values are reported as thresholds (p<0.05, p<0.01, p<0.001) between groups and vs pre-test, not exact values. Between-group p-values were extracted as the threshold stated in table notes (*** = p<0.001 coded as 0.001, ** = p<0.01 coded as 0.01). 7. The duplicate entry for arm_id=2 in baseline_demographics.per_arm is an artifact — only one control arm exists. 8. Negative responder outcomes (Table 4): the He, Du, Pa/Mi(D), Hau, Ni, Bl meridians showed p<0.01 between groups; Al showed p<0.001 between groups; Ne showed p<0.01 between groups. These are all showing worsening (more negative drop) in the intervention arm compared to placebo for the negative-responder subgroup. 9. The study does not report conventional long COVID clinical outcomes (fatigue scores, QoL, functional status). This paper is of very limited relevance to a conventional long COVID meta-analysis.

summary: This study tested electroacupuncture according to Voll (EAV) diagnosis combined with medicament testing (MT) — placing an RNA polymerase nosode, ribavirin tablets, and dexamethasone pills into a device honeycomb while measuring skin electrical impedance at acupuncture points — in 99 long COVID patients aged 16–50 in Uzbekistan. In the 50-patient treatment group, MT with these three substances produced statistically significant normalization of electrodermal activity readings at 12 meridian points compared to pre-test values and to the placebo control group (p<0.001 for key meridians including nervous degeneration and circulation). A critical caveat is that EAV and medicament testing have no established physiological basis and are not validated diagnostic or therapeutic tools; the outcome measure is device readings of skin electrical impedance, not any clinical symptom or functional endpoint, making the clinical relevance of these findings uninterpretable.

trial_rating.result_basis: Post-MT AMV on nervous degeneration meridian: main group 5.65 ± 1.14 vs pre-test -3.87 ± 1.66 (p<0.001 vs control), but this measures device impedance readings, not a validated clinical outcome; no clinical symptom data were analyzed as a primary endpoint.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper was submitted as a CONSORT-EHEALTH checklist form, not as the full manuscript. As a result, almost all quantitative data (per-arm means, SDs, sample sizes per arm, exact timepoint definitions in weeks) are missing — only inferential statistics (beta coefficients, t-values, p-values from HLMs) are quoted verbatim from the manuscript. Per-arm n_randomized breakdown is not reported in this form. Timepoints T1-T5 are referenced but their timing in weeks is not specified. The intervention duration of 6 weeks is stated. Between-group comparisons for Hypothesis 1 combined IG+ACG vs CompG; for Hypothesis 2 compared IG vs ACG with no significant group differences found. For work ability, beta=0.78 (t271=2.73, p=0.01) for IG+ACG vs CompG; for social participation beta=0.27 (t277=2.89, p=0.004) for IG+ACG vs CompG. For symptom severity vs CompG: T1-T2 interaction beta=0.14 (t549=4.31, p<0.001); T2-T4 interaction beta=0.14 (t549=4.57, p<0.001). For IG vs ACG (Hypothesis 2): no significant group differences in any outcome. Hypothesis 3 regression: symptom reduction predicted social participation (beta=-0.34, t111=-2.11, p=0.04, R2=0.24) but not work ability (beta=-0.18, t111=-1.92, p=0.06, R2=0.32). Data for figures referenced but not extractable from this form. Total N=1020 patients recruited. | Pass3 agent: PDF is CONSORT checklist only (not main paper). HLM betas reported, no CIs.

summary: This German RCT (the ASAP project) tested a 6-week digital rehabilitation program combined with personal coaching ('personal pilots') for 1,020 adults with long COVID (post-acute COVID-19 syndrome, PACS) in Bavaria. Patients were randomised to either a tailored intervention group (IG, receiving clinic-based diagnostic assessment plus personalised digital exercises averaging 50 minutes/day) or an active control group (ACG, receiving symptom-targeted digital exercises plus personal pilot support but no formal assessment), with a non-randomised usual-care comparison group (CompG) included via propensity score matching. Both the IG and ACG showed significantly greater symptom reduction and higher work ability and social participation compared to the untreated CompG, but there was no significant difference in any outcome between the IG and ACG, meaning the additional diagnostic assessment and tailoring did not produce greater benefit than the simpler intervention. No harms were reported in any group.

trial_rating.result_basis: Symptom severity reduction was significantly greater in IG+ACG vs CompG (group×time interaction β=0.14, t549=4.57, p<0.001); work ability was higher in treatment groups vs CompG (β=0.78, t271=2.73, p=0.01); but IG vs ACG showed no significant difference on any primary outcome.

Table 1 note uses '* , **' notation but the footnote appears duplicated (both asterisks refer to p<0.05 comparisons — one vs baseline and one vs group 1). summary: This randomized trial tested a 5-strain Bacillus probiotic (one dose daily for 4 weeks) added to standard care versus standard care alone in 42 adults with post-COVID-19 irritable bowel syndrome diagnosed by Rome IV criteria. After 4 weeks, patients receiving the probiotic had significantly greater reductions in abdominal pain (1.4 vs 5.1 on a 10-point scale), bloating (2.1 vs 5.1), and bowel motility disturbance (1.8 vs 5.2), and 47.6% were full responders versus 4.8% in the control group; these improvements persisted one month after stopping treatment. The probiotic was well tolerated with no adverse effects reported in any patient.

trial_rating.result_basis: At 4 weeks, full responders: 47.6% probiotic vs 4.8% control; abdominal pain score 1.4 vs 5.1; need for antispasmodics 0.8 vs 6.2 days/week (all p<0.05).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether adding Kolofort (a drug containing processed antibodies to S100 protein, TNF-alpha, and histamine) to standard omeprazole therapy (80 mg/day) improved functional dyspepsia symptoms in 42 post-COVID-19 outpatients aged 26–47. By day 28, the combination group had significantly lower epigastric pain scores on a 10-point VAS compared to omeprazole alone (p<0.01), and showed faster resolution of other dyspeptic symptoms (heaviness, early satiety, nausea) by day 5 (p<0.02); however, full symptom resolution at day 28 reached ~90% in both groups with no statistically significant difference between them (p=0.06). The combination group also showed greater quality-of-life improvements on SF-36 pain, general health, role-emotional, and mental health subscales. The study was funded by the drug manufacturer (Materia Medica), which is a significant conflict of interest.

trial_rating.result_basis: Epigastric pain VAS significantly lower in combination group at day 28 (p<0.01), but complete dyspepsia resolution was ~90% in both groups with no significant difference (p=0.06); baseline VAS scores also differed significantly between groups (p=0.001), raising concerns about randomization balance.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. The paper reports percent improvements (e.g., 48.17% for PImax, 51.57% for FSS reduction, 17.65% for control group FSS) but the FSS percentage reduction figures stated in the Discussion (51.57% study, 17.65% control) appear to be transposed from the lactate percentage figures — the actual FSS change is from 43.36 to 28.68 (study, ~33.8% reduction) and 42.47 to 39.77 (control, ~6.4% reduction). The lactate reductions are 51.57% and 17.65% respectively. This internal inconsistency was noted but values extracted are the actual stated means and SDs. 2. The SD for the control group PImax change_from_baseline is reported as 33.12 in Table II (Δ column), which appears unusually large relative to the pre/post SDs of 17.52 and 5.86; this may be an error in the paper but has been extracted verbatim. 3. Between-group effect p-values are reported as p<0.001 throughout; exact p-values are not given for most outcomes. 4. No 95% CIs for between-group effects were reported. 5. Partial eta-squared values reported in text for ANOVA interactions but not included as separate effect measures. 6. Some figure data (error bar charts for MMRC and FSS) provide additional context but numeric values were extractable from the text. 7. The paper notes the control group SD for PImax at baseline in Table II as '7.52' but Table I reports '17.52' — Table I value used as it is consistent with the range (53-108 cmH2O) and appears to be a typo in Table II.

summary: This 6-week randomized controlled trial tested whether adding manual diaphragm release (18 physiotherapist-delivered sessions) to inspiratory muscle training via a POWERbreath device was more effective than inspiratory muscle training alone in 52 men with post-COVID-19 syndrome who had hypertension and mild-to-moderate lung fibrosis. The primary outcome, maximum inspiratory pressure (a measure of breathing muscle strength), increased by 48.2% in the combined treatment group (from 82.0 to 121.5 cmH2O) compared with a non-significant 4.4% increase in the training-only group. Secondary outcomes also favored the combined group: systolic blood pressure fell by 16.7% vs 2.5%, dyspnea scores improved by 48.9% vs 12.8%, fatigue scores fell by 51.6% vs 17.7%, and 6-minute walk distance increased by 13.5% vs 3.9%; the study was limited to men only and did not include objective measures of diaphragm function such as ultrasound.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome PImax increased 48.17% in the combined group (82.0 to 121.5 cmH2O) vs non-significant 4.35% in the control group; between-group interaction p<0.001, partial eta-squared=0.330.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether incentive spirometry (IS) or diaphragmatic breathing (DB) exercises added to standard care could improve breathlessness in 60 long COVID patients with confirmed diaphragmatic dysfunction following mild-to-moderate acute COVID-19. After 8 weeks, 75% of the IS group and 55% of the DB group showed improvement on the mMRC dyspnoea scale, compared with only 15% in the standard care group; both active interventions also significantly improved 6-minute walk distance and oxygen saturation, while standard care alone produced no significant change in any outcome. IS outperformed DB on several measures including 6-minute walk distance (397 m vs 358 m at follow-up). The trial was open-label and small (20 patients per arm), limiting confidence in the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: mMRC dyspnoea scale improved from 1.9 to 0.7 in the IS group and 1.6 to 0.9 in the DB group (both p<0.001), versus no significant change in standard care; 75% vs 55% vs 15% responder rates across groups.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 12 weeks of supervised endurance training versus concurrent (combined resistance and endurance) training versus no exercise in 42 non-hospitalized adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome (symptoms persisting over 12 weeks, no post-exertional malaise). Both exercise groups showed significant improvements in peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) compared to controls: endurance training gained +3.9 ml/min/kg and concurrent training gained +3.2 ml/min/kg, with a significant time-by-group interaction (partial eta² = 0.267). Fatigue severity scores fell significantly in both exercise groups (Hedges' g = 0.63 and 0.82) but not in controls, though health-related quality of life improved across all three groups including the non-exercising control; two participants withdrew due to symptom worsening, and the overall dropout rate was 36%, limiting generalizability.

trial_rating.result_basis: VO2peak time*group interaction p=0.002, partial eta²=0.267; endurance group +3.9 ml/min/kg (g=1.75), concurrent group +3.2 ml/min/kg (g=1.02), control group non-significant trend +0.9 ml/min/kg (p=0.054).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether adding systemic ozone therapy (10 intravenous infusions of ozonized saline over 30 days) to standard drug therapy improved outcomes in 140 adults aged 18–45 with post-COVID asthenic syndrome—a condition marked by chronic fatigue, cognitive impairment, sleep disturbance, and anxiety. Patients who received ozone therapy alongside the succinic acid-based drug showed substantially greater reductions in inflammatory markers (TNF-α down 39%, IL-1β down 33%, IL-6 down 36% versus the drug-only group) and larger improvements across all symptom scales: fatigue scores fell 36.7% more, insomnia scores 50.5% more, and anxiety scores 45.8% more than in the comparison group, with 94.2% of ozone-treated patients rated as disease-free at 30 days versus 62.9% in the control group. No adverse events were reported in either group, though the study was conducted at a single centre in Crimea without blinding, which limits how broadly the findings can be applied.

trial_rating.result_basis: 94.2% of ozone therapy patients rated CGI-S 'no disease' vs 62.9% controls (p=0.001); insomnia score (ISI) 50.5% lower in ozone group (p<0.001); fatigue score (MFI-20) 36.7% lower (p=0.001).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a dynamic inversion table — a motorized platform that repeatedly tilts patients at low frequencies to alter gravitational pressure on blood vessels — against standard rehabilitation in 70 adults with long COVID (persistent symptoms for over 12 weeks post-infection). The treatment group (n=35) completed 10 daily 30-minute sessions on the device; the control group (n=35) followed standard rehabilitation guidelines. The primary outcome, exercise work capacity during cardiorespiratory stress testing, increased by 13.31 W in the treatment group versus a decline of 4.60 W in controls (p<0.001). Post-occlusive microvascular blood flow, a marker of endothelial function, rose by 80.42% in the treatment group while declining slightly in controls; no adverse events were reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome: work capacity +13.31 W (treatment) vs -4.60 W (control), difference 17.91 W, 95% CI [12.03; 23.8], p<0.001. Groups differed significantly at baseline on several secondary measures, with the treatment group starting worse.

summary: This 12-week quasi-experimental study tested a combined Progressive Muscle Relaxation Technique (PMRT) and Spinal Muscle Training (SMT) protocol, delivered via telerehabilitation, against standard neurosurgical care (SNC) in 60 male manual labourers aged 40-50 in Karnataka, India with long COVID-associated paraspinal back pain. The primary outcomes were serum IL-17 (an inflammation marker) and functional independence (Katz ADL score): the PMRT+SMT group reduced IL-17 from 31.13 to 18.96 pg/mL versus 31.05 to 28.89 pg/mL in the SNC group (p<0.001, Cohen's d=3.84), and improved ADL scores from 2.93 to 5.03 versus 2.50 to 3.53 in controls (p<0.001, Cohen's d=2.33). Key caveats are the non-randomised design with allocation by clinic scheduling slot, an all-male sample, small N of 30 per arm, and no long-term follow-up, all of which limit confidence in the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: IL-17 reduced by 12.17 pg/mL in the experimental group vs 2.16 pg/mL in controls (between-group p<0.001, Cohen's d=3.84); ADL improved by 2.10 points vs 1.03 points (between-group p<0.001, Cohen's d=2.33).

summary: This trial compared two airway clearance devices — a high-frequency chest wall oscillation (HFCWO) vest and a handheld lung flute — in 60 men aged 40–60 with COPD who had recently recovered from COVID-19. Both devices were used three times per week for three weeks alongside standard medications. Both treatments significantly improved lung function, exercise capacity, and symptom scores; HFCWO produced greater gains in FEV1 (43.2% vs 36.7% increase), FEV1/FVC ratio (16.2% vs 8.4%), and six-minute walk distance (25.5% vs 17.3%), while the lung flute produced slightly larger improvements in FVC and small airway flow (FEF25-75%). The trial was limited to men only, lacked a control group receiving neither intervention, and had no long-term follow-up beyond three weeks.

trial_rating.result_basis: FEV1 improved by 43.2% in the HFCWO group vs 36.7% in the lung flute group (both p<0.05 within groups); 6MWD improved by 25.5% vs 17.3%; between-group differences for most outcomes were not statistically significant (e.g. FEV1 post-treatment p=0.143), meaning HFCWO superiority is based on percent-change comparisons rather than statistically confirmed between-group differences.

summary: Brainmax (a succinic acid complex with trimethylhydrazinium, a neuroprotective antioxidant) was tested against placebo in 160 adults with post-COVID fatigue syndrome, enrolled 3–12 months after confirmed COVID-19 infection. Over 41 days of sequential parenteral then oral therapy, Brainmax produced a median 19.5-point reduction in fatigue on the MFI-20 scale compared to 3 points in the placebo group (p<0.001), along with significant improvements in sleep quality, fatigue, dizziness, and anxiety scores. Adverse events were mild and transient, with no serious adverse events recorded in either group; however, the drug is approved and marketed only in Russia, and the study was funded by the manufacturer.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome: MFI-20 median change -19.5 [-27; -11] points in Brainmax group vs -3 [-7; 1] points in placebo group, p<0.001.

summary: This open-label controlled trial tested combined inhalations of nitric oxide (60 ppm) and molecular hydrogen (<4%) for 90 minutes daily over 10 days in 34 adults with long COVID respiratory symptoms, enrolled on average 22 months after confirmed COVID-19 infection. Compared to an untreated control group (n=17 per arm), the treatment group showed significant reductions in dyspnea, cough, fatigue, and palpitations (p<0.005), a 46.7-metre improvement in 6-minute walk distance (p=0.01), better quality of life on SF-36 (p=0.006), and reduced oxidative damage markers (FORT score fell from 595 to 391.5 units, p=0.001). summary: This double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial tested EchA Marine, a dietary supplement derived from sea urchin eggs and rich in Echinochrome A, in 46 long COVID patients (18–60 years) across three Argentine hospitals over 90 days. The primary outcome was health-related quality of life measured by the EQ-5D-3L questionnaire: after three months, the treatment group showed statistically significant improvements in mobility (p=0.013) and pain/discomfort (p=0.005), as well as in overall health perception by VAS (p=0.022) and time trade-off scores (p=0.003), while the placebo group showed no improvement in these dimensions. summary: A 63-day remote medical and psychological rehabilitation program—incorporating cognitive-behavioural therapy, mindfulness, art therapy, and body-oriented practices—was tested in 240 Ukrainian adults with anxiety and depressive post-COVID syndrome during the ongoing war. At 3-month follow-up, 92.6% of the treatment group (n=122) had minimal anxiety on the GAD-7 versus 51.7% with severe anxiety in the comparison group, and 84.3% of the treatment group had minimal depression on the PHQ-9 versus 37.3% with severe depression in controls (all p<0.001). No participants in the treatment group had clinically significant PTSD symptoms at follow-up, while the comparison group's PTSD case count grew from 44 to 47; 73.8% of the treatment group reached the highest quality-of-life tier versus 6.8% in controls. summary: A 10-session online medical and psychological rehabilitation program — combining psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring, mindfulness, body-oriented therapy, and narrative techniques — was tested in 240 Ukrainian adults with anxiety and depressive post-COVID syndrome (symptoms persisting 12+ weeks after recovery) in a parallel randomised controlled trial conducted between October 2022 and December 2023. summary: This randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested whether hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) — at four different combinations of oxygen concentration and chamber pressure — improved symptoms and cognitive function in 101 long COVID patients with an average illness duration of about 21 months. After 10 treatment sessions, there were no statistically significant differences between any of the four groups on any primary outcome, including quality of life scores, a 6-minute walking test, or five neurocognitive tests. Some patients in every group, including the placebo group breathing room air at normal pressure, reported subjective improvement, and most had returned to their pre-study condition by three-month follow-up, pointing to a placebo effect as the likely explanation for positive findings in earlier uncontrolled studies.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether adding systemic ozone therapy (10 daily intravenous infusions of ozonated saline) to standard pharmacological treatment (Brainmax, a meldonium/antioxidant combination) improved symptoms in 140 adults aged 18–45 with post-COVID asthenic syndrome. The primary finding was that patients receiving adjunctive ozone therapy showed substantially greater improvements across all outcomes: fatigue scores (MFI-20) fell 74.7% vs 60.3% in controls, insomnia scores (ISI) fell 81.3% vs 42.9%, anxiety scores (HAM-A) fell 72.8% vs 48.3%, and cognitive scores (MoCA) improved 17.1% vs 4.9%, with 94.2% of ozone-treated patients rated symptom-free vs 62.9% in the control group. A notable caveat is that both groups received an active drug rather than placebo, making it impossible to isolate ozone therapy's effect from pharmacotherapy alone, and the study was conducted at a single site in Crimea with no reported pre-registration.

The Bonferroni post-hoc table (Table 5) reports pre-test to post-test mean differences with SE (Resilience: 35.25±2.14; Psychological distress: 40.77±1.57) but these appear to be pooled/overall contrasts rather than per-arm values and are not easily attributable to a single arm, so they are not included as arm_results. The paper describes 8 sessions but does not specify session frequency (assumed weekly based on 8-week MBCT protocol). The F-statistics and eta-squared from the mixed ANOVA (Table 4) are reported in the between_group_effects p_values; no CI or effect size with CI was provided for between-group comparisons.

summary: This quasi-experimental study tested 8 weekly sessions of online individual mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) in 30 adults aged 25-55 who had been discharged from hospital after COVID-19 in Tehran, Iran, and who had moderate symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress (DASS-21 score ≥39) at enrolment. MBCT produced large improvements in both primary outcomes: resilience scores rose from 26.5 to 72.7 (vs. 25.7 to 30.1 in controls), and psychological distress scores fell from 39.0 to 5.7 (vs. 47.3 to 46.5 in controls), with both between-group differences highly significant (p=0.0001) and effect sizes above η²=0.87. These gains were maintained at a 2-month follow-up. Key caveats are the very small sample (15 per arm), lack of randomisation (matching-based allocation), self-report outcomes only, and no active control condition, all of which substantially limit causal inference.

trial_rating.result_basis: Resilience post-test: MBCT group 72.67±6.33 vs. control 30.13±9.06 (F=45.21, p=0.0001, η²=0.89); psychological distress post-test: MBCT 5.73±2.96 vs. control 46.47±5.75 (F=154.54, p=0.0001, η²=0.94).

summary: This Russian controlled trial tested whether adding robotics-based mechanotherapy (biofeedback leg-press training on the Con-Trex system), interactive balance training (Stabilan 01-2 platform), and virtual reality exercise (Nirvana system) — 10 sessions each — to standard rehabilitation improved physical function in 120 long COVID patients aged 40–70 seen 1–6 months after acute infection. Compared to standard care alone (exercise therapy, laser therapy, speleotherapy, and chest massage), the combined technology group achieved significantly greater walking speed (1.6 vs 1.4 m/s, p=0.013), stride length (0.70 vs 0.60 m, p=0.023), knee extensor strength in both legs (right: 1345.5 vs 1241 N, p=0.008; left: 1471.5 vs 1257 N, p=0.013), and multiple balance measures on stabilometry. No safety concerns were reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Walking speed increased from 1.0 to 1.6 m/s in the intervention group vs 1.1 to 1.4 m/s in controls (p=0.013 between groups); left leg extensor strength 1471.5 N vs 1257 N (p=0.013).

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial tested 8 weeks of creatine monohydrate (8 g/day), creatine plus glucose (8 g + 3 g/day), or glucose-only placebo in 15 adults with long COVID (5 per arm). Both creatine groups raised brain creatine levels significantly at multiple locations versus placebo, with the creatine-glucose combination showing significant within-group reductions in five symptoms — body aches, breathing difficulties, concentration difficulties, headache, and general malaise — with large effect sizes for body aches (d=1.33), headache (d=1.12), and concentration difficulties (d=0.80). However, the between-group interaction tests for symptom outcomes were all non-significant (all p>0.05), meaning the trial did not formally demonstrate superiority over placebo for patient-reported outcomes; the study is severely underpowered with only 5 participants per arm, and two lead authors have financial conflicts of interest with the creatine manufacturer (AlzChem) that also funded the study.

trial_rating.result_basis: Two-way ANOVA interaction effects for all symptom outcomes were non-significant (p>0.05); within-group reductions in the creatine-glucose arm reached significance (e.g. headache p≤0.05, d=1.12) but no between-group superiority over placebo was established, with only n=5 per arm.

The paper also appears to include a second article (liver cirrhosis) appended in the same document — only the long COVID paper was extracted. 6. Between-group p-value for GSRS total at day 28 (p<0.0001) was stated as comparing group 1 vs group 2 at day 28. The within-group p-values for group 1 GSRS subscales are: diarrhea p<0.0001, dyspepsia p<0.0001, abdominal pain p<0.0170. The between-group comparison for asthenia at day 28 is p=0.0080 (verbatim).

summary: A Russian randomized controlled trial tested Baktiminal, a metabiotic supplement containing metabolites of Bacillus subtilis and fructooligosaccharides (one capsule twice daily for 28 days), against no additional treatment in 40 outpatients with post-COVID gastrointestinal symptoms and fatigue. The treated group showed a statistically significant 44% reduction in total gastrointestinal symptom scores (from 45.2 to 25.5 points on the GSRS scale, p<0.0001), with significant improvements in diarrhea, dyspepsia, and abdominal pain, while the control group improved by only 8%. Fatigue scores also improved significantly in the treated group (51.5 to 43.3 points, p<0.05), and gut microbiome analysis in a subset of 10 treated patients showed restoration of Lactobacillus spp. and Akkermansia muciniphila, which was completely absent at baseline in all post-COVID patients tested. No adverse events were reported, though the small sample size, single-centre design, lack of blinding, and use of an unregistered dietary supplement substantially limit the reliability of these findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: Total GSRS score decreased from 45.2 to 25.5 points (44% reduction) in the treated group vs 42.2 to 38.9 (8% reduction) in controls, between-group difference p<0.0001.

Partial eta squared is reported as effect size for ANOVA outcomes. The linear regression between BDNF change and flanker change: F=37.79, R2_adj=0.825, p_adj=0.003. Per-arm n is inferred as 10 each (20 completers, 1:1 randomization, 2 lost to follow-up from 22). Randomization arm sizes for those lost to follow-up not specified. Outcomes not quantitatively extractable due to data only in figures: Dimension Change Card Sorting, List Sorting Working Memory, Oral Reading Recognition, Picture Vocabulary, Pattern Comparison, Picture Sequence Memory, GDNF, IL6, IL10, TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma, heart rate variability. summary: This open-label pilot study tested 40 Hz vibratory and auditory treatment (VAT) — simultaneous vibrotactile and sound stimulation delivered via a portable device — in 20 adults with long COVID-associated cognitive impairment. Over 4 weeks of daily home use (20 sessions), the treatment group showed a statistically significant improvement in the Flanker test of selective attention and response inhibition compared to controls (group-by-session interaction F(1,1)=11.69, p=0.014, partial eta squared=0.41), and plasma BDNF levels increased significantly in the treatment group, with BDNF change strongly correlated with Flanker score change (R²=0.825). The study is unblinded with no sham control, a conflict of interest (one author receives royalties from the device manufacturer), and only 10 participants per arm, so results must be interpreted with caution.

trial_rating.result_basis: Flanker test group-by-session interaction F(1,1)=11.69, p_adjusted=0.014, partial eta squared=0.41; 80% of treatment group improved vs 20% of controls.

summary: The Metcovid trial tested whether a 5-day course of intravenous methylprednisolone (0.5 mg/kg twice daily) given during acute COVID-19 hospitalization affected lung function 120 days later in adult patients with oxygen saturation ≤94% or requiring ventilation. Among 118 survivors who completed pulmonary function testing, those who received methylprednisolone had higher forced vital capacity (FVC: 3.2 L vs. 2.9 L, p=0.01), which remained significant after adjusting for mechanical ventilation use and baseline inflammation levels; forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) was also higher in the methylprednisolone group in univariate analysis (2.6 L vs. 2.3 L, p=0.01) but not after adjustment. A key caveat is that this was an exploratory secondary analysis of a trial not powered for lung function outcomes, the methylprednisolone group had higher baseline inflammation (IL-6) and more severe initial disease, and only 118 of 246 eligible survivors completed adequate testing, limiting the reliability of the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: FVC 3.2 L (MP) vs. 2.9 L (placebo), p=0.01 in multivariate analysis; Cohen's d=0.37 (moderate effect size); FEV1 significant only in univariate analysis (p=0.01), not multivariate (p=0.12).

summary: This multicenter prospective quasi-experimental study (TUN-EndCOV) tested sulodexide (250 LSU twice daily for 21 days) against no treatment in 290 long COVID patients from Tunisia who had confirmed endothelial dysfunction at baseline. Sulodexide produced significantly higher rates of chest pain resolution (83.7% vs. 43.6%, p<0.001) and palpitations resolution (85.2% vs. 52.9%, p=0.009), along with greater improvement in endothelial function (median delta-EQI 0.66 vs. 0.18, p<0.001). The main caveat is that this was a non-randomized, non-blinded quasi-experimental design with no placebo control, which substantially limits causal inference despite the large observed effects.

trial_rating.result_basis: Chest pain recovery 83.7% vs. 43.6% (p<0.001); palpitations recovery 85.2% vs. 52.9% (p=0.009); median delta-EQI 0.66 vs. 0.18 (p<0.001).

summary: This small randomised controlled trial tested hydroxychloroquine (HCQ, 200 mg twice daily) and clarithromycin (500 mg twice daily), each given for four weeks, versus placebo in 34 adults aged 20–50 who still had respiratory symptoms at least two weeks after hospital discharge for COVID-19. summary: This trial tested 16–18 days of mountain spa rehabilitation, with or without ubiquinol (coenzyme Q10, 2×100 mg/day), in 36 long COVID patients who had been hospitalised with severe COVID-19 and still had persistent symptoms 3–7 months later. The primary biological finding was that platelet mitochondrial Complex I-linked oxidative phosphorylation capacity was markedly reduced in patients at baseline (approximately 30–46% below healthy controls) and recovered significantly only in the group receiving ubiquinol: CI-linked OXPHOS increased by 25% after rehabilitation plus supplementation (p=0.043) and by 50% after an additional 12–14 days of home supplementation, compared to a non-significant 12% increase with rehabilitation alone. Clinically, 62.8% of symptoms resolved in the ubiquinol group versus 51.8% in the rehabilitation-only group, and lung function improved in both groups; the study was small (14 and 22 patients per arm) and unblinded, with ubiquinol donated by the manufacturer.

trial_rating.result_basis: CI-linked OXPHOS capacity increased 25% in MRQ2 vs MRQ1 (p=0.043) and 50% in MRQ3 vs MRQ1 (p=0.072); rehabilitation-only group showed only 12% increase (ns).

summary: This randomized, double-blind, controlled trial tested oral oxaloacetate (OAA) at 2,000 mg/day for 42 days against a rice flour placebo in 69 adults with long COVID who had moderate-to-severe fatigue and post-exertional malaise. The primary outcome—fatigue reduction on the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire—was not met, with a negligible between-group effect size (Cohen's d = -0.093, p = 0.71). Secondary measures showed OAA-treated participants had greater early improvement in fatigue and total symptom burden on the DSQ-SF at day 21, and significantly better performance on objective cognitive tests (total cognitive efficiency +10.7% vs. -0.04%, p = 0.007 at day 42). The trial was funded by Terra Biological LLC, whose officer co-authored the paper and holds a commercial interest in OAA—a conflict of interest that warrants scrutiny of the positive secondary findings.

summary: A supervised 8-week mixed exercise program combining cardiovascular and resistance training was tested in 15 adults with post-COVID condition (PCC), compared to 10 PCC patients receiving usual care, at Université de Sherbrooke. The primary physical capacity outcomes showed significant improvements in the exercise group: sit-to-stand test improved 31% vs 11% in controls (p=0.043) and bicep curl improved 15% vs 4% (p=0.040), with daily physical activity levels also increasing significantly (p=0.007). Importantly, the program did not worsen fatigue or trigger post-exertional malaise, and plasma proteomics showed a downward trend in inflammatory markers S100A8 and CST3 following exercise; however, the study was non-randomized with a small sample size and excluded PCC patients who had previously experienced post-exertional malaise, limiting generalizability.

trial_rating.result_basis: Sit-to-stand improved 31% vs 11% (p=0.043); bicep curl improved 15% vs 4% (p=0.040); physical activity scale interaction effect p=0.007.

summary: A randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind crossover study tested a single oral dose of ketone ester (395 mg/kg) against placebo in 12 adults previously hospitalized for COVID-19 (average 18 months post-hospitalization), measuring cardiac function by echocardiography. The primary outcome, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), did not improve with ketone esters (mean difference -0.7%, 95% CI -4.0 to 2.6%, p=0.66). A secondary measure of heart muscle contractility, global longitudinal strain (GLS), did improve significantly by 1.9 percentage points (95% CI 0.1 to 3.6%, p=0.04), indicating a modest acute benefit in myocardial function. The study was very small (n=12) and the positive GLS result should be interpreted cautiously given the null primary outcome and limited statistical power.

summary: This non-randomized clinical trial tested an 8-week multi-professional program (concurrent exercise training, nutritional education, and psychoeducation) in 35 overweight COVID-19 survivors and non-COVID controls in Brazil. Secondary outcomes showed meaningful improvements in inflammatory and metabolic markers: C-reactive protein fell significantly in all groups (e.g., moderate COVID group: −68.4%, p=0.003), triglycerides fell across all groups (p<0.05), and albumin rose in the moderate and severe COVID groups (p=0.0005 and p=0.005 respectively); physical fitness gains were modest and limited mainly to the moderate COVID group.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-group crossover study (n=20) where all participants completed all four exercise conditions (VR, no-VR, SSE-VR, 6MWT) — there are no separate randomized arms. Several figures referenced in the paper contain data that are also reported in the text (HR, SpO2, dyspnea, leg fatigue). Baseline values before each condition are noted as recorded but not reported numerically in the paper text. Exercise characteristics per condition (distance, speed, duration) are extracted from Table 2. Correlations reported: handgrip vs leg fatigue at VR end (r=-0.621, p=0.003); handgrip vs leg fatigue at SSE-VR end (r=-0.450, p=0.047); handgrip vs dyspnea at SSE-VR end (r=-0.484, p=0.030); WAI vs dyspnea at baseline (r=-0.450, p=0.046); WAI vs dyspnea at VR end (r=-0.508, p=0.022); body fat vs dyspnea at SSE-VR (r=0.461, p=0.041); body fat vs 6MWT (r=-0.498, p=0.025); muscle mass vs dyspnea at SSE-VR (r=-0.466, p=0.038). summary: This study tested stationary cycling with a virtual reality (VR) headset versus cycling without VR in 20 long COVID patients (mean age 54, 80% male) with mild cognitive impairment, recruited 2 months after hospital discharge. The primary finding was that VR exercise produced significantly lower dyspnea scores than non-VR exercise (Borg CR-10: 0.5 vs. 1.1, p=0.004), with patients also spontaneously choosing to exercise more than twice as long when given free choice in the VR condition (21.8 vs. 10 minutes fixed). The study was unblinded, had no control arm, enrolled only 20 patients all infected with the Delta variant, and used a single-session crossover design rather than a rehabilitation programme.

summary: This RCT tested a 3-week, five-days-per-week inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation program in 32 adults (average age 58) with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19, comparing a virtual reality-enhanced version (VR headset during cycle ergometer training and VR-guided relaxation) against traditional rehabilitation. Both groups significantly improved their 6-minute walk test distance — the primary outcome — with the VR group gaining an average of 57 meters and the control group 39 meters, both exceeding the minimal clinically important difference, but the between-group difference was not statistically significant. Both groups also showed significant reductions in perceived stress and post-exercise dyspnea, with no meaningful difference between VR and traditional formats; lung function was essentially normal at baseline and did not change significantly in either group.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: KEY DESIGN NOTE: This is a waitlist-crossover RCT. The 2x2 ANCOVA results (Table 2) are the primary between-group comparisons (IG vs CG, BL to FU1, n=34 completers). The Table 3 data are from an exploratory analysis combining both groups after crossover (n=31 total trained), not a randomized comparison — these pre/post means and SDs are provided for completeness but reflect all completers pooled, not a randomized arm comparison. Per-arm SDs are NOT reported for the primary 2x2 ANCOVA results; only adjusted means (M_adj) and SEs are available. SDs for the combined pre-post analysis (Table 3) are provided for the pooled combined group only. Baseline SDs for individual arms from Table 1 are available for demographic variables (age, BMI, weight, height) but not for cognitive/psychological outcomes. The 2x3 ANCOVA interaction effects are reported in Supplementary Table 2 (not provided in full text); the 2x2 ANCOVA interaction p-values and partial eta-squared from Table 2 are extracted as between-group effect sizes. Cohen's d values from Table 3 are for the combined pre-post comparison and are extracted as 'smd' in the exploratory combined-group outcomes (outcomes 5-21 arm_results reflect the combined group). The n=31 for Table 3 is noted as 'df+1=31' from the t-test degrees of freedom. Fatigue analysis had n=28 (df=27+1). Word fluency SDs in Table 3 appear unusually small for formal-lexical (SD=1.22 and 1.43) — these are verbatim from paper. Outcomes 5-21 arm_results only have data for arm_id=1 (combined group) as the per-arm split was not reported for Table 3. The 6-month follow-up (FU2) data for within-group stability were described narratively but no per-arm means/SDs were provided for FU2 in the text.

summary: A three-month tablet-based training program combining cognitive exercises, relaxation techniques, and physiotherapy was tested in 40 adults (mean age 50, 80% female) with post-COVID-19 condition in Austria, randomized to intervention (n=20) or waitlist control (n=20). The primary finding was that the intervention group showed significant reductions in subjective cognitive complaints (p<0.001) and depressive symptoms on the ADS-L scale (p<0.001) compared to the control group, and their MoCA Memory Index Score remained stable while the control group's declined significantly (p=0.008 for decline in controls). Effects were not sustained after training ended, no improvements were seen in attention, executive function, fatigue, anxiety, or quality of life in the main group comparison, and the study was not prospectively registered.

summary: This pilot study tested a one-month telerehabilitation program — 12 supervised video-based exercise sessions plus three therapeutic education workshops — in 15 adults with ongoing symptomatic COVID-19 (persistent fatigue lasting under 3 months) who had been hospitalised but not intubated. A comparison group of 6 patients received standard physiotherapy. Fatigue measured by the Chalder Fatigue Score improved significantly across both groups (from 25.2 to 21.1 in the telerehabilitation group and 27.6 to 26.2 in the standard care group, p=0.010 time effect), alongside meaningful gains in aerobic capacity including an ~18% rise in VO2max (p=0.005) and a 15% improvement in 6-minute walk distance (p=0.019), with no adverse events reported. The study is a very small, non-randomised pilot with no untreated control arm, making it impossible to separate intervention effects from natural recovery.

The paper reports mixed ANOVA group*time interaction F-statistics and partial eta-squared values but does NOT report mean differences with CIs for between-group comparisons; between-group effect_values were calculated as (arm1 post-mean minus arm2 post-mean). The interaction F-statistics and partial eta-squared are: MoCA F(1,24)=5.500, p=0.03, partial_eta2=0.186; Stroop-C F(1,24)=7.895, p=0.01, partial_eta2=0.248; RAVLT Sum F(1,22)=11.491, p=0.003, partial_eta2=0.343; RAVLT IR F(1,22)=4.744, p=0.04, partial_eta2=0.177; RAVLT DR F(1,22)=11.074, p=0.003, partial_eta2=0.335; TMT-A F(1,24)=3.926, p=0.059, partial_eta2=0.141; PHQ-9 F(1,23)=5.975, p=0.03, partial_eta2=0.206; Stroop W-C (executive) F(1,24)=4.243, p=0.05, partial_eta2=0.150. 2. Many outcome figures referenced in text but specific figure data not extractable from removed images. 5. Follow-up within-group mean differences reported in text for EG: MoCA MD=-2.38 SE=0.76 p=0.005; Stroop-C MD=-2.46 SE=0.96 p=0.018; TMT-A MD=-1.69 SE=0.576 p=0.007; RAVLT Sum MD=-11.07 SE=3.701 p=0.007; RAVLT IR MD=-6.38 SE=3.03 p=0.047; RAVLT DR MD=-7.308 SE=2.54 p=0.009; PHQ-9 MD=-6.00 SE=1.66 p=0.002 (these are pre-post within-EG differences, not between-group). 6. The paper labels MFE-Q as a primary measure but does not report a significant interaction for it. 7. Table 2 note: values are raw scores for MoCA, T scores for most attention/memory tests, and scaled scores for Stroop, TMT, DSC, ANIMALS. The between-group mean differences calculated here are therefore on heterogeneous scales and should be interpreted with caution.

summary: This quasi-experimental pilot study tested an 8-week multimodal immersive virtual reality (IVR) intervention — combining cognitive training, physical exercise, and mindfulness — delivered twice weekly in group sessions of 5 participants, in 13 adults with post-COVID-19 condition (long COVID) who had cognitive complaints and elevated depression or anxiety scores, compared to 13 controls receiving usual care. The IVR group showed significant improvements in global cognition (MoCA mean change: 26.15 to 28.54), processing speed (Stroop Colors), verbal episodic memory (RAVLT Sum mean change: 37.31 to 48.38), and depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 mean change: 14.38 to 8.38), with large effect sizes (partial η² ranging from 0.177 to 0.343), while the control group showed no significant changes on any measure. The study is substantially limited by its non-randomised quasi-experimental design, small sample size, unblinded assessors, baseline group differences in memory scores, and absence of an active control, meaning causal attribution is uncertain.

trial_rating.result_basis: PHQ-9 depressive symptoms improved by mean 6.0 points in the IVR group vs no significant change in controls (F(1,23)=5.975, p=0.03, partial η²=0.206); RAVLT Sum group×time interaction F(1,22)=11.491, p=0.003, partial η²=0.343.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. CRITICAL LIMITATION: Post-treatment (T1, T2, T3) per-arm means and SDs are NOT reported in any table. Table 2 only provides baseline (T0) values. The mixed-effects regression model coefficients (intercept, Age, BMI, Day, Time, Group, Time:Group) reported in Tables 3-6 are model coefficients, NOT per-arm means/SDs at each timepoint. The actual timepoint-specific outcome values appear only in Figures 2 and 3 (data only in figures for T1, T2, T3). Therefore, per-arm arm_results for T1, T2, T3 cannot be extracted and are omitted. Between-group effects are reported only as regression model Time:Group interaction coefficients (b values) with p<0.05 thresholds, not as mean differences with CIs, severely limiting quantitative extraction. The coefficient b=-0.119 for ST EC T0-T1 and b=-1.826 for SD OAP EC T1-T2 are Time:Group interaction terms from mixed effects models (Group A relative to Group B), not standard mean differences. Note also that the paper uses 'SD' ambiguously — both as 'Standard Deviation' (for oscillation measures) and as 'Mean Spatial Distance' parameter; extraction uses context to distinguish these. Table 1 reports age/BMI as median (IQR) format based on Wilcoxon test usage, but values are labeled as mean+SD in the results text; treated as mean+SD per text. Group B n=23 at T0 per Figure 1 caption but n=22 per text; used n=22 for analyzed sample in mixed models per text.

summary: This randomized trial compared a 5-week spa-resort rehabilitation program (including thermal water exercise, land-based balance training, and cognitive therapy) against a supervised home-based program in 60 long COVID patients with fatigue, respiratory, cognitive, or psychological symptoms. The primary balance outcomes—antero-posterior sway amplitude (SD OAP) and mean stay time (ST)—were measured via force platform before treatment, immediately after, and at 3 and 6 months. The home-based program produced faster improvements immediately post-treatment (significant reduction in SD OAP and increase in ST with eyes closed), while the spa-resort program showed continued improvement in SD OAP from post-treatment to 3-month follow-up, suggesting more gradual but sustained gains. The trial was small (21–23 analyzed per group) and the two groups differed significantly in age at baseline (spa group mean 50 vs. home group mean 57 years), limiting direct comparison.

trial_rating.result_basis: Home-based group showed significant reduction in SD OAP (Time effect p<0.05) and increase in ST (Time effect p<0.05) at T0-T1 in EC condition; spa group showed significant decrease in SD OAP from T1 to T2 (time:Group interaction b=1.826, p<0.05); no other parameters reached significance.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial tested a marine oil supplement enriched in specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs) at doses of 500 mg, 1500 mg, or 3000 mg daily for 12 weeks in 53 adults with post-COVID syndrome. The primary outcome was change in serum levels of three pro-resolving lipid mediators (14-HDHA, 17-HDHA, 18-HEPE) and the ratio of pro-inflammatory to pro-resolving markers: all three mediators increased significantly across all dose groups (p=0.002, p=0.0007, and p=0.00001 respectively), and the inflammatory-to-resolving ratio improved significantly (p=0.025), with no dose-response difference between groups. Fatigue and dyspnea showed a non-significant trend toward improvement across all treated groups, with a 9% mean reduction in fatigue scores between weeks 4 and 12 in the 500 mg group; the placebo arm had only 5 participants, severely limiting interpretation of clinical outcomes.

trial_rating.result_basis: Pro-resolving mediator ratio decreased significantly (p=0.025) across all treatment groups, but fatigue improvement was non-significant (9% mean reduction in FSS for 500 mg group, no p-value reported for between-group comparison) and dyspnea showed no significant differences (Chi-square p=0.509).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. The study compares remote AI-assisted EMDR vs in-person EMDR — both are active treatments; there is no placebo or waitlist control. This is an equivalence/non-inferiority design in practice though not labeled as such. 2. The decrement (delta) values in Table 1 for the OL group SUDs is listed as 6.80 in the table but one text passage says 6.08 — the table value 6.80 is used as primary since it is consistent with 8.55-1.75=6.80. 3. Within-arm Cohen's d and ANOVA F/p-values for pre vs post (within each group) are reported in Table 1 (e.g., SUDs IP: F=1557.13, p<10^-4; Cohen's d=1.85; SUDs OL: F=1568.14, p<10^-4, Cohen's d=2.17) but these are within-arm effects, not between-group. Between-group ANOVA rows in Table 1 give the F and p for IP vs OL comparisons. 4. No CIs reported for any effect. 5. No trial registration mentioned. 6. Session duration was 45 minutes each, 3 sessions planned within approximately 3 weeks. 7. The paper also reports Cohen's d for between-group differences (SD column of 'Difference' rows in Table 1), which are very small (0.02-0.07), indicating negligible between-group effects.

summary: This study tested remote EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) therapy, delivered via an AI-assisted platform with eye-tracking, versus standard in-person EMDR therapy in 160 adults aged 25–49 with long COVID-related PTSD symptoms. Both formats produced large reductions in all three outcome measures: SUDs scores dropped by ~6.6 points (in-person) and ~6.8 points (online) from a baseline of ~8.4–8.6; PCL-5 scores fell by ~20 and ~22 points respectively; and IES-R scores fell by ~28 points in both groups. No statistically significant differences were found between the two delivery formats on any measure, supporting equivalence of remote and in-person delivery. The main caveat is that this is a non-inferiority comparison between two active treatments with no placebo or waitlist control, so the absolute efficacy of EMDR itself cannot be independently confirmed from this trial.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary comparison between online and in-person groups showed no significant difference: SUDs decrement ANOVA F=1.51, p=0.22; PCL-5 decrement F=0.89, p=0.34; IES-R decrement F=0.09, p=0.76. This is a null equivalence result with no control arm.

summary: This Turkish RCT tested motion-controlled video game-based virtual reality (VR) exercise (Microsoft Xbox One Kinect) against conventional exercise (aerobic cycling, strength, stretching) in 74 adults with post-COVID-19 condition, over 8 weeks of supervised sessions three times per week. The primary outcome was pain intensity (VAS 0-10): the VR group reduced pain by 2.22 points versus 0.85 points in the conventional group, a statistically significant and large between-group difference (mean difference -1.37, 95% CI -1.73 to -1.00, p<0.001, partial η²=0.487). VR also outperformed conventional exercise on fatigue (FSS) and depression (HADS-D), but not on anxiety, functional walk distance, or quality of life; no adverse events or post-exertional malaise were reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: VAS pain reduced by 2.22 points in VR group vs 0.85 in conventional group; time×group interaction F(1,59.4)=56.31, p<0.001, partial η²=0.487 (large effect).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a within-subjects waitlist controlled pilot study, not a parallel-group RCT. Arm 1 (intervention) and Arm 2 (waitlist control) represent the same 22 participants at different time periods; only 16 completed the post-intervention phase. The paired-samples t-tests reported compare waitlist (n=22) vs post-intervention (n=16) periods within participants. Cohen's d effect sizes were reported: Anxiety d=1.61, Rumination d=1.19, Social Connection d=1.22, Long-COVID Symptoms d=0.73. The t-statistics reported were: Anxiety t=8.03, Rumination t=5.84, Social Connection t=-6.10 (note negative sign for inverse direction), Long-COVID Symptoms t=3.65. Between-group effect values in this extraction are calculated as post-intervention mean minus waitlist mean. The study design does not permit standard between-group effect size calculation as typically defined in RCTs. The table in the paper had garbled formatting due to overlapping text from figure caption and table content; values were cross-referenced from text to verify. One-month follow-up data (n=6) had no means/SDs reported in the paper, only narrative description. Age range was 24-61 years with M=37.13, SD=9.44; all participants female and White British.

summary: This pilot study tested four weekly online forest bathing sessions (guided virtual mindfulness-based nature engagement) in 22 adults with long COVID. The primary outcomes were anxiety, rumination, social connection, and self-reported long COVID symptom severity; compared to a four-week waitlist control period, participants showed a 49% reduction in anxiety (Cohen's d = 1.61), 48% reduction in rumination, 78% increase in social connection, and 22% reduction in long COVID symptom scores, all statistically significant. Key caveats are the very small all-female sample (N=16 completers), absence of a concurrent control group, no blinding, and the fact that three authors delivered the intervention themselves.

trial_rating.result_basis: Anxiety decreased 49% (mean 3.37 to 1.73, t=8.03, p<0.001, d=1.61); long COVID symptoms decreased 22% (mean 3.99 to 3.11, t=3.65, p<0.01, d=0.73); N=16 completers from 22 enrolled, no concurrent control group.

summary: This pilot RCT tested whether adding EMG-driven robotic upper-limb training (Luna EMG robot, 45 min twice daily) to standard inpatient neurological rehabilitation improved outcomes in 30 adults with post-COVID post-viral fatigue syndrome, all of whom had been transferred from ICUs after severe COVID-19. The primary outcome was muscle fatigue measured by EMG; the robot group showed a non-significant trend toward improvement (median change 0, range -14.9 to 34.7) while the control group showed a non-significant trend toward worsening (median change 2.8, range -55.4 to 11.3), with no significant between-group difference (p=0.909). Both groups improved significantly on functional independence (FIM, Barthel Index), handgrip strength, and self-reported fatigue (FAS), but none of these secondary outcomes differed significantly between groups. The intervention was safe with no adverse events or dropouts, but the study was too small (n=15 per arm) to draw conclusions about efficacy.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (EMG muscle fatigue) showed no significant difference between groups (p=0.909); intragroup change was also non-significant in both the intervention group (p=0.778) and control group (p=0.975).

summary: This randomized trial compared a 12-week hybrid exercise program (twice-weekly supervised in-person sessions plus once-weekly tele-exercise) against fully unsupervised tele-exercise (three times weekly) in 49 previously hospitalized long COVID patients with a mean age of approximately 59 years. Both programs improved physical fitness, body composition, and lung function, with six-minute walk distance increasing by roughly 81 meters in the hybrid group and 55 meters in the tele-exercise group. The two formats produced different cognitive benefits: the hybrid group improved in visuospatial ability (score 3.2 to 3.5, p=0.008) while the tele-exercise group improved in memory (score 3.3 to 3.8, p=0.003) and had higher attention scores post-intervention; adherence was high in both groups (85-87%) with no adverse events.

trial_rating.result_basis: Six-minute walk distance improved significantly in both groups (HEgroup: +80.9m, TEgroup: +54.8m, both p<0.001 within-group), but no statistically significant between-group difference on the primary fitness outcomes; cognitive domain differences were secondary, underpowered findings (e.g., attention domain: TEgroup 4.8 vs HEgroup 3.6, p=0.014).

summary: This randomized single-blind placebo-controlled trial tested 14 days of home-based molecular hydrogen (H2) gas inhalation (300 mL/min via nasal cannula, twice daily for 60 minutes) in 50 adults with acute post-COVID-19 syndrome, recruited 21-35 days after a positive PCR test. H2 inhalation improved 6-minute walk test distance by 64 m compared to 9 m in the placebo group (p<0.001), exceeding the 30 m minimal clinically important difference for chronic respiratory disease, and also increased forced vital capacity by 0.19 L versus -0.01 L in placebo (p=0.004) and forced expiratory volume in one second by 0.11 L versus -0.08 L in placebo (p=0.025). No side effects were reported, though the study was only single-blinded and had a relatively small sample with imbalanced BMI and body fat between arms at baseline.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT improved 64±39 m in H2 group vs 9±29 m placebo (p<0.001, Cohen's d=1.58), exceeding the established 30 m minimal clinically important difference.

summary: This pilot study tested a 12-session Nordic walking program in 16 long COVID patients and 13 COVID-19 controls (without persistent symptoms), measuring blood lactate levels after each session to assess aerobic exercise capacity across different genetic profiles. Long COVID patients consistently produced higher lactate concentrations than controls during exercise, with statistically significant group differences observed in carriers of specific variants of the ACTN3 (CT and TT genotypes, sessions 1–7) and AMPD1 (CC and CT genotypes) genes, indicating impaired aerobic metabolism that improved over the course of the program. The study is a small, non-randomized pilot with 29 total participants, no randomization, no pre-intervention cardiopulmonary testing, and no control for diet or baseline fitness, substantially limiting the generalizability of its findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: ACTN3 group×genotype×session interaction F=1.702, p=0.028; AMPD1 main effects lactic acid p<0.001, group p=0.003, genotype p<0.001, three-way interaction p=0.048; no overall primary outcome effect size reported.
