extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Study duration stated as 'two months' with 15 sessions over alternating days (3x/week); 8 weeks estimated as treatment duration. Mid-intervention timepoint (T1) estimated at approximately week 4 (halfway through 8 weeks). The abstract reports PPT C5-C6 values as 2.1 to 3.5 kg/cm2 for EG which differ from Table 2 values (1.43 to 1.87); Table 2 values extracted as primary data source. SDNN abstract states '30.42 to 39.11 ms' for EG and '31.88 to 28.73 ms' for CG which also differ from Table 2 values; Table 2 values extracted as primary. The inter-group p-value for SDNN (p=0.021) is reported in the text as a group difference but the time-by-group interaction F-value (0.579; p=0.567) is non-significant — the p=0.021 appears to refer to the between-groups main effect from ANOVA. Body weight data reported per arm: EG 61.71 (4.71) kg, CG 61.94 (3.39) kg — BMI not calculable without height. Cortisol also reported in µg/dL (EG T0: 0.24, T1: 0.43, T2: 0.36; CG T0: 0.26, T1: 0.13, T2: 0.54) but nmol/L values extracted as primary. No post-treatment follow-up period beyond end of intervention.

summary: This pilot RCT tested superficial neuromodulation (NESA XSIGNAL device, 15 sessions over two months) versus a sham placebo device in 16 women with post-COVID-19 condition and dysautonomia. The primary outcome was heart rate variability (HRV): SDNN increased in the treatment group (49.06 to 69.68 ms) but decreased in controls (84.65 to 42.26 ms), with a statistically significant between-group difference (p=0.021), though no significant time-by-group interaction was found. Fatigue, sleep quality, and pain threshold improved in both groups equally, with no significant differences between real and sham treatment, and the authors concluded a placebo effect cannot be ruled out. The study was severely underpowered, enrolling only 16 of a planned 60 participants.

trial_rating.result_basis: SDNN between-group difference p=0.021, but no significant time-by-group interaction; all other primary outcomes (MFIS p=0.978, PSQI p=0.352, PPT C5-C6 p=0.844) showed no significant group differences, with both real and sham groups improving equally.

summary: A 14-day telerehabilitation program of daily breathing and strength exercises (30 minutes/day, 12 reps per exercise) was tested against relative home rest in 48 non-hospitalized adults with post-COVID-19 symptoms lasting at least 40 days. The exercise group showed large, statistically significant improvements across all five outcomes: perceived exertion on the Borg Scale dropped by 4.25 points (vs. 0.25 in controls), dyspnea scores fell by 10.21 points on the MD-12 (vs. 0.37), fatigue improved by 2.00 points on the visual analog scale (vs. 0.17), six-minute walk distance increased by 148 metres (vs. no change), and sit-to-stand repetitions increased by 3.08 (vs. 0.21), all p<0.001 with large effect sizes (R² 0.235–0.693). No adverse events were reported, but the trial had no follow-up beyond day 14, so durability of benefit is unknown.

trial_rating.result_basis: Borg Scale improved by 4.25 points in the exercise group vs. 0.25 in controls (between-group p<0.001, R²=0.693); 6MWT improved by 147.92 metres vs. -0.37 metres (p<0.001, R²=0.294).

Table 1 and Table 2 report baseline PWV for rehab group as 8.2 (1.4) m/s and 8.2 (1.3) m/s respectively (minor SD discrepancy: 1.4 in Table 1, 1.3 in Table 2 and abstract); 8.2 (1.3) used for T0 arm_results per Table 2 which is the outcomes table. 2. The between_group_effects p-value for FMD interaction is reported as p<0.001 (interaction), for PWV p<0.001 (interaction), for AIx p=0.005 (interaction); these are p-values for the group-by-time interaction from repeated-measures ANOVA, not direct between-group comparisons at T1 — they are reported as the primary between-group effect measure in this paper. Calculated mean differences at T1 are provided. 3. Subgroup IL-6 analyses for outcome_id 4 and 5: two arm_results entries per arm_id represent the two IL-6 strata (high and low) rather than two separate arms — this is a within-arm subgroup. 4. The paper also reports a healthy control group (n=60) for baseline comparison but this is not a randomized arm and is not included in the RCT extraction. 5. summary: A 3-month cardiopulmonary rehabilitation program was tested in 60 adults recovering from COVID-19 (randomized 1:1 to rehabilitation or no rehabilitation, starting one month post-acute disease). The primary outcome was endothelial function measured by flow-mediated dilation (FMD): the rehabilitation group improved from 6.2% to 8.6% (+2.4 percentage points), versus 5.9% to 6.6% (+0.7 percentage points) in controls, with a statistically significant between-group interaction (p<0.001). Rehabilitation also reduced arterial stiffness (pulse wave velocity fell from 8.2 to 6.6 m/s, p<0.001) and augmentation index (25.9% to 21.1%, p<0.001), with no significant changes in the control group; patients with higher baseline IL-6 levels showed greater FMD benefit.

trial_rating.result_basis: FMD improved by 2.4 percentage points in the rehabilitation group vs 0.7 in controls (p for interaction <0.001); PWV fell from 8.2 to 6.6 m/s in the rehabilitation group vs no change in controls (p<0.001).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 12 weeks of face-to-face versus asynchronous online Mat Pilates (three sessions per week) in 49 adults aged around 52 years with long COVID, all presenting with fatigue as a defining symptom. Only the face-to-face group showed significant improvements in the primary fatigue outcome: total Fatigue Assessment Scale scores dropped from 33.5 to 26.7 (p<0.01), alongside gains in upper limb endurance (16 to 23 repetitions), trunk flexion isometric strength (6.6 to 12.7 kg), and 6-minute walk distance (463 to 514 m). Online Pilates produced no significant changes on any outcome, and neither format affected body composition or cardiometabolic blood markers. Notably, the inactive control group showed significant increases in systolic (114 to 122 mmHg) and diastolic (75 to 81 mmHg) blood pressure over the 12 weeks, suggesting ongoing cardiovascular deterioration without exercise.

trial_rating.result_basis: Face-to-face group total FAS score improved from 33.5 to 26.7 (p<0.01, Cohen's d not directly reported for fatigue); 6-minute walk improved from 463 to 514 m (p<0.05, Cohen's d=0.87); trunk flexion strength doubled from 6.6 to 12.7 kg (p<0.01, Cohen's d=1.17).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL LIMITATION: All primary and secondary outcome quantitative data (means and SDs for IFNγ, TNFα, MDA, protein carbonyls, SOD) appear only in figures (Figures 1-5) with no numerical values in text or tables. Only p-values, F-statistics, and partial eta-squared values for between-group effects were reported in text. Per-arm means and SDs cannot be extracted. RPE and VAS data reported as mode (range) only in Table 1, not mean±SD. The 4 AEs reported were described as occurring across both HIIT groups combined (n=4, 5.97%), not separated by arm. Within-group p-values extracted: HIIT IFNγ p=0.047, TNFα p<0.001; Combined IFNγ p=0.033, TNFα p<0.001; Control IFNγ p=0.860, TNFα p=0.496; HIIT MDA p=0.037, protein carbonyls p=0.047; Combined MDA p=0.014, protein carbonyls p=0.018; all groups SOD p<0.001. Between-group interaction F-statistics: IFNγ F(2,36)=0.179, η2=0.010, p=0.837; TNFα F(2,8)=2.189, η2=0.354, p=0.175; MDA F(2,56)=0.345, η2=0.012, p=0.710; protein carbonyls F(2,38)=0.032, η2=0.002, p=0.968; SOD F(2,62)=0.610, η2=0.019, p=0.546. Note: the paper states n=104 total analyzed but CONSORT details suggest initial randomization was ~112 across 3 groups; exact per-arm n at randomization not stated, only at analysis.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 8 weeks of cycling-based high-intensity interval training (HIIT), with or without daily Triphala herbal supplementation (1000 mg/day), in 104 young adults (mean age 22 years) with long COVID symptoms including fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Both the HIIT-only and HIIT-plus-Triphala groups showed significant within-group reductions in the pro-inflammatory cytokines IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha, and in oxidative stress markers MDA and protein carbonyls, compared to no change in the placebo control group; however, the between-group interaction effect was not statistically significant for any primary outcome (IFN-gamma: p=0.837; TNF-alpha: p=0.175), meaning the trial did not formally demonstrate superiority of HIIT over control. Triphala added no statistically significant benefit beyond HIIT alone and was safe with no liver or kidney toxicity detected.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcomes IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha showed within-group reductions in HIIT groups but no significant group-by-time interaction: IFN-gamma F(2,36)=0.179, p=0.837; TNF-alpha F(2,8)=2.189, p=0.175.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) The paper_id is the preprint DOI (10.21203/rs.3.rs-2847841/v1); the placeholder ID in the template (10.3390/jcm12196244) was replaced. 2) Absolute VO2max values (not relative) are reported to increase significantly in AQUA (p=0.001) and LAND (p=0.004) within-group, but only relative VO2max group x time interaction is shown in Table 2 (p=0.017); absolute VO2max values are not given in tables — only relative ml/kg/min. 3) Table 2 F and p values represent the repeated-measures ANOVA group x time interaction across all 3 groups, not pairwise comparisons. Post-hoc pairwise p-values are only reported for AQUA vs CONTROL VO2max (p=0.023) and LAND parent PedsQL (p<0.01). 4) Between-group CIs reported for AQUA vs CONTROL use 'AQUA minus CONTROL' direction per table header ordering; LAND vs CONTROL CIs were extracted as stated. 5) Supplementary Table S1 (fatigue complaint rates per symptom) and Supplementary Table S2 (PedsQL subscales) were not available in the provided text — subscale data (physical, emotional, social, school functioning) not extracted. 6) The table footnote for Body mass LAND SD appears to be a typo (1.6 instead of plausible ~11.6); extracted as stated (43.4, SD=1.6). 7) No between-group statistical test p-values are given for most outcomes other than overall F-test p-values in Table 2. 8) Within-group pre-post p-values not tabulated; only stated in text for VO2max (AQUA p=0.001, LAND p=0.004, CONTROL p=0.999) and PedsQL parent LAND (p<0.01).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested eight weeks of twice-weekly supervised water-based (AQUA) or land-based (LAND) exercise training versus no exercise in 74 children aged 10-12 years with post-COVID-19 condition. Both exercise programs significantly increased absolute VO2max compared to baseline (AQUA p=0.001, LAND p=0.004), and post-intervention VO2max was significantly higher in the AQUA group versus the control group (p=0.023); relative VO2max increased significantly only in the AQUA group (p=0.017). Neither exercise program reduced fatigue scores, and no adverse events were recorded in either training group.

trial_rating.result_basis: Relative VO2max group-by-time interaction F=4.32, p=0.017; post-intervention difference between LAND and CONTROL was 4.3 ml/kg/min (95% CI 0.01 to 8.6), with no significant between-group differences for AQUA vs LAND or AQUA vs CONTROL at post-intervention.

summary: This Swedish randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week multidisciplinary group telerehabilitation program (combining breathing exercises, mindfulness, ACT-based therapy, physical training, and psychoeducation delivered via Microsoft Teams) in 109 adults with long COVID who had persistent symptoms for at least 12 weeks after SARS-CoV-2 infection. The primary outcome was functioning and activity measured across 38 ICF categories; the telerehabilitation group showed improvements in more ICF categories than the waiting-list controls, particularly in activities and participation domains such as recreation, household tasks, stair climbing, and lifting, though statistically significant between-group differences were rare — breathing function actually improved more in the waiting-list group at 8 weeks (p=0.034). At 6 months, many participants in both groups still reported severe fatigue and cognitive impairment, highlighting the chronic nature of the condition.

trial_rating.result_basis: Between-group differences were rarely statistically significant on the primary ICF outcomes; within-group improvements were seen across multiple ICF categories in the telerehabilitation group (e.g. pain at multiple sites: Wilcoxon p=0.003; climbing stairs: p=0.02), but the between-subjects group factor was non-significant across nearly all regression model outcomes (all group F p-values >0.05).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested moderate-intensity aerobic interval training (IT) versus continuous training (CT) on cycle ergometers in 110 long COVID patients (mean age 49, average 260 days post-infection) undergoing 4-6 weeks of inpatient medical rehabilitation in Germany. The primary outcome, peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak), improved by a mean of 2.7% across all PCS patients, but the difference between IT and CT was not statistically significant (IT: +0.8% vs CT: +4.1%, p=0.157), meaning neither modality was superior to the other. Both groups showed significant improvements in fatigue, anxiety, depression, and quality of life, and the overall gains in exercise capacity were comparable to those seen in coronary artery disease patients undergoing guideline-based cardiac rehabilitation; no post-exertional malaise or training-specific fatigue was detected in either group.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome VO2peak improvement did not differ between IT and CT (IT +0.8% vs CT +4.1%, p=0.157); the trial was designed to detect equivalence, not superiority, and the non-significant between-group result is the primary finding.

Table 3 reports both mean and median for QOL outcomes. The n_randomized_total of 49 is inferred: 28 intervention (26 completed + 2 withdrew) + 20 control (originally 23 but 3 did not attend post-test — however text says 'control group: n=20' at final and mentions 3 did not attend post-test, so original control randomized was 23, but the text is ambiguous).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week resistance training program (twice weekly, 60 minutes per session at 70% of 1-repetition maximum) in 46 adults aged 65 and older who had recovered from COVID-19 and reported ongoing post-COVID symptoms such as dizziness, fatigue, and balance problems. The primary finding was a significant improvement in overall postural stability (overall stability index with eyes open) in the training group compared to controls (Z = -3.12, p = 0.0017, effect size R = 0.533), along with reduced fall risk on an unstable surface (fall-risk index 6-2, Z = -2.06, p = 0.04, R = 0.354). The training group also showed greater improvements in psychological wellbeing and social relationship domains of quality of life, and higher health satisfaction scores, compared to controls. The trial was small (26 intervention, 20 control) and conducted at a single site using gym-based resistance machines, limiting generalizability.

trial_rating.result_basis: Overall stability index (eyes open) improved significantly in the intervention group vs control: Z = -3.12, p = 0.0017, R = 0.533 (large effect by rank-biserial correlation).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a 6-week outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation program — combining aerobic cycle training, resistance exercise, respiratory training, and stretching — in 59 post-COVID-19 patients with persistent symptoms, comparing an active inspiratory muscle training (IMT) group (n=39) against a placebo IMT group (n=22). The primary outcome, maximum inspiratory pressure (PImax), improved significantly in both groups (p<0.001), with a median increase of 52% in the IMT group and 47.5% in the placebo group, but there was no statistically significant difference between the two groups (p=0.28), meaning the additional resistive breathing device did not provide extra benefit over the general exercise program. The IMT group did show greater improvement in spirometric parameters — FEV1 rose 8.02%, FVC by 13.24%, and PEF by 9.67% — but the unequal group sizes (39 vs 22) and the preliminary nature of this dataset limit the strength of these conclusions.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome PImax improved in both groups (p<0.001 within-group) but the between-group comparison was non-significant (p=0.28, r=0.141), meaning the key experimental question — whether IMT adds benefit — was not confirmed.

The 'Height' and 'Weight' values in Table 1 appear to be switched (height ~65cm, weight ~166cm), suggesting a data entry error in the paper. 4. Within-group p-values for Long-COVID pre vs. post: MFIS physical p=0.011, cognitive p=0.031, total p=0.009; SF-36 physical functioning p=0.001, social functioning p=0.011, bodily pain p=0.003, total SF-36 p=0.004. These are within-group comparisons only. 5. No between-group effect sizes (mean differences with CIs) were reported by the authors; all calculated between-group mean differences are from endpoint values only. 6. Two-way ANOVA group x time interaction results for SF-36 (F=4.632, p=0.002) and EQ-5D (F=4.340, p=0.014) indicate differential change between groups. 7. Non-randomized design with retrospective trial registration limits validity.

summary: A 12-week Nordic Walking program (one 45-minute session per week) was tested in 16 long COVID patients and 13 healthy controls in Spain. Long COVID patients showed consistently higher blood lactate concentrations after exercise than controls throughout the program (group effect F=5.604, p=0.024), indicating impaired aerobic metabolism. Long COVID patients also improved on quality-of-life measures after the program: total SF-36 score rose from 37.2 to 48.4 (p=0.004) and EQ-5D from 41.3 to 58.8 (p=0.005), and fatigue scores (MFIS total) fell from 59.6 to 48.6 (p=0.009). Key caveats include the non-randomized design, small sample, predominantly female long COVID group (94%), and that the lactate meter frequently exceeded its upper range in long COVID patients, meaning true values may have been even higher.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (lactate group difference) was statistically significant (F=5.604, p=0.024) but showed no time or interaction effect; SF-36 total improved by 11.2 points in long COVID group vs. 1.4 in controls (interaction p=0.002), a modest change against a low baseline.

summary: This Romanian RCT tested whether adding daily 20-minute progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) sessions to a standard 21-day pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) program improved outcomes in 61 long COVID patients (aged 54–74) with persistent dyspnea and fatigue. The primary finding was that the PR+PMR group showed significantly greater improvements in mental health, anxiety, and sleep quality compared to PR alone: GAD-7 anxiety scores dropped by approximately 5 points (to a mean of 4.96 vs. 8.23 in the PR-only group, p<0.001), and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores fell by 4.74 points (median 4 vs. 7, p<0.001), crossing the threshold from poor to good sleep quality. Exercise capacity (6-minute walk test) improved in both groups but did not differ significantly between them (366.60 m vs. 391.54 m, p=0.171). The study is limited by its small sample, short 21-day follow-up with no post-intervention monitoring, and a predominantly older male population from a single centre.

trial_rating.result_basis: GAD-7 post-intervention: PR+PMR group mean 4.96 vs. PR-only mean 8.23 (p<0.001); PSQI median 4 vs. 7 (p<0.001); PSQI reduction of 4.74 points exceeds the 3-point MCID threshold.

Between-group effect sizes (Cohen's d) are reported only as within-group comparisons, NOT as between-group differences. No between-group p-values are reported for continuous outcomes except for HADS Anxiety binary outcome at 8 weeks (p<0.01, stated as '**'). Symptom duration reported as mean 51 (SD 27) weeks for rehabilitation group and 58 (SD 31) weeks for waiting list — converted to months as approximately 11.8 (SD 6.3) and 13.4 (SD 7.2) months respectively. The paper reports Cohen's d within the rehabilitation group for SF-36 outcomes (8 weeks): physical functioning=0.5, role physical=0.4, bodily pain=0.5, vitality=0.7, social functioning=0.6, role emotional=0.3, mental health=0.9, PCS=0.3, MCS=0.7. Waiting list within-group Cohen's d (8 weeks): physical functioning=0.5, social functioning=0.4, mental health=0.4. At 6 months: physical functioning=0.6, vitality=0.6, mental health=0.8. HADS within-group Cohen's d (TR): anxiety d=0.4 (p<0.01) at 8 weeks, d=0.6-0.7 (p<0.001) at 6 months; depression d=0.6-0.7 (p<0.001) at 8 weeks, 6 months. summary: An 8-week multidisciplinary telerehabilitation programme delivered via Microsoft Teams was tested in 67 adults with long COVID (mean age 43, 78% women) who had persistent symptoms for at least 12 weeks after mild SARS-CoV-2 infection, compared against 42 people on a waiting list. The primary outcomes were health- and pain-related parameters measured by SF-36 and ICF pain categories; the telerehabilitation group showed moderate-to-large within-group improvements across most SF-36 subscales (Cohen's d 0.3–0.9), but no statistically significant between-group differences were found for any primary outcome. The only statistically significant between-group difference was a reduction in clinically elevated anxiety (HADS): 6% of the telerehabilitation group screened positive after 8 weeks versus 24% of the waiting list (p<0.01).

trial_rating.result_basis: No statistically significant between-group difference was found for any primary outcome (SF-36 or ICF pain categories) by one-way ANOVA; within-group pain intensity reduction in the telerehabilitation group was Cohen's d=0.3, p=0.026, but the between-group comparison was non-significant.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 8 weeks of moderate-intensity resistance training (twice weekly, 60 minutes per session, 70% of one-repetition maximum) in 41 adults aged 65 and older with long COVID symptoms, recruited approximately 9 months after infection. The primary outcome was change in body mass and body composition measured by both DXA and bioelectrical impedance analysis; neither method detected any statistically significant changes in body mass, fat mass, or fat-free mass in the training group compared to controls. The authors conclude that 8 weeks at this frequency is insufficient to drive body composition changes in this population, and suggest that programs of at least 12 weeks with higher training frequency and increased protein intake may be needed.

trial_rating.result_basis: No significant changes in body mass or body composition were detected; ANOVA group-by-session interaction for DXA fat mass p=0.726 (F=0.12, η²=0.003) and fat-free mass p=0.518 (F=0.43, η²=0.012).

summary: This Phase II feasibility trial tested heart rate variability biofeedback (HRV-BF) — 10 sessions over 5 weeks using the HeartMath emWave system — added to standard care (analgesics and antidepressants) versus standard care alone in 18 adults with long COVID who met diagnostic criteria for CFS/ME. The primary outcome was change in severe fatigue: 3 of 8 participants in the HRV-BF group (37.5%) moved out of the severe fatigue category compared to 0 of 9 in the control group, while 2 control participants worsened (Kruskal-Wallis H=4.083, p=0.043). The trial was explicitly a feasibility study with a very small sample, quasi-random (non-random) allocation, and multiple outcomes tested simultaneously, so the fatigue result must be treated as a preliminary signal only and not evidence of efficacy.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week gym-based resistance training program (twice weekly, 70% of 1-repetition maximum, seven machine exercises) in 46 adults aged 65 and older with long COVID symptoms including muscle weakness and exercise intolerance. The primary functional outcome was the Chair Stand Test: the intervention group significantly improved both speed (5-repetition sit-to-stand improved from ~9.1s to 6.7s in men and 8.8s to 7.0s in women) and number of repetitions in 30 seconds (men: 15 to 24; women: 18 to 25), while the control group showed no change. Isometric strength improved significantly across most muscle groups in both sexes, with the largest gains in trunk extensors (~22% in men, ~23% in women); however, isokinetic torque improvements did not reach significance for the group-by-session interaction. The program was safe and well-tolerated, with a 93% average attendance rate and only two dropouts due to unrelated musculoskeletal pain.

subgroup_analyses.variable: outlier status (unusually high RMSSD at baseline)
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Five participants (4 in OMT, 2 in sham; note: table lists 6 outliers total) had RMSSD far above normal (mean 88.3 vs 20.5 ms for full population). Outlier OMT group showed increase in RMSSD at T2 followed by significant decrease at T3. No effect sizes calculated due to small n. 75% of outliers had been hospitalized during acute COVID.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. The Hedges' g values reported in the paper appear to represent within-group effect sizes (change from T1 to T2 within OMT arm), NOT between-group effect sizes; they have been extracted in between_group_effects as the best available effect measure since no true between-group effect statistics (mean differences with CIs) were reported for most outcomes. 2. Per-arm data for the sham group across most HRV outcomes (RMSSD, SDNN, LF, HF, TP, mean HR, mean RR, Stress Index) were NOT reported numerically in text or tables — only the OMT arm values and select sham LF/HF ratio values were given. Sham arm HRV data therefore not extractable. 3. The n values for OMT arm vary across outcomes (14–19 of 21 randomized), suggesting some missing measurements, but the paper provides no explanation for discrepancies. 4. The RMSSD g value at T3 (g=-0.55) has an asymmetric CI [-0.96, 0.18] crossing zero, indicating non-significant decline. 5. FAS was used for eligibility screening; post-intervention FAS values were mentioned as reduced but no numeric post-intervention data were provided. 6. Subjective dyspnea questionnaire (0–10 scale) and subjective well-being were listed as secondary outcomes but no quantitative results were reported. 7. The follow-up duration of 48 hours was converted to approximately 0.3 weeks. 8. The outlier table (Table 2) lists n=6 outliers but the text states n=5 participants with 4 in osteopathy and 2 in sham — a discrepancy noted in the paper itself. 9. LF/HF ratio results were only reported for the sham group (T2 vs T3 within-group change); OMT group LF/HF was stated to be 'statistically unchanged'. 10. Outcome data appear only in text/figures for most HRV parameters; no summary table of results by arm and timepoint was provided.

summary: A single 45-minute session of osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) was tested against a sham treatment in 42 long COVID patients (mean age 51 years) with persistent fatigue lasting at least 12 weeks. The primary outcome was heart rate variability (HRV); immediately after OMT, RMSSD increased from 17.8 ms to 21.6 ms (Hedges' g = 0.82), SDNN rose from 19.6 ms to 26.0 ms (g = 0.80), mean heart rate dropped from 67.3 to 62.3 bpm (g = -1.10), and the Baevsky stress index fell significantly — all indicating a short-term shift toward parasympathetic dominance. These gains fully reversed within 48 hours, and no long-term or clinically meaningful benefit was demonstrated from a single session.

trial_rating.result_basis: RMSSD increased from 17.8 ms to 21.6 ms immediately post-treatment (Hedges' g = 0.82, 95% CI [0.19, 1.40], p < 0.01), but returned to baseline by 48-hour follow-up (17.4 ms), indicating only a transient effect with no sustained benefit.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Non-randomized study; allocation was based on patients' ability to attend supervised sessions (logistical/transport issues). The paper reports the overall age SD as 4.5, which appears to be an error (given the range 21-79 and per-group SDs of ~14-15); the per-arm SDs of 14.42 and 15.04 are more plausible and were used for per-arm baseline demographics. The overall SD of 4.5 was extracted verbatim as stated. Time since infection was reported as means of ~100-101 days (~3.35-3.39 months); these were calculated from reported days. No between-group p-values were reported for any outcome at the final timepoint (only within-group pre-post p-values reported); between-group effect mean differences at week 8 were calculated as arm1 endpoint minus arm2 endpoint. The dyspnea outcome was analyzed with non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon/Mann-Whitney) due to non-normal distribution; means and SDs are still reported in tables.

summary: A non-randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week supervised physiotherapy program — combining interval aerobic exercise on a cycle ergometer with resistance training (2 sessions/week) — in 20 adults with long COVID syndrome. In the 10 participants who completed the exercise program, quadriceps muscle strength increased by 5.86 kg (right leg, p=0.03) and 8.26 kg (left leg, p=0.01), functional capacity on the 60-second sit-to-stand test improved by 3.7 repetitions (p=0.01), and perceived breathlessness fell by 0.95 points on the Borg scale (p=0.02) — none of these improvements reached statistical significance when comparing directly against the control group. The study is severely limited by its very small sample size (n=10 per group) and non-randomized allocation, with control group membership determined by inability to travel to the hospital rather than random assignment.

trial_rating.result_basis: Within-group improvements in the exercise group: left quadriceps +8.26 kg (p=0.01), right quadriceps +5.86 kg (p=0.03), 60s sit-to-stand +3.7 rises (p=0.01), Borg dyspnea -0.95 points (p=0.02); however, between-group comparisons were non-significant for all outcomes.

No explicit reporting of dropouts or missing data; all enrolled patients appear to have completed assessments, but no CONSORT-style flow data for attrition is reported.
Objective outcomes (CPET, 6MWT, muscle strength) are well-standardized. Patient-reported outcomes (FACIT, mMRC, CAT, HADS) are validated instruments, but assessors were not described as blinded.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) This is a non-randomized quasi-experimental study (propensity-matched), not a true RCT; allocation to PR vs UC was based on patients' ability to attend supervised sessions. 2) Per-arm baseline and endpoint values for 6MWT, quadriceps force, handgrip strength, SPPB, and 60s sit-to-stand were reported only as change scores or in figures without explicit per-arm pre/post means+SDs in tabular form — 6MWT, QF, and handgrip extracted as change_from_baseline only. 3) WRpeak SD for change from baseline listed in abstract as 10W (PR group: +19±10W); Table 2 shows pre 94±46 and post 113±50, consistent. Abstract also states 19±10W change. 4) VE and Vt in Table 2 show slight discrepancy with Table 3 (peak pre values): VE 56.7 vs 55.2 and Vt 1.63 vs 1.587 — likely rounding or slightly different subsets; both extracted as reported. 5) HR in Table 2: PR group pre 127±19 (Table 2) vs 127±18 (Table 3) — minor rounding, both extracted. 6) SPPB total score and components (balance score, 4m walk test, 5-rep sit-to-stand) data appear only in Figure 3 without tabular values — not extracted numerically. 7) The p-values reported as 0.001 in text are likely p<0.001 displayed as exact; flagged as p_value_exact=false where stated as 0.001 throughout. 8) Omitted from detailed extraction (data in figures only): SPPB total score and individual components. 9) WR%predicted and VO2%predicted extracted in Table 2 but not separately included as outcome objects to manage JSON size; key data: PR pre WR%pred=70±26, post=86±29; UC pre=75±29, post=78±30; PR pre VO2%pred=66±17, post=75±18; UC pre=65±20, post=62±19.

summary: A 12-week hybrid pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) programme — comprising 8 supervised outpatient sessions followed by 24 home-based walking sessions — was tested in 27 previously hospitalised long COVID patients (mean age 57, average 140 days post-discharge) with severe fatigue, compared to 15 usual care controls. Peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) increased by 2.4 mL/kg/min (15%) and peak work rate by 19 watts (20%) in the PR group, with no improvement in either measure in the usual care group; 6-minute walk distance also improved by 72 metres, exceeding the minimum clinically important difference. The study was non-randomised and underpowered relative to its own sample size calculation, which limits the strength of conclusions.

trial_rating.result_basis: VO2peak improved by 2.4 mL/kg/min in the PR group vs no change in usual care (p=0.001); peak work rate improved by 19 watts (p=0.001); 6MWT improved by 72 metres (p=0.001).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Most quantitative outcome data appears only in figures (Figures 5 and 6); per-arm means and SDs were only explicitly reported in the abstract for post-intervention values of MFIS physical subdomain, MFIS psychosocial subdomain, and EQ-VAS. Baseline per-arm means and SDs for outcome measures are NOT reported in text or tables — only in figures. ANOVA F-statistics and p-values for group x period interactions are reported in text for all outcomes. The p-values stated for MFIS physical (p<0.001) and psychosocial (p<0.001) in the abstract appear to refer to post-intervention between-group comparisons, not the ANOVA interaction (which shows p=0.187 and p=0.014 respectively); this inconsistency is noted. Body composition outcomes (weight, segmental fat, body water, segmental muscle) all showed non-significant results with no meaningful between-group differences; omitted from outcomes array due to data only in figures and no clinical relevance for fatigue meta-analysis. EQ-5D-5L individual dimension results (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) reported only as chi-square p-values with no per-arm counts or means; omitted from detailed extraction. The study enrolled only women, all vaccinated, recruited Feb-Apr 2022 from a patient association (AMACOP). Non-randomized design with pragmatic allocation based on scheduling availability.

summary: A 12-week supervised plank-based core stabilisation program (MORETA methodology, 2 sessions/week) was tested in 39 women with long COVID (mean symptom duration ~20 months) in a non-randomised pilot trial in Madrid. The primary outcomes were fatigue (Modified Fatigue Impact Scale, MFIS) and health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L and EQ-VAS): the intervention group improved physical fatigue domain scores by 39.1% vs 16.7% in controls, and EQ-VAS self-rated health by 19.6% vs 1.1% in controls, with a statistically significant group-by-time interaction for EQ-VAS (F=4.347, p=0.046) and psychosocial fatigue domain (p=0.014), though the total MFIS interaction was not significant; no post-exertional symptom exacerbation was reported. The non-randomised design with self-selected group allocation and small sample size (n=20 intervention, n=19 control) introduce substantial risk of selection bias, limiting causal inference.

trial_rating.result_basis: EQ-VAS group×time interaction F=4.347, p=0.046 (intervention +19.6% vs control +1.1%); psychosocial MFIS interaction p=0.014; total MFIS group×time interaction p=0.551 (non-significant).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a quasi-experimental before-after study, not an RCT; there is no randomization and the two groups (COVID-19 patients vs. healthy controls) are not randomized comparators but rather separate cohorts each serving as their own pre-post controls. Between-group effect sizes in this extraction reflect pre-vs-post within-arm differences (paired comparisons), not between-arm comparisons, as that is the primary analysis structure used. The study reports only acute effects from a single 20-minute scTS session assessed 15 minutes post-intervention; there is no extended follow-up. FVC % predicted values are reported per individual in Table 1 (mean 68±3% predicted). Blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, and VAS pain were monitored as safety measures but no numeric results were reported for these. Time since infection reported as 59±48 days (mean±SD); converted to months as 1.97±1.60 months. All spirometry data (PIF, PEF, tPIF, tPEF, FVC) are reported as mean±SD in text; no figures-only data were extracted.

summary: A single 20-minute session of transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (scTS) applied over the T5 and T10 thoracic spinal segments was tested in 10 adults with post-acute COVID-19 respiratory deficits (mean age 55, all with FVC around 68% predicted). Peak inspiratory flow increased from 94 to 134 L/min (p=0.040) and peak expiratory flow increased from 88 to 109 L/min (p=0.049) immediately after stimulation, with faster time-to-peak for both measures, indicating improved neuromuscular activation of respiratory muscles. Total lung capacity (FVC) was unchanged, suggesting the effect is neural rather than structural. The study is very small, unblinded, uncontrolled, and used a single session design with unmatched healthy controls, so results are exploratory only.

trial_rating.result_basis: PIF increased from 93.99 to 133.67 L/min (p=0.040) and PEF from 87.84 to 108.85 L/min (p=0.049) in n=10 patients with no control arm for the COVID group.

domains.support: Fixed-block randomization with SPSS is described, but allocation concealment method is not reported. Baseline characteristics appear well balanced across groups.

Single-blind design; participants were blinded but the treating researcher was not, as blinding investigators was deemed impossible in physical therapy. Sham TENS used low-frequency, low-amplitude current on abdomen rather than true inert control.

10-15% attrition across arms; 82 of 93 randomized patients completed treatment and 82 completed follow-up (with minor variation per arm). Reasons for dropout are reported but analysis population is not explicitly stated as ITT or per-protocol.
IIEF-15 is a validated patient-reported measure and patients were blinded. Hypoesthesia was assessed on a 10-point scale which is relatively subjective, acknowledged as a study limitation.

Trial is registered (ISRCTN47534508) but registration date (December 2024) appears concurrent with or after study start (first participant December 2024), raising concerns about prospective pre-registration. All stated endpoints appear reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. Per-arm endpoint means and SDs at post-treatment and follow-up timepoints are NOT reported in text or tables for most outcomes — the paper reports only percentage change from baseline within each arm plus between-group t-tests and Cohen's d. Absolute endpoint values are only available at baseline. 2. The overall baseline mean for orgasmic function (3.43±1.2), sexual desire (3.52±1.12), intercourse satisfaction (5.74±1.9), and overall satisfaction (2.99±0.90) are stated as grand means across groups, not per-arm breakdowns. 3. Figure data (post-treatment and follow-up absolute scores) appears only in bar graphs with no accompanying tables; result_source set to 'not_reported' for these cells. 4. Cohen's d values are reported for within-arm pre-post comparisons and between-arm comparisons but are not extractable as standardized between-group effect sizes in the conventional meta-analytic sense (they appear to be reported for within-group change). 5. The TENS arm comparison for orgasmic function gives t=3.75, p=0.0006, Cohen's d=1.25 (53.6% improvement vs control); LLLT gives t=4.32, p=0.0001, Cohen's d=1.44 (69.5% improvement). 6. The intercourse satisfaction and overall satisfaction baseline means are reported as grand means across groups, not per arm individually. 7. EMG exploratory outcome data extracted in study but not included as formal outcome objects due to small, non-comparable subgroup and inability to attribute to specific treatment arms in follow-up. 8. Post-treatment (3-month) follow-up percentage changes for orgasmic function: LLLT +5.05%, TENS +4.43%, LLLT+TENS +5.17% (noted as not statistically reliable).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested low-level laser therapy (LLLT), transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) of the pudendal nerve, and their combination against sham treatment in 82 men who developed erectile dysfunction within one month of COVID-19 infection and had symptoms lasting 6–12 months. On the IIEF-15 erectile function domain, LLLT improved scores by 38% and TENS by 27% compared to baseline, while the combination improved scores by 64% — outperforming LLLT alone by 20% (p=0.003). TENS was markedly more effective than LLLT at reducing genital hypoesthesia (49% vs 17% reduction), and the combination achieved a 61% reduction; all treatment gains were sustained at 3-month follow-up with no adverse effects reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Erectile function domain improved 38% with LLLT (p≤0.01, Cohen's d=0.85) and 27% with TENS (p≤0.01, Cohen's d=1.26); combined LLLT+TENS improved scores by 64% vs baseline and by 20% over LLLT alone (p=0.003, Cohen's d=1.05).

Primary comparisons are arm1 vs arm2 for long COVID-specific effects. Post2 data (follow-up ~1 week post-intervention) only available for G-Int arm. Table 4 CRT Post1 RT for G-Int reads 535±83 ms in the table; the abstract states RTpost2=521±86 ms; Post1 value extracted as 535±83 from table. Between-group effects for cognitive outcomes are not directly reported as formal between-group statistics; group-time interaction ANOVA stats are reported and noted in text but pairwise between-group values at post not provided; calculated mean differences from arm means. Outcomes omitted due to space constraints: Pattern Comparison CO trials RT (baseline G-Nor=975±121, G-Con=1371±467, G-Int=1277±393; Post1: G-Nor=949±145, G-Con=1353±388, G-Int=1198±331; Post2 G-Int=1128±281), Pattern Comparison accuracy CO and IN trials, Simon CO RT and accuracy, Simon IN accuracy, Pursuit Rotor mean deviation, Corsi longest sequence. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a four-week neuro-meditation program (Rebalance®, combining sound therapy, coach-guided meditation, and light stimulation) in 34 long COVID patients with confirmed cognitive and psychological impairment. The intervention group (n=17) completed ten 30-minute sessions and showed significantly faster reaction times on three cognitive tasks compared to the untreated control group: choice reaction time improved by 12.1% (593ms to 521ms, p<0.001), pattern comparison by 13.3% (1244ms to 1079ms, p<0.001), and Simon task by 8.4% (539ms to 494ms, p<0.01). Subjective measures also improved significantly, including large reductions in physical fatigue (-13 points), mental fatigue (-7.7 points), depression (-5.2 points), and anxiety (-3.6 points), all p<0.001; however, the study is small (17 per arm), lacked a placebo or active control, and the Rebalance® device is a commercial product of an institution connected to the authors.

trial_rating.result_basis: Choice reaction time: 593ms baseline vs 521ms post-intervention (p<0.001); physical fatigue reduced by 13.0 points vs -0.6 in controls (p<0.001); n=17 per arm.

summary: This single-blind randomized controlled trial tested twice-daily oral supplementation of 1.66 g L-arginine plus 500 mg liposomal vitamin C against placebo for 28 days in 46 adults (median age 51, 65% women) with long COVID and persistent fatigue. The primary outcome, 6-minute walk test distance, improved by a median of 30 m in the treatment group versus 0 m in the placebo group (mean difference 50 m, 95% CI 20–80 m, p=0.001), exceeding the 35 m minimal clinically important difference threshold. Secondary outcomes also favored the supplement: handgrip strength increased by 3.4 kg versus 1.0 kg (p=0.03), flow-mediated dilation reached 14.3% versus 9.4% (p=0.03), and fatigue persisted in only 9% of the treatment group versus 80% of the placebo group at day 28. The trial was small (23 per arm, single center) and single-blind rather than double-blind, limiting the strength of conclusions.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6-minute walk distance improved by median 30 m (treatment) vs 0 m (placebo), mean difference 50 m, 95% CI 20–80 m, p=0.001, exceeding the 35 m minimal clinically important difference.

summary: This randomised trial tested whether 1-methylnicotinamide (1-MNA), a niacin metabolite with anti-inflammatory and antithrombotic properties, could improve exercise tolerance and fatigue in 50 non-hospitalised adults with persistent post-COVID-19 symptoms. After one month of daily 58 mg 1-MNA supplementation, participants in the treatment group walked a mean of 42 m further in the 6-minute walk test compared to a 13 m improvement in the unsupplemented control group (p=0.0016), and 92% of treated patients improved versus 60% of controls. The proportion of patients with severe fatigue (FSS ≥4) was significantly lower in the 1-MNA group at follow-up (20% vs 56%, p=0.008); however, the study used alternating allocation rather than true randomisation, had no placebo control, and enrolled only 25 patients per arm over a single month.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT mean difference between groups: 42 m vs 13.28 m (absolute between-group difference 28.72 m, p=0.0016); severe fatigue rate 20% vs 56% (p=0.008).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study is NOT an RCT; it is an open-label two-cohort observational study where both cohorts (PCIBS n=16 and IBS-control n=28) received the same intervention (Curcuma + Boswellia + low-FODMAP diet). The 'arm_id=1' is the long COVID (PCIBS) group and 'arm_id=2' is the IBS-without-COVID control group. There is no placebo or untreated control arm. Between-group effect direction convention: control minus PCIBS (arm2 minus arm1) as reported in Table 2. The 'n_lost_to_followup' for PCIBS arm represents screened (28) minus completed (16)=12 excluded at screening; similarly control screened 35 minus completed 28=7 excluded at screening — these are screening exclusions, not post-enrollment dropouts. GAE data: PCIBS — grade 1: n=1 (6.3%), grade 2: n=2 (12.5%), grade 3: n=8 (50.0%), grade 4: n=5 (31.3%); Control — grade 1: n=0 (0%), grade 2: n=2 (7.1%), grade 3: n=9 (32.1%), grade 4: n=17 (60.7%). Grade ≥3 response: PCIBS 81.3%, Control 92.8%, p>0.05. Table 2 CI for abdominal pain in PCIBS: lower bound listed as '-5.593' and '-5.008' in the extracted table — based on the table structure, PCIBS delta change CI 95% is (-7.560; -5.008) and Control delta change CI 95% is (-7.511; -5.593). The between-group difference for pain CI is (-1.879; 1.373). Adverse events reported as 'No adverse effects related to the supplementation were reported during the study' — applies to all participants combined, not broken down per arm.

summary: This pilot study tested 30 days of supplementation with lecithin-based formulations of Curcuma longa (500 mg twice daily) and Boswellia serrata (150 mg twice daily), combined with a low-FODMAP diet, in 16 adults with post-COVID-19 irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-like symptoms 60–120 days after infection) compared to 28 adults with IBS who had no prior COVID-19 infection. Both groups showed statistically significant reductions in abdominal bloating (the primary outcome), but the effect was smaller in the post-COVID group (score change: −1.950) than in the IBS-only group (−2.850), with the between-group difference reaching significance (p=0.001). A key caveat is that gut dysbiosis, measured by urinary indican, improved significantly only in the IBS-only group (−36.2 units) and not in the post-COVID group (+7.9 units, i.e., no improvement), suggesting that post-COVID dysbiosis may require different treatment strategies; the study had no placebo arm, was open-label, and enrolled very small numbers.

trial_rating.result_basis: Abdominal bloating (primary outcome) decreased significantly within the post-COVID group (intra-group Δ −1.950, CI95% −2.238 to −1.662), but the between-cohort comparison showed the post-COVID group improved less than the IBS-only group (difference −0.899, CI95% −1.270 to −0.528, p=0.001); no placebo control was included.

summary: This pilot randomized controlled trial tested whether drinking hydrogen-rich water (HRW, 500 mL twice daily for 14 days) reduced fatigue and breathlessness in 32 long COVID patients with self-reported fatigue and dyspnea. The primary fatigue outcome (Fatigue Severity Scale) showed a significantly greater percent reduction in the HRW group compared to placebo (p=0.046, Cohen's d=0.696), and HRW also improved six-minute walk distance, chair stand test performance, and sleep quality. However, dyspnea scores (mMRC) did not improve significantly with HRW versus placebo (p=0.556), and no improvements in mood or anxiety were detected.

trial_rating.result_basis: FSS percent change was significantly greater in HRW vs placebo (p=0.046, 95% CI -20.607 to -0.198, d=0.696), but this was a secondary percent-change analysis; the primary mixed-effects model showed no significant group effect (p=0.122) or interaction (p=0.184), and the primary dyspnea outcome was null (p=0.556).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a pilot RCT with very small per-protocol sample sizes (n=8 probiotic, n=13 placebo after dropout). Most quantitative outcome data (means, SDs) are reported only in supplementary tables (S7-S20) which were not included in the provided paper text, or in figures only — therefore arm-level numeric values are not_reported for nearly all outcomes. Only p-values for between-group comparisons are available in the main text. The mild COVID group (n=10) served as an observational non-randomized comparator and is not an RCT arm; it was not included in arm_results. Outcomes omitted due to data only in supplementary tables or figures: SF-36 physical functioning, GIQLI physical function and symptoms, GIQLI medical treatment burden, mMRC dyspnea scale, recovery scale, serum lipoprotein components (HDL cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, Apo-A2, etc.), stool metabolites (DOPAC, fumaric acid, tyrosine, proline, deoxyuridine, cholic acid, malonic acid, L-DOPA), gut permeability markers (DAO, zonulin, LBP, sCD14), macrophage markers (sCD163, sMR), neutrophil chemotaxis parameters, full T-cell and B-cell subpopulation panels, multi-omics factor analysis scores. The dropout difference between arms (5/13 probiotic vs 0/13 placebo, p=0.039) is a major methodological concern. Butyric acid increase at 6 months noted as significant but exact p-value not stated in main text; data in Figure S14.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial tested a five-strain probiotic (OMNi-BiOTiC Pro-Vi 5, taken twice daily for six months) in 21 adults who had experienced severe COVID-19 roughly 10 months earlier, comparing them to 10 mild-disease controls. The probiotic significantly increased gut microbial richness at 3 months (p=0.047) and 6 months (p=0.014), reduced fatigue scores on the ARTIQ questionnaire at 3 months (p=0.014), improved psychological burden (p=0.022), increased stool butyrate at 6 months, and reduced neutrophil ROS production and CD4+ TEMRA cells at 3 months; however, increased intestinal permeability and the reorganization of Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae remained unaffected. The trial was small (8 probiotic completers vs 13 placebo) with a notable 38% dropout rate in the probiotic arm, making all findings preliminary and hypothesis-generating.

trial_rating.result_basis: Microbial richness improved in the probiotic group at 6 months (p=0.014); fatigue reduction at 3 months (p=0.014); these are secondary/exploratory endpoints and the trial was not powered for a single primary outcome, with only 8 completers in the probiotic arm.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This is a 4-arm trial stratified by COVID severity (severe vs moderate), with a healthy donor control group (n=25, arm_id 5) that was not included in randomized arms as it received no intervention. 2. All cytokine biomarker data (IL-6, IL-8, IL-17A, IFN-gamma), nitrate/nitrite ratio, antioxidant activity (AOA), PMN ATP levels, and phagocytosis index quantitative data appear ONLY in figures (Figure 1, Figure 2, and referenced additional figures) with no tabulated numeric values extractable from text — these outcomes were noted as significant but numeric means/SDs were not reported in text. Outcomes omitted due to data-only-in-figures: IL-6, IL-8, IL-17A, IFN-gamma plasma levels, plasma nitrate/nitrite ratio, antioxidant activity, PMN ATP content, phagocytosis index (%), intracellular bacterial killing (%). 3. The Borg scale is labeled 1-10 but Group 3 baseline values (10.8) exceed this range — likely the scale used differs or values represent a different metric (possibly a modified Borg or dyspnea visual analogue scale); values extracted as reported verbatim. 4. Table 2 had extensive merged/duplicate rows with the same values appearing for multiple answer score levels (e.g., '2-great' and '1-moderate' rows show identical means); only one set of values per question item was extracted. 5. ECG data reported as counts at two time points (30-40 days and 50-60 days post-discharge), corresponding to baseline and end-of-trial respectively. 6. No primary outcome was designated; paper lacks trial registration. 7. Oral-nasal-pharyngeal microbiota data not tabulated quantitatively. 8. A 5th group (healthy donors, n=25) served as a normative reference and was not randomized; excluded from arm-level extraction. 9. The Borg score for severe COVID groups is presented such that improvement = score increases (counterintuitive direction); values extracted verbatim. Higher Borg score in this paper's context may indicate improved exercise tolerance rather than worse dyspnea — this is ambiguous from text; higher_is_better set to false as Borg score conventionally measures dyspnea/exertion.

summary: This randomized placebo-controlled trial tested daily oral supplementation with 28g of fermented Carica papaya and Morinda citrifolia syrups (BioRex Papaya and BioRex Noni) added to standard rehabilitation care in 188 adults recovering from moderate or severe COVID-19 (primarily the delta variant). After 20 days, patients receiving the fermented fruit supplements showed significantly greater reductions in plasma IL-6 and IL-8 levels, normalization of elevated nitrite/nitrate levels, improved immune cell function (phagocytosis restored toward normal range in severe COVID survivors), and greater improvement in self-reported symptoms including weakness, physical and mental working capacity, heart pain, arrhythmia, and tachycardia compared to placebo. The study has notable limitations: it was single-center with no pre-registration, blinding adequacy is unclear, several co-authors have commercial ties to the tested products, and the placebo (diluted honey water) may not have been inert.

trial_rating.result_basis: Total average symptom score decreased from 1.2±0.2 to 0.5±0.1 in FFS group vs 0.9±0.1 in placebo (severe COVID, p<0.05); IL-6 normalized in FFS groups vs remained significantly elevated in placebo groups (p<0.01); oxygen desaturation during 6-minute walk test occurred in 53.3% of FFS patients vs 71.4% of placebo patients.

summary: This 12-week open-label randomized controlled trial tested vitamin D replacement therapy guidance (25 µg daily vitamin D3 supplement plus dietary counseling, sun exposure, and exercise) versus alfacalcidol (active vitamin D preparation) alone in 85 adults with ME/CFS developing after COVID-19 infection or vaccination who had vitamin D insufficiency or deficiency (serum 25(OH)D <30 ng/mL). The intervention group reduced their ME/CFS symptom count by a mean of 6.7 symptoms versus 1.2 in the control group (between-group difference -5.6; 95% CI: -7.2 to -3.9; p<0.001), and 16 of 42 intervention participants versus 1 of 38 controls no longer met ME/CFS diagnostic criteria at 12 weeks. Key caveats are the open-label design (no blinding), 83.5% of participants enrolled from a single clinic, and the use of a simple symptom count rather than validated quality-of-life measures as the primary endpoint.

trial_rating.result_basis: Mean symptom reduction -6.7 (intervention) vs -1.2 (control), between-group difference -5.6 (95% CI: -7.2, -3.9; p<0.001); 38% of intervention participants vs 3% of controls no longer met ME/CFS diagnostic criteria.

summary: This 24-week randomized controlled trial tested daily supplementation with 2000 IU vitamin D3 and 240 µg vitamin K2 (MK-7 form) against standard of care in 151 adults with established long COVID (at least 2 moderate symptoms persisting 3+ months after confirmed infection). The vitamin K2/D3 group showed a 7.1% decrease in the proportion meeting the RECOVER Long COVID Research Index threshold of ≥12, compared to a 7.2% increase in the standard-of-care group (p=0.01); in adjusted models, the LC Research Index was 3.2 points lower in the treatment arm (p=0.04), and the treatment group had nearly 2 fewer total symptoms (-1.7, 95% CI -3.2 to -0.1, p=0.02). The trial lacked a placebo control, which is a meaningful limitation, though vitamin D levels rose only in the treatment arm, supporting adherence; no adverse events were attributed to the intervention.

trial_rating.result_basis: LC Research Index 3.2 points lower in K2/D3 arm vs SOC in adjusted model (p=0.04); total symptom count -1.7 (95% CI -3.2, -0.1, p=0.02); proportion with index ≥12 decreased 7.1% vs increased 7.2% in SOC (p=0.01).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper is in Russian with English abstract and table. The table provides all primary numeric data with means and SDs (labeled Хср ± σ). No primary outcome is formally designated; all five outcomes extracted. Between-group p-values for mMRC, SpO2, and Adaptation Potential are reported as U=0 in the table (Mann-Whitney U=0 implies p very small but exact value not given beyond p<0.05); only FAS (p=0.0002) and Carlisle HR (p=0.0003) have explicit p-values for between-group comparison. Wilcoxon T=0 for most within-group comparisons indicates p<0.05; the Carlisle HR control group Wilcoxon T=2 with p=0.03. The intergroup comparison rows show absolute difference in post-intervention means and percent improvement ratio relative to control group change — these are not standard effect sizes. Between-group mean differences for mMRC, SpO2, and AP were calculated from post-intervention means. The study is described as a 'pedagogical experiment' with no mention of randomization; classified as quasi-experimental. Age range 45-59 years given for overall sample but per-arm age statistics not reported. No per-arm sex breakdown reported.

summary: This trial tested individually dosed hypoxi-hyperoxic therapy (IDHHT), alternating cycles of low-oxygen (FiO2 ~11-13%) and high-oxygen (FiO2 ~35-40%) breathing using the Oxyterra device, added to a standard physical therapy programme in 40 middle-aged adults (45-59 years) with confirmed post-COVID syndrome. After 3 weeks, the IDHHT group showed significantly greater improvements than the physical-therapy-only control group across all measured outcomes: fatigue (FAS score) fell by 41.5% vs 25.1%, oxygen saturation rose by 3.3% vs 1.4%, dyspnea (mMRC) improved by 55.3% vs 34.0%, and cardiovascular adaptation potential improved by 23.7% vs 13.8%. No adverse effects were reported in the IDHHT group.

trial_rating.result_basis: FAS fatigue score decreased by 11.99 points (41.5%) in the IDHHT group vs 7.15 points (25.1%) in controls; between-group difference 4.84 points, p=0.0002 (Mann-Whitney U test).

Most outcome data over time (severity scores for fatigue, headache, respiration problems, organoleptic disorders, hair loss, cough, pain, sweatiness, anxiety, depression, cognitive performance) are presented only in figures (Figures S1-S13 in Supplement 2) with no tabulated per-arm means and SDs at intermediate or final timepoints — only baseline values are in Table 1. Workout time data is similarly only in figures. The IL-6 end-of-study values (Day 21) for each arm were extracted from narrative text in the Discussion section (4.730±0.329 pg/mL for ADAPT-232 and 5.981±0.530 pg/mL for placebo), where ± appears to indicate SEM not SD. The workout (daily walk time) baseline values in Table 1 appear to use SEM not SD given the very small values (0.0628 and 0.0757). Note that baseline 'Physical activity (daily walk) min' values of 5.534 and 5.162 minutes appear unusually low and may represent log-transformed or differently scaled data. The p=0.0148 for workout interaction and p<0.0001 for between-group comparison are from figure captions only. Creatinine between-group p=0.0012 is from Figure 2 caption. Omitted from outcomes due to data only in figures: fatigue severity score over time, headache severity score, respiration severity score, organoleptic severity score, hair loss severity score, cough severity score, pain severity score, sweatiness severity score, HAM-A score change over time, HADS score change over time, d2 test change over time. summary: This randomized, quadruple-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested Chisan®/ADAPT-232 — an oral combination of Rhodiola, Eleutherococcus, and Schisandra extracts — in 100 adults with long COVID symptoms (mean age 49) who had been discharged from hospital, ICU, or isolation and had at least three persistent symptoms. The primary outcomes showed mixed results: ADAPT-232 reduced the duration of fatigue by one day and pain by two days in 50% of patients, with significantly fewer patients still experiencing pain on Day 9 (39% vs. 57%, p=0.0019) and fatigue on Day 11 (28% vs. 43%, p=0.0157), and it significantly increased daily workout time compared to placebo (p<0.0001); however, overall symptom severity scores did not significantly differ between groups for most measures. ADAPT-232 also significantly reduced blood creatinine compared to placebo (p=0.0012), suggesting a possible kidney-protective effect, though the study was small, funded by the manufacturer of the test product, and described by the authors as a pilot trial.

trial_rating.result_basis: Fewer patients had pain on Day 9 (39% ADAPT-232 vs. 57% placebo, p=0.0019) and fatigue on Day 11 (28% vs. 43%, p=0.0157); workout time difference p<0.0001; but overall symptom severity showed no significant between-group difference for most endpoints.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL LIMITATION: This paper reports all outcomes collapsed across both arms combined (overall pre vs. post), not disaggregated by experimental vs. control arm. Per-arm means, SDs, and Ns are NOT reported for any outcome. The arm_id fields for arm_results are set to null to reflect this. The between_group_effects p-values reported are for within-group (pre vs. post overall) paired tests, NOT between-arm comparisons; no experimental vs. control between-group statistics are reported anywhere in the paper. This severely limits the trial's usability for meta-analysis. Table 1 reports overall pre/post for 1-min STS (26.75±5.04 vs 28.75±5.6, p=0.002119), Fatigue NRS (2.72±1.33 vs 2.26±1.19, p=0.0223), and L-Test (19.18±5.08 vs 18.24±3.64, p=0.006627). Table 2 reports overall pre/post hand grip strength for right (14.27±4.39 vs 14.35±4.75, within p=0.8722) and left (14.05±4.58 vs 14.0±4.45, within p=0.8965) with changes of 0.08±2.7 and 0.06±2.37 respectively (between-hand change comparison p=0.9717). Some data appear only in figures (Figures 1-4) with no additional numerical values beyond those in tables. The conclusion text contains an apparent error: it states 'subjects took less time in pretest compared to post test' for the STS, but the data show higher count post-test (improvement), suggesting a narrative error. summary: A one-week structured physiotherapy program — including seated and standing limb exercises plus breathing exercises — was tested against general mobility exercises in 30 post-COVID-19 patients (non-ICU, mild-to-moderate disease, post-quarantine) at a hospital in Dharwad, India. The main group (n=46) received acupuncture combined with therapeutic exercise incorporating yoga elements and small-group psychotherapy; comparator groups received massage plus physiotherapy, acupuncture alone, or home exercise only. The combined acupuncture-plus-exercise group showed the largest improvements across all outcomes: the six-minute walk test distance increased by 18% (from ~364m to ~430m), dyspnoea on the Borg scale fell by 53%, depression severity on the HADS fell by 66.7%, and quality-of-life scores (EQ-5D) rose from ~57 to ~87 points (+53%), all significantly better than comparator groups (p<0.05). The study had no blinding, no placebo control, and outcomes were self-reported, which limits confidence in the findings.

summary: This pilot study tested two bacteriophage cocktails — one oral and one inhaled — in 30 post-COVID patients who had persistent gut dysbiosis and lung involvement at least 3 months after hospital discharge. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested the addition of audiovisual stimulation (binaural brainwave entrainment shifting from beta to theta activity over 22-minute sessions) and cognitive behavioral therapy (5 sessions of 40 minutes each) to standard rehabilitation in 59 long COVID patients with emotional disturbances 1–6 months post-infection, mean age ~60 years. In the intervention group (n=29), anxiety and depression scores on the HADS improved significantly compared to the control group receiving standard rehabilitation alone, with 93.1% of treated patients showing no signs of anxiety or depression after treatment versus 64% in controls; situational anxiety on the Spielberger-Khanin scale dropped from a median of 46 to 42 points (p<0.001), and high-level situational anxiety was eliminated in all 21 patients who had it at baseline (p<0.001 between groups). The main caveat is that three of the five authors hold a patent on the intervention, and the lead editor of the publishing journal is also a study author, raising conflict-of-interest concerns.

trial_rating.result_basis: Situational anxiety median fell from 46 to 42 in the intervention group vs unchanged (45.5 to 45.5) in controls (p<0.001 between groups); 93.1% of intervention patients had no anxiety/depression post-treatment vs 64% in controls (p<0.05).

summary: This single-blind randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week calisthenics exercise program (jumping jacks, burpees, squats, planks, and related movements) in 176 adults with post-COVID syndrome, comparing therapist-supervised sessions against a home-based program. Both groups showed statistically significant improvements across all five EQ-5D-3L quality-of-life dimensions and the general health score, with the home exercise group's health score rising from 58.5 to 75.8 and the supervised group's from 58.0 to 68.6. No significant difference was found between the two delivery formats, suggesting that a well-instructed home program is as effective as supervised exercise for improving quality of life in this population.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested acupuncture added to a standard multi-modal rehabilitation program versus rehabilitation alone in 160 post-COVID-19 patients (average age 61, 76% women) hospitalized at a rehabilitation center in Kazakhstan. Patients receiving acupuncture plus rehabilitation showed statistically significant improvements across all four outcome measures — dyspnea (MDS improved 40%), exercise tolerance (6-minute walk test improved 29.5%), perceived exertion (Borg scale improved 35%), and daily function (Barthel index improved 2.2%) — while the rehabilitation-only group showed significant improvement only on the dyspnea and Borg scales. A key caveat is that the two groups were not well-matched at baseline (the acupuncture group had more comorbidities including higher rates of hypertension and motor system disease), there was no blinding, and the combination design makes it impossible to isolate acupuncture's specific contribution.

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested a rehabilitation programme combining robotic mechanotherapy with biofeedback (Con-Trex lower-limb trainer), interactive balance therapy (Stabilan 01-2), and virtual reality training (Nirvana system) against a standard rehabilitation programme (therapeutic gymnastics, low-intensity laser, speleotherapy, chest massage) in 120 adults aged 40-70 with post-COVID syndrome assessed 1-6 months after infection. The experimental group showed significantly greater gains in cardiorespiratory fitness: maximum work performed increased by 12.9% versus 3.0% in controls (post-rehabilitation difference 25.3% higher, p=0.006), oxygen consumption at the first ventilatory threshold rose 6.3% versus 5.0% (p=0.016 between groups), and diastolic blood pressure at peak exercise fell by a mean of 7 mmHg (p=0.003). Dyspnoea severity also improved more in the experimental group: the proportion with moderate-to-severe dyspnoea fell from 78.3% to 13.3%, and 86% had mild or no dyspnoea after treatment, compared with 58.3% in the control group. No safety concerns were reported, but notable conflicts of interest exist: four authors hold a patent on the intervention tested.

trial_rating.result_basis: Maximum work performed increased 12.9% in the intervention group vs 3.0% in controls, with post-rehabilitation values 25.3% higher in the intervention group (p=0.006); diastolic BP at peak load fell by 7 mmHg (p=0.003); proportion with mild or no dyspnoea reached 86% vs 58.3% in controls (p<0.001 for mild dyspnoea category).

summary: This randomized trial tested whether adding personalized normobaric interval hypoxic-hyperoxic therapy (NBIHHT) — alternating breathing of low-oxygen (10–15% O2) and high-oxygen (up to 40% O2) gas mixtures, individually dosed via real-time pulse oximetry feedback — to a standard rehabilitation program improved outcomes in 120 adults (mean age 62) with persistent symptoms more than 12 weeks after moderate COVID-19 pneumonia. Patients in the NBIHHT group (n=60) showed significantly greater improvements than the standard rehabilitation group (n=60) across all primary outcomes: six-minute walk distance increased by 19.9% vs 12.0%, vital lung capacity by 12.8% vs 8.1%, breath-hold time on inspiration by 51.2% vs 24.1%, resting heart rate fell by 13.3% vs 7.3%, and anxiety and depression scores dropped by ~64% and ~61% vs ~52% and ~43% respectively (all p<0.001). Quality-of-life gains were sustained at 3 months in the NBIHHT group and stable at 6 months, whereas the control group showed a declining trend by 6 months; no safety concerns were reported, though the trial lacked a sham-control arm and did not pre-register.

trial_rating.result_basis: Six-minute walk test improved by 19.87% in the NBIHHT group vs 12.01% in controls (p=0.000 within group; between-group p=0.051 at endpoint), with breath-hold time improving 51.15% vs 24.14% (p=0.000 and p=0.006 respectively).

summary: This study tested 16-18 days of mountain spa rehabilitation with or without ubiquinol (reduced coenzyme Q10, 200 mg/day) in 36 non-vaccinated post-COVID-19 patients (3-6 months after hospitalization) at a high-altitude sanatorium in Slovakia. summary: The EXER-COVID trial tested a 6-week supervised muscle power resistance training program (two sessions per week, 50–70% of daily 1RM, performed at maximum speed) in 100 adults with long COVID (mean age 48, 68% women) in a randomized crossover design conducted in Spain. The primary outcome, peak VO2, improved by 2.10 mL/kg/min (95% CI 1.25–2.94, p<0.001) compared to usual care. The program also increased upper and lower body strength, reduced psychological distress, improved quality of life and cognitive performance, and reduced 7 of 22 long COVID symptoms including dyspnea (RR=0.56, 95% CI 0.39–0.82) and weakness (RR=0.75, 95% CI 0.59–0.95), with no notable safety signals reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Peak VO2 improved by 2.10 mL/kg/min (95% CI 1.25 to 2.94, p<0.001) in the exercise vs. usual care condition; per-protocol analysis showed 2.40 mL/kg/min (95% CI 1.56 to 3.25, p<0.001).

summary: This pilot trial tested 4 g/day of creatine monohydrate plus breathing exercises (2-3 times daily for 10-15 minutes) versus breathing exercises alone in 8 long-COVID patients with moderate fatigue lasting at least 3 months. trial_rating.result_basis: Time to exhaustion improved by 54 s in the creatine group (p=0.05, 95% CI -201 to 309 s); post-exertional malaise group difference p=0.03; n=4 per arm.

summary: This randomised-design study tested whether adding balloon blowing exercise (30 min/day) to diaphragmatic breathing (10 min/day) for 8 weeks improved lung function, exercise tolerance, and quality of life in 30 post-COVID-19 survivors aged 25–50, compared to diaphragmatic breathing alone. The trial is severely limited by its small sample (n=15 per arm), convenient sampling, non-blinded design, single centre, and lack of pre-registration.

summary: This pilot RCT tested individualized homeopathic treatment versus placebo in 77 adults with long COVID (mean symptom duration ~9 months, 80% female) over 12 weeks via telemedicine. The primary outcomes — Fatigue Assessment Scale (FAS), and the physical and mental composite scores of the SF-36 — showed no significant difference between the homeopathy and placebo groups at any time point (4, 8, or 12 weeks). Repeated-measures ANOVA found a statistically significant interaction favoring placebo over verum for fatigue (FAS: F(3,210)=3.3, p=0.021) and physical health (PCS: F(3,210)=3.28, p=0.022), meaning the placebo group improved earlier; both groups improved overall, likely reflecting natural recovery. The verum group reported nearly twice as many transient symptom worsening events (19 vs. 10), which the authors attribute to a homeopathic aggravation effect.

trial_rating.result_basis: No significant between-group difference at any time point for FAS, PCS, or MCS; the only significant ANOVA interaction (FAS p=0.021, PCS p=0.022) favored placebo over verum.

summary: A 6-week, 18-session outpatient cardiopulmonary rehabilitation programme (combining aerobic training, resistance training, and respiratory exercises) was tested against a sedentary control in 30 Tunisian long COVID patients with persistent dyspnoea (mMRC ≥2) at least three months post-diagnosis. The primary outcome, 6-minute walk distance, improved by 168 m in the rehabilitation group versus 5 m in controls — a difference that far exceeded the 30 m minimal clinically important difference. Dyspnoea also improved meaningfully (mMRC decreased by 1.5 points vs. 0.1 in controls, exceeding the 1-point MCID threshold), though spirometric measures did not differ between groups.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWD increased by 168 ± 99 m in the intervention group vs. 5 ± 45 m in controls (p=0.001 for group-session interaction), exceeding the 30 m MCID; effect size was small by partial eta-squared.

summary: This prospective study tested nintedanib (a tyrosine kinase inhibitor used in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis) added to standard treatment versus standard treatment alone in 50 adults who developed CT-confirmed lung fibrosis after recovering from COVID-19. summary: A 3-month hybrid integrated care program combining 8 outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation sessions with 24 home-based ICT-supported sessions was tested in 27 long COVID patients with significant fatigue (mean FACIT score 26), compared to 15 patients receiving usual care. summary: This study tested osteopathic manual treatment (sessions every two weeks for 10–12 weeks) in 20 adults with post-COVID fatigue and autonomic symptoms (astheno-neurotic syndrome), compared against 20 untreated controls. The primary outcome was severity of asthenia on the Scale of Asthenic State (SAS): the treated group improved by 4.7 points versus 0.8 points in the control group. Treated patients also showed normalization of autonomic balance (Kerdo index moving from −3.29 to −0.35) and improvements in mental health and general health on the SF-36. The trial was small, unblinded, and conducted at two Russian osteopathic medicine institutes with a non-treatment (rather than sham) control group, introducing high risk of placebo and expectation bias.

trial_rating.result_basis: SAS asthenia score decreased by 4.7 points in the treated group (p=4.16E-17) versus 0.8 points in the control group (p=1.30E-3); no between-group statistical comparison reported, and the absolute difference of ~4 points on a scale of 30–120 is modest.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week circuit training program combining aerobic, strength, and breathing exercises (50 minutes, three times per week, at 65-75% maximum heart rate) in 60 Indonesian women with post-COVID-19 syndrome. The exercise group showed significantly greater improvements than controls in FEV1 (forced expiratory volume; interaction p=0.010, effect size d=-0.66), FEV1/FVC ratio (interaction p=0.006), peak expiratory flow (interaction p=0.009, effect size d=-0.67), and oxygen saturation (interaction p=0.041), while FVC and maximum voluntary ventilation improved in both groups equally. The FEV1/FVC ratio actually declined in the control group over the 8 weeks, underscoring the value of the exercise program, though the study was limited to women only and lacked long-term follow-up beyond the intervention period.

summary: This systems immunology study analyzed immune profiles of 152 adults with long COVID (symptoms persisting more than 90 days, average duration over 16 months) who participated in the STOP-PASC randomized controlled trial of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) versus placebo. The antiviral treatment produced transient changes in plasma proteins related to monocyte, complement, and lysosomal pathways at day 15, but these normalized by week 10 and the drug did not improve patient-reported outcomes or change the Long COVID immune signature score. A cross-cohort meta-analysis of nine independent datasets identified a conserved 60-protein Long COVID signature reflecting persistent activation across neutrophil, monocyte, and T/NK cell compartments (AUROC 0.783 in discovery, 0.759 in validation), which may serve as a future biomarker endpoint for clinical trials.

trial_rating.result_basis: The Long COVID Signature score showed no significant treatment-associated change between NMV/r and PBO/r arms at day 15 (p=0.1208) or week 10 (p=0.969), consistent with the primary trial finding of no therapeutic benefit.
