summary: This randomized controlled trial compared physiotherapist-supervised synchronous telerehabilitation (STR) against unsupervised asynchronous telerehabilitation (ATR) in 31 Brazilian adults with post-COVID syndrome, using an 8-week progressive exercise program including aerobic, strengthening, and breathing exercises. The primary outcome—lower limb functional strength measured by the Five Times Sit-to-Stand Test—improved significantly within the STR group (from 11.02s to 9.63s at 8 weeks, p=0.03) and showed a statistically significant between-group difference (p=0.027, Cohen's d=0.52), though post-hoc testing did not confirm this between-group difference. STR also produced significant within-group improvements in dyspnea, fatigue, stress, and quality of life, while ATR improved only fatigue and anxiety; notably, dropout was substantially higher in the ATR group (13 of 21 lost by 20-week follow-up vs. 8 of 23 in STR), limiting the reliability of comparisons.

trial_rating.result_basis: Between-group difference in FTSTS was p=0.027 (Cohen's d=0.52), but post-hoc testing did not confirm this difference; within-group improvement in STR was from 11.02s to 9.63s (p=0.029, 95% CI 0.10–2.40).

summary: This randomized trial tested daily home-based transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS), delivered via a standard TENS device clipped to the left ear tragus, in 114 adults with post-COVID fatigue. Among the 24 participants in the active treatment arm who met minimum adherence (at least 1 hour/day on at least 50% of days), fatigue measured on a Visual Analogue Scale improved by 11.9 points (±17.8) after 8 weeks, compared to non-significant reductions of 8.0 points in both the sham and placebo groups; the active group also showed significant improvement across all domains of the Fatigue Impact Scale and in an objective measure of peripheral muscle fatigue. A major caveat is that this is a per-protocol subgroup analysis of adherent participants only — one-third of the 114 enrolled did not meet minimum usage — and the main between-group intention-to-treat analysis is reported separately; the experimenter was also not blinded after randomization.

trial_rating.result_basis: VAS fatigue score improved by 11.9 ± 17.8 points in the active nVNS group (p=0.003, Cohen's d=0.939, N=24), versus non-significant reductions in sham (p=0.018) and placebo (p=0.141) groups; this is a per-protocol subgroup analysis, not the pre-specified primary analysis.

summary: This double-blind randomized controlled pilot trial tested 2,100 mg/day of omega-3 fatty acids (EPA+DHA) versus a soybean oil placebo for 12 weeks in 18 healthcare workers with long COVID symptoms including shortness of breath, cough, fatigue, and loss of taste and smell. summary: This randomized trial compared 15 sessions of continuous aerobic training (CT) at 40% peak workload versus low-intensity interval training (LIIT, alternating 3-minute loaded and 1-minute unloaded intervals at 40% peak workload) in 63 COVID-19 survivors with residual symptoms including dyspnea, fatigue, and reduced walking distance. Both groups improved significantly in six-minute walk test (6MWT) distance, exercise capacity, hand grip strength, dyspnea scores, anxiety, depression, and quality of life. The LIIT group showed greater improvements than CT in three key measures: 6MWT distance increased by 123m versus 56m (p=0.010), resting heart rate fell by 10 bpm versus 2 bpm (p=0.026), and dyspnea grade (mMRC) improved by a median of 2 versus 1 point (p=0.032); however, the LIIT group had more severely ill patients at baseline, which limits direct comparison.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT distance increased by 123m in LIIT vs 55.6m in CT (p=0.010); within-group improvements were significant in both arms (LIIT: 254m to 377m, p<0.001; CT: 371m to 427m, p=0.001).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. The paper does not report baseline (pre-MBSR) outcome scores — all reported values are from 6-month and 12-month post-MBSR timepoints. No baseline means/SDs available for BPI-SF, HADS, or ISI. Weeks_from_randomization for the two timepoints are estimated as ~32 weeks (8 weeks treatment + ~6 months follow-up) and ~58 weeks (8 weeks treatment + ~12 months follow-up). 2. HADS anxiety and depression mean scores are reported in text/Figure 3 but SDs are not provided for these continuous scores. ISI continuous means (9, 13.6 at 6 months; 9.1, 11.1 at 12 months) are also reported without SDs. T-statistics are given for HADS-A (t=-3.636, t=-5.167) and HADS-D (t=-2.823, t=-2.458) and ISI (t=-8.801, t=-3.569) but not CIs. 3. The insomnia categorical outcome (absence of insomnia 53.2% vs 30.4%) was reported with chi-square statistic (x=4.944, p=.026) — this appears to be the chi-square value not the ISI mean score as stated in the abstract. 4. The abstract states insomnia score '53.2 vs 30.4' which matches the categorical percentages in Table 2 (not ISI continuous scores), suggesting the abstract conflated percentage data with score data. 5. Control group n at 12 months is 43 per Table 2 (not 46), consistent with 3 additional dropouts noted in limitations. 6. Baseline demographic table shows n=93 for analyzed population but randomization was 105 total (52 IG + 53 CG). The 12 missing patients (5 IG + 7 CG) are the dropouts. 7. The paper uses 'psychoeducation' as the label for the MBSR intervention in the abstract methods section but the intervention is clearly MBSR throughout.

summary: This Italian RCT tested an 8-week Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) program (2 hours per week in small groups) added to usual drug therapy versus usual care alone in 105 COVID-19 survivors who had been admitted to intensive care and developed new-onset chronic pain, anxiety, depression, or insomnia. The primary outcome was chronic pain assessed by the Brief Pain Inventory; the MBSR group showed statistically significant reductions in 'least pain in the last 24 hours' at 6 months (0.91 vs 1.43, p=0.035) and 12 months (2.20 vs 2.83, p=0.012), alongside significant improvements in anxiety (HADS score 11.28 vs 13.15, p<0.001), depression (9.95 vs 11.23, p=0.007), and insomnia at 6 months (53.2% vs 30.4% absence of insomnia, p=0.026). The authors themselves noted that the pain reductions, while statistically significant, appeared clinically small, and the study was single-centre with a sample size below its original target of 125.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (least pain in last 24h) improved by 0.52 points at 6 months (0.91 vs 1.43, p=0.035) and 0.63 points at 12 months (2.20 vs 2.83, p=0.012); authors themselves characterised these reductions as statistically but not clinically significant.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Binary logistic regression showed high baseline CRP positively associated with O3-MAH response. subgroup_analyses.results_summary: LCTM identified two groups. Improving group had shorter time since infection (373 vs 555 days, ASD=0.78), higher 1-min sit-to-stand (26.9 vs 19.5, ASD=0.58). No difference in NMV/r proportion (64.7% vs 66.2%). Severe group had more cardiovascular symptoms as most bothersome (16.2% vs 0%) and more low-dose naltrexone use (20% vs 5.9%, ASD=0.43).

Worsening group had higher proportion of NMV/r (81.8% vs 63.8%, ASD=0.41), lower proportion female (31.8% vs 63.8%, ASD=0.68), longer time since infection (625 vs 517 days, ASD=0.39). No clear benefit of NMV/r in either group.

Four groups identified. Severe group had lower 1-min sit-to-stand (10.6), more cardiovascular symptoms as most bothersome (27.3%), more low-dose naltrexone use (45.5%, ASD=0.649). Improving group had shorter time since infection (374 days). NMV/r proportion similar across severe (63.6%), moderate (69.4%), and improving (66.7%) groups but lower in normal/mild (38.5%).

Three groups identified. Severe group had higher proportion of NMV/r (90% vs 64.5% moderate vs 53.1% improving, ASD=0.590) and higher proportion female (70% vs 63.2% vs 46.9%, ASD=0.32). Time since infection similar across groups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a secondary/exploratory analysis of the STOP-PASC RCT (primary publication: Geng et al., JAMA Intern Med 2024). Quantitative outcome data (per-arm means, SDs, effect sizes) are NOT reported in this paper — it focuses on latent class trajectory modeling (LCTM) and characterization of trajectory subgroups. No per-arm numeric results for primary or secondary outcomes are available in this paper; all arm_results arrays are empty. Between-group treatment effects are stated as null/no significant difference but no numeric values are given. Baseline demographics per treatment arm are stated to be 'previously reported' in the primary publication and are not reproduced here (only trajectory-group-level demographics in Tables 1-2). The overall sample mean time from index infection to baseline was 536 days (SD=275 days). Trajectory group characteristics reported in Tables 1 and 2 are descriptive of LCTM-defined subgroups, not treatment arms. Key trajectory-group statistics extracted: PGIS improving group mean days from infection=372.82 (SD=177.55), n=17; PGIS severe group mean days from infection=554.66 (SD=280.20), n=136; PGIS improving group 1-min sit-to-stand mean=26.88 (SD=15.16); PGIS severe group=19.54 (SD=9.35). PGIC improving group: n=130, 63.8% female, 63.8% NMV/r, mean days from infection=516.96 (SD=272.82); PGIC worsening group: n=22, 31.8% female, 81.8% NMV/r, mean days from infection=625.00 (SD=284.66). Outcome data only in figures (heatmaps and alluvial plots) — no numeric values extractable. Supplementary tables referenced but not provided in the paper text.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a secondary analysis of heterogeneous treatment effects from a primary RCT (McNarry et al. 2022, Eur Respir J). Per-arm means and SDs for individual outcomes at baseline and follow-up are NOT reported in this paper — only between-group mean differences with 95% CrI (Bayesian credible intervals, not frequentist CIs) and SD differences are provided. The CrI values have been placed in ci_95_low/ci_95_high fields as the closest equivalent, though they are 95% credible intervals not confidence intervals. The SMIP between-group mean difference upper bound (42.7) appears to be a typographical error in the paper (Table 3 states '141.2 (68.0 to 42.7)'); the lower bound 68.0 is clearly correct and 42.7 is likely a formatting error — the true upper CI is not determinable from the text. Outcome data for MIP and SMIP appears primarily in figures (Figure 3) with distribution shapes shown but no tabular per-arm means/SDs. The primary RCT data (McNarry et al. 2022) would need to be consulted for per-arm baseline and endpoint values. Proportion of response estimates extracted: MIP 0.84 (95% CrI 0.63-1.0), SMIP 0.95 (95% CrI 0.76-1.0). Table 4 dose-response beta coefficients extracted in subgroup_analyses section. BDI baseline values: IMT group 5.8 (SD 2.5), Control group 5.4 (SD 2.9) — these are baseline dyspnea index scores, not outcome change scores.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a quasi-experimental two-arm study without randomization; both arms receive active intervention differing only in number of sessions (16 vs 24). There is no control/comparator arm receiving no treatment or usual care. Mid-term timepoint differs between arms: Group 1 mid-term is at week 4 (after 8th session), Group 2 mid-term is at week 6 (after 12th session), so mid-term weeks_from_randomization is approximate. End-of-intervention is week 8 for Group 1 and week 12 for Group 2; a single timepoint_id=3 was used for both but the absolute calendar time differs. The main statistical results are within-group time effects (mixed ANOVA), not between-group comparisons: SDSD F(2,32)=3.674, p=0.037, partial eta2=0.187; SDNN F(2,32)=4.237, p=0.023, partial eta2=0.209; RMSSD F(2,32)=4.303, p=0.022, partial eta2=0.212; pNN50 F(2,32)=3.019, p=0.063, partial eta2=0.159 (marginal). Pairwise mean differences (pooled across groups, baseline to mid-term): SDSD MD=0.059ms p=0.033; SDNN MD=0.066ms p=0.037; RMSSD MD=0.079ms p=0.044. No between-group interaction effects were significant for any measure. Frequency-domain measures showed no significant time or interaction effects. Between_group_effects entries for time-domain outcomes reflect group-x-time interaction p>0.05 (not significant). The study notes that mid-term for Group 1 is the 8th session and for Group 2 is the 12th session — these are not exactly equivalent time points.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IMPORTANT: This paper is a systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 RCTs, NOT a primary RCT. All between-group effects are pooled meta-analytic estimates (random-effects models), not single-trial results. Per-arm means and SDs were extracted from forest plot tables embedded in the text (Figures 3 and 5) for individual studies where legible; several individual-study SD values were partially obscured or garbled in the forest plot text rendering (particularly Almazan 2022 and Elyazed 2024 fatigue arm SDs). The Li 2021 6MWD values (mean 80.2 and 17.09) likely represent change-from-baseline rather than endpoint values given their low magnitude; this is flagged but extracted as reported. The total duration and treatment duration across studies ranged from 4-12 weeks but are not uniform. Heterogeneity was substantial for most outcomes (I2=68-96%). The meta-analysis included 5 studies for 6MWD and MIP, 4 studies for dyspnea and fatigue, and 5 studies for HRQoL. Fatigue forest plot n_analyzed sums (96/97 total) suggest 4 studies contributed. The dyspnea forest plot per-arm data were mentioned as in Figure 4 but the data table was not fully readable in the provided text. Quality of life forest plot (Figure 6) data were referenced but the table was not readable. MIP forest plot (Figure 7) data were also not fully readable. Only outcomes with extractable per-arm data from forest plot tables were populated with means/SDs.

CRITICAL DATA LIMITATION: Table 2 reports pooled totals across BOTH arms combined (not per-arm), making it impossible to extract per-arm means or SDs. The table columns are labeled 'Total Pre-test' and 'Total Post-test' representing combined group means (n=35). No per-arm disaggregated data are reported anywhere in the paper. Table 3 reports p-values for between-subjects effects and within-subjects contrasts but without means, SDs, or effect sizes per arm. The FEV1/FVC ratio values (288.69 to 147.86) are anomalous — normal FEV1/FVC is ~0.7-0.8 or 70-80%; these values may represent a different metric or reporting error. outcomes.name: Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy Item GP5

domains.support: Centralized randomization using Stata with stratified block randomization across 8 strata; electronic data capture system with coded lot numbers; permissions configured to prevent unintentional unmasking.

Double-blind design with participants, clinicians, and study team masked; ritonavir added to placebo to mimic taste effects; however, notable difference in dysgeusia rates (48% vs 6%) suggests some unmasking may have occurred.
10% missing data on primary outcome; multiple imputation using fully conditional specification applied; sensitivity analyses in mITT and per-protocol populations consistent with primary ITT analysis.
Validated PROMIS-29 instrument used; self-reported outcomes via electronic diaries; no assessor blinding concern as outcomes are patient-reported.
Trial pre-registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05668091); statistical analysis plan published in appendix; primary and secondary endpoints clearly pre-specified.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: No differences in changes from baseline in PROMIS PHSS or MHSS between treatment groups across age subgroups; analysis was descriptive without statistical testing.
No differences in changes from baseline across sex subgroups; analysis was descriptive without statistical testing.
No differences in changes from baseline across race subgroups; analysis was descriptive without statistical testing.
No differences in changes from baseline across vaccination status subgroups; analysis was descriptive without statistical testing.
No differences in changes from baseline across US census region subgroups; analysis was descriptive without statistical testing.

sensitivity_analyses.description: Modified ITT analysis (participants adhering to >=80% of prescribed intervention, analyzed by assigned treatment)
Per-protocol analysis (participants completing trial without major protocol deviations, analyzed by treatment received)

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. Per-arm data at day 15 and week 6 for primary outcome (PROMIS-29 PHSS) reported as 'can be found in figure 2 and the appendix' — specific numeric values not provided in the main text, so only baseline and day 28 values extracted. 2. Between-group effect sizes for most secondary endpoints (MHSS, PROPr, cognitive function, GSQ-30, COVID Core Outcome Measures, EQ-5D-5L, EQ-VAS, Patient Global Impression scales) stated as not statistically significant but exact effect values, CIs, and p-values are in tables (table 2 and table 3) that were not included in the paper text provided — only narrative summaries available. 3. Baseline per-arm demographics (age, sex, BMI, time since infection) not broken down per arm in text — only overall mean age and overall percent female reported. 4. Safety population n=46 (arm 1) and n=49 (arm 2); n_any_ae cannot be directly extracted as the paper states 79 of 95 total participants had AEs but does not break this down per arm. 5. FACIT GP5 higher scores likely indicate worse tolerability/side effects in context (medication-related symptoms); scoring direction noted as uncertain. 6. Omitted from outcomes due to insufficient quantitative data in text: Patient Global Impression of Severity, Patient Global Impression of Change, additional long COVID symptom questions (26 items), individual PROMIS-29 domain scores.
